What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season.
  • One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.
  • With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis).

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

In a recent development, for Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

In a recent development, he is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

In a recent development, “I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the major mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

“Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

In a recent development, “I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

According to recent reports, “I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”.

Sources indicate that “Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s important is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

Industry observers note that “If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”.

According to recent reports, the founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

“Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”.

“Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

“In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a upcoming position gradually.”.

“This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the big training blocks start.”.

Industry observers note that head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’.

It has been revealed that “I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

Recent findings suggest that “For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”.

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the upcoming technique as you can sustain, and no more.

“You can’t ingrain a upcoming technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”.

A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

It has been revealed that “You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

“For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”.

“A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”.

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

“A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”.

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most key session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”.

It has been revealed that (h/t to Leo, our awesome illustrator who makes these images for us from scratch! 🙌 ) ​ Meet Major Overload.

Do this. Never do that. Fasted cardio. Never fasted cardio. Carbs are fine. Carbs are the enemy.

The Major loves it when you have 100 tabs open on your browser, but haven’t done a workout yet.

He wants to keep you plugged in to The Matrix. He feeds off of you staying stuck in planning mode while he drains your batteries.

My client Eric ran into him a few months ago.

Recent findings suggest that he’d spent weeks searching for “best at-home workouts to lose fat”. ​ In his words:.

It’s the way I felt when I tasked myself with running Nerd Fitness’s Instagram.

A million different opinions on how to do it. Hours spent researching. And weeks later, I still hadn’t filmed an actual video yet. 😅.

I was firmly stuck in analysis paralysis.

In a recent development, same boss battle as Eric. Different rabbit hole.

What got me unstuck was the same thing that helped Eric.

It wasn’t finding the “perfect” strategy or blueprint.

1) Follow one plan and block out everything else for now.​ ​ ​2) Commit to taking some small action, most days of the week.

The first one turned Major Overload’s volume down.

I didn’t need every voice. I needed a simple starting point. One that didn’t have a gajillion hoops to jump through.

The second one is where the learning actually happened.

In a recent development, I didn’t have to be perfect. I had to commit to imperfect reps.

I’ve learned more from a couple of weeks of posting than from all the agonizing I did beforehand.

Here’s what I told Eric, and what I’d tell you, too:.

Unless you’re Doctor Strange, scrubbing through 14 million possible futures to find the one where everything works out, you can’t know what perfect looks like. Neither can I. Nor anyone on the internet, no matter how loud they get.

Luckily, you don’t need a perfect proposal.

In a recent development, enough structure to get out there and do the thing. Not so convoluted that you never get started.

That’s why we built the Beginner Bodyweight Workout and our Strength Training Templates.

So you stop getting stuck at the starting line, and start putting in the reps.

Moving from planning to action does two things at once.

It breaks the inertia, and it teaches you what fits in YOUR life.

And that’s where the real magic happens.

It’s where you learn that, actually, training later in the evening works better for you than trying to force yourself up at 5AM.

It’s how you discover that splitting your workout up into two 15-minute chunks works better for your schedule.

Or that you prefer training with weights to training with bands.

You won’t know those things until you get out there and try.

It’s just as important to learn what DOESN’T work for you as what does.

Three weeks of taking imperfect action will tell you more about what works for you than three months of listening to Major Overload ever could.

Instead of searching for the “perfect” plan, build your action plan.

1 or 2 actions you can take this week, small enough to test and see how they feel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

Someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“.

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.).

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

Industry observers note that the drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again promptly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

Sources indicate that A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

“Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”.

It has been revealed that this got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”.

That win got them back on the routine.

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

“How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”.

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”.

It’s getting the next available win.

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

To be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.).

In a recent development, “Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪.

I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”.

This is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

According to recent reports, including if the evidence claims that something MASSIVE needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

Industry observers note that but the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate promptly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

Industry observers note that to be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health challenges (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”.

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition plan. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

You might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

Recent findings suggest that the salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

Recent findings suggest that with no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you blueprint to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

If you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is at the moment facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.).

In a recent development, with 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

Despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

Led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

It has been revealed that made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”.

According to recent reports, the flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

As a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s the client story this comes from.

This was the first thing a new client said to me.

When we dug into it, here’s the pattern that emerged:.

-> See something newly introduced, give that a try.

Strength training, then running, then a yoga challenge, then back to lifting with a different app.

Nerd Fitness Coaching was the latest in a long line of fresh starts.

And here’s the thing: all of it was GOOD.

She was moving. She was trying newly introduced things. She was having fun (at least at first).

But she was frustrated with herself.

She felt like she kept starting over and never getting anywhere.

And she wanted help figuring out what to do.

Let’s be real: trying something new is exciting.

Industry observers note that A new program, a new class, a new challenge. There’s a buzz to it.

According to recent reports, and that buzz isn’t bad. Enjoying it is a major part of what keeps people moving.

The catch is that most goals need some repetition.

Industry observers note that getting stronger, running farther, learning a skill. You get better at the things you practice again and again.

So the question isn’t “how do I stop getting bored?”.

It’s “how do I keep some of that newly introduced-thing fun AND repeat things enough to see progress?” 🧐.

That’s what we worked on together.

When I built her program, I kept its overall shape the same week to week.

According to recent reports, but inside it, a few key exercises got a target. Something like:.

“Once you can do 12 reps with 25 pounds, we level up.”.

The targets were far enough away to stretch her, and close enough that she could hit them in 2 to 6 weeks of focused practice.

Industry observers note that when she hit one, we leveled up that exercise: new reps or weight, or a new variation. Everything else stayed put.

So something was always changing.

There was always a target she was closing in on and a level she’d recently beaten.

According to recent reports, but the frame stayed the same. We were still working on the same overall qualities.

And that’s what let her progress stack up instead of resetting every few weeks.

She was able to stay really consistent with her program.

According to recent reports, she still fell off some. (Life happens.).

But when she came back, she wasn’t looking for something new.

She was excited to pick up her program and keep progressing.

And sure, sometimes her goals would change.

We spent 6 months training for her first half marathon, then switched gears to focus on building muscle.

But that was a choice, not a restart.

If you love bouncing between things and you’re happy doing it, keep bouncing.

This is for when the bouncing starts to feel frustrating.

Before you reach for a latest program, try a new level.

✅ Set a target you could reach in 2 to 6 weeks (a rep count or a weight).

In a recent development, ✅ When you hit it, level up that one exercise with newly introduced reps, a new weight, or a new variation. Leave everything else alone.

Sources indicate that I’m excited to see what you come up with. 😃.

#172893. Breaking: Biological age tests: Should you get one?

Breaking: Biological age tests: Should you get one?

📅 28 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson, the subject of the Netflix documentary Don’t Die, says he’s on a quest to achieve the lowest possible “biological age” (also known as bio age).
  • He reportedly spends millions each year on anti-aging treatments—dozens of daily supplements, weekly acid peels for his skin, injections to boost collagen production, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and plasma infusions extracted from his 17-year-old son’s body.
  • Recent findings suggest that to determine what’s working, Johnson has undergone numerous tests to assess his bio age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson, the subject of the Netflix documentary Don’t Die, says he’s on a quest to achieve the lowest possible “biological age” (also known as bio age).

He reportedly spends millions each year on anti-aging treatments—dozens of daily supplements, weekly acid peels for his skin, injections to boost collagen production, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and plasma infusions extracted from his 17-year-old son’s body.

Recent findings suggest that to determine what’s working, Johnson has undergone numerous tests to assess his bio age. Johnson claims these tests show his age is now 5.1 years younger than when he embarked on his anti-aging quest.

Apparently, he’s aging in reverse.

Industry observers note that granted, not everyone’s buying it. A New York Times exposé, for example, claims Johnson’s biological age, in reality, has increased by 10 years.1.

Still, Johnson’s “don’t die” crusade is gaining traction.

Industry observers note that bio age tests are a frequent topic on popular podcasts by Peter Attia, Joe Rogan, and Andrew Huberman. Google “bio age testing” and you’ll see dozens of ads for mail-order blood or urine testing kits that claim to reveal your biological age, pace of aging, and more. With prices tumbling into affordability, it’s natural to wonder….

In a recent development, if so, which test is best? Just as importantly, what should you do with the information?

Sources indicate that your biological age (bio age) refers to how your cells function. It’s not necessarily the same as your chronological age, which refers to the number of candles on your birthday cake.

For example, let’s say Chang, a 50-year-old man, works at a desk, spends his free time in front of the TV, lives in the most polluted city in the world, eats a candy bar for lunch, and smokes. On the other hand, Jabari, a different 50-year-old man, hits the gym several times a week, lives in the mountains, doesn’t smoke, relishes his five servings of veggies a day, meditates, and spends most evenings in his garden.

Genetics aside, you’d be wise to wager that Jabari’s bio age is younger than Chang’s.

Bio age testing kits measure one or more biological markers of aging, also known as biomarkers.

For example, some tests focus on the size of your telomeres, the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes. Others measure DNA methylation, a physiological process that chemically alters DNA.

Once a company isolates and measures these markers from your blood or urine, it plugs the bio data into a formula that calculates your bio age.

However, if you see a doctor with any regularity, you’re likely already tracking some biomarkers of aging. For example, biomarkers such as blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and blood glucose can help predict your risk of future cardiovascular disease, a leading cause of premature death.

Biomarker testing can help you monitor your wellness proactively rather than waiting for disease symptoms to appear.

It has been revealed that for some, it also serves as a motivator. If you learn you have the bones of someone 20 years older, this may give you the nudge you need to start strength training consistently.

Industry observers note that in addition, biomarkers provide objective data, allowing you to track and evaluate various health-related actions quantitatively. By monitoring your blood pressure, you might learn that consistent exercise helps, but your late-afternoon energy drink does the opposite.

You don’t have to be a billionaire (or even a millionaire) to track biomarkers of aging.

In this section, we’ll cover several massively underappreciated, scientifically validated tests you can use to gain insight into your bio age—for FREE.

Before scientists developed high-tech blood-based bio age tests, researchers used these free tests to calculate the pace of aging in the people they studied.

People who are fitter and stronger tend to live longer.2.

That’s because muscles do more than just move us around. They also secrete anti-inflammatory substances, help to regulate blood sugar, slow cellular aging, protect the lining of the arteries, and more. All this helps reduce the risk of age-related diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease, a phenomenon we explore in our article, The New Science of Muscle.

Related to strength, your ability to balance is also key. If you’re middle-aged or older and can’t stand on one foot for at least 10 seconds, your risk of dying in the next seven years is double that of someone who can stand for longer, according to a study of 1,700 people.3.

The Sitting-Rising Test (SRT) is one way to assess both strength and balance at the same time.

People with low scores on this test have a higher risk of dying from cardiovascular disease, according to a 12-year study of 4,200 adults between the ages of 46 and 75.4.

Lower yourself to the floor with your legs in a crisscross position. Then, with your legs in the same position, stand back up. As you stand, notice if you must use a part of your body—hand, shin, knee—as leverage.

It has been revealed that to score yourself, start with 10 points. Then, for each body part you used to stand, deduct a point. Subtract a half point if you became unsteady or lost your balance.

Keep in mind that this (and other tests) serve as a proxy for your fitness. A low score indicates that your balance and coordination, muscle strength and power, and mobility may all require some attention.

Like the SRT test, your grip strength provides insight into your overall fitness. If the muscles in your hands are weak, the muscles throughout your body are more likely to be weak, too.

Poor grip strength can also predict future muscle weakness. In one study, people with a weak grip were more likely to walk slowly and be unable to rise from a chair, complete rigorous housework, or climb a flight of steps 25 years later.5.

Low grip strength has also been associated with:6.

According to one study, grip strength was a better indicator of longevity (or lack thereof) than blood pressure.7.

Grab a standard tennis ball, and squeeze as hard as you can, for as long as you can.

In a recent development, if you can manage 15 to 30 seconds before your grip fatigues, you’re doing fine. Ninety seconds puts you well above average—anything over 90 ranks you solidly in the upper-third percentile.

Sources indicate that if you’re below 15, keep in mind that this test is also just one indicator of your overall strength. (And squeezing balls to improve grip strength without training the rest of your body is unlikely to make significant improvements in your overall health and fitness.).

A hand-held dynamometer—available for use at most occupational therapists’ and some gyms—can also test grip strength. (If you’re willing to shell out some cash, you can buy your own for somewhere between $100 and $500.).

An ability to balance on one foot for an extended period can help reduce your risk of falls, one of the leading causes of injury-related death among older adults.

In addition, many different bodily systems—the eyes, inner ear, skeletal muscles, and brain—must work together to help you stay upright.

Conditions like diabetes, heart disease, and cancer can all affect balance. As a result, an inability to stand on one foot can serve as a warning sign for eroding health and fitness.8.

Industry observers note that stand near a wall or chair for safety. Keep your eyes open and hands on your hips. Then, lift your dominant leg and start timing yourself. Once you put your foot down, stop the clock. Repeat the test with your non-dominant leg.

Once you have your times, compare them to the following averages, from a study out of Duke University, to see how you did compared to your age-matched peers.9.

Sometimes you know why you’re tired, such as the morning after binge-watching the last few episodes of a thriller. Once you catch up on your sleep, the weariness lifts.

According to recent reports, that’s not the same thing as fatigue, which describes persistent exhaustion that worsens over time and interferes with life. In addition to feeling physically tired, someone who’s fatigued feels mentally dull and emotionally exhausted.

Think of fatigue as an early sign that something’s off, especially if you don’t know the cause.

According to recent reports, let’s say you’ve already ruled out the usual suspects like too much caffeine, dehydration, too much alcohol, medication side effects, chronic stress, or too much or too little exercise. What’s left is likely a sleep disorder or a developing health problem such as anemia, obesity, depression, cancer, or diabetes, to name a few.

If you’re 60 or older, fatiguability—or how worn out you feel after an activity—can also predict longevity.

According to research out of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, the higher someone scores in fatiguability, the higher their risk of death in the future.10 Other research has linked high fatiguability with declines in gait speed, walking ability, and other tests of fitness.11.

Industry observers note that to measure fatigability, use a tool called the Pittsburgh Fatigability Scale. Using a 0 (no fatigue) to 5 (extreme fatigue) scale, rate how fatigued you think you would feel after completing the following activities:.

According to recent reports, if you score less than 15, you’re doing well. Scores between 15 and 24 are a warning sign. Anything 25 and above is regarded as severe, and worth mentioning to your healthcare professional.12.

Despite popular belief, both too little and too much body fat can influence health for the worse, as we explore in our infographic, Is body fat good or bad for you?

Your muscle mass also plays a role, which is why someone’s body composition matters more than their weight.

The gold standard methods that estimate body composition—underwater weighing, air displacement (Bod Pod), and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA)—certainly aren’t free.

However, a recent study determined that a good old-fashioned (and cheap) tape measure can provide a comparably accurate estimate of body composition.13.

To use a tape measure to keep track of your body fat percentage, measure:.

It has been revealed that ensure the tape is snug but not so tight that it cuts into the skin. Once you have your measurements, plug those numbers—along with your age, sex, height, and weight—into our FREE Body Fat Calculator, which will take it from there.

Sources indicate that depending on where you live in the world, the following tests may not be free. However, as part of routine preventative care, your insurance might cover them.

If your primary care doctor recommends yearly blood work, it’s for good reason.

By keeping tabs on several blood markers, you can see if your health is trending toward type 2 diabetes or heart disease, both leading causes of premature mortality.

Sources indicate that many blood markers can also be influenced relatively rapidly (within 6 to 12 weeks) through lifestyle changes, supplement protocols, or medications. This makes them practical tools for monitoring whether various lifestyle or medical modifications are working.

If you’re not already doing so, consider having the following blood markers tested annually. Then, talk to your health care professional about what your numbers mean. They might use the following numbers, along with your blood pressure, to calculate a cardiovascular disease risk score.

*Milligrams per deciliter of blood **Milligrams per liter.

When researchers study healthy super-agers aged 90 and older, strong bones are one of their defining features.14.

That may be because, like muscles, bones are live organs that secrete substances that may be beneficial to overall health and longevity.15.

Recent findings suggest that for example, bones secrete osteocalcin, a hormone that plays a role in bone remodeling. When osteocalcin circulates in the body, it’s thought to play a role in everything from helping muscles to produce ATP to regulating brain neurotransmitters.

Sources indicate that because of these varied roles, it’s thought that, as bones wear away, osteocalcin levels drop, contributing to many age-related health problems, including diabetes, low muscle mass, and cognitive problems.16 17 (At least, that’s the theory. Most of this research has been done on mice.).

Osteocalcin aside, loss of bone density can, of course, lead to fractures, which can increase your risk of death for up to 10 years after a break.18.

It’s especially notable to keep tabs on bone health if you’re in any of these high-risk categories:.

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans are a type of X-ray that measures the amount of bone mineral content packed into a square centimeter of bone.

Insurance often won’t cover these scans for people younger than 65 unless there’s a documented risk of developing osteoporosis. Out of pocket, the average cost is about $300.

In a recent development, when you receive your DEXA results, you’ll see a T-score that represents how your bone density compares to the average bone density of a young adult with peak bone mass. A T-score of +1.0 to -1.0 means you have normal bone mineral density for someone your age. Anything below -1.0 means you might have osteopenia (low bone mineral density) or osteoporosis (porous bones that are prone to fracture).

If you have some money to burn, you can learn an awful lot about your body.

Here, you’ll find a quick run-down on some of the more high-tech tests you can get and what they can tell you.

However, before we get into the details, we want to point out a few caveats:.

In a recent development, ▶ Biological age can vary over time, and by organ. Someone may go through a period of accelerated aging—saying, during a period of intense stress—then their rate of aging may slow as they focus more on recovery. Additionally, organs can age at different rates. For example, someone with heart disease may have a relatively older heart than their kidneys. (Not all tests measure individual organ age, but it’s becoming more common.).

Recent findings suggest that ▶ Commercial tests won’t always accurately reflect the changes you’re making. Until more research supports the reliability of these tests, evaluate your behaviors over isolated test results. If you’re eating more fruits and veggies, exercising more consistently, managing stress, and otherwise slaying the healthy lifestyle department, don’t sweat your results. Focus on doing the things we know improve health.

Sources indicate that ▶ If a tech giant pairs your test results with a hard sell for a proprietary and expensive supplement protocol, be wary. It’s better to share and discuss your results with a trusted health professional than take health advice from a profit-seeking stranger over the internet.

Recent findings suggest that DNA methylation is a biological process that chemically alters DNA. Because the rate of methylation accelerates with aging, it can be used to estimate someone’s biological age and life expectancy, finds research.19 20 21.

According to recent reports, the Horvath Clock and DunedinPACE both measure specific biomarkers that can be used to better understand someone’s methylation rate. Scientists developed these tests to help other scientists study how various lifestyle factors, environmental exposures, and medicines affect aging. They didn’t develop the tests as a way for the average person to pinpoint their biological age. (Which hasn’t stopped companies from selling DNA methylation testing kits to the public.) They cost about $300.

According to recent reports, if you decide to get one of these tests, keep in mind your results won’t give you a complete picture of your health and longevity. Aging typically occurs at varying rates throughout the body. Your liver might age faster than your heart or brain, for example. So if you measure DNA methylation in your blood, that’s all you know about. Put another way, a DNA methylation test isn’t a substitute for your annual wellness checkup or blood work.

Sources indicate that telomeres—the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes—wear away with age. The length of a telomere can predict how many times a specific cell can divide before dying.

Abnormally short telomeres are associated with several genetic diseases. For this reason, when physicians suspect someone might have inherited a genetic disease, they’ll order a specific type of telomere test—the flow-FISH test—to measure the telomere length in all the cells in a blood sample.22 23.

It’s more debatable whether telomere tests can predict aging in healthy people.

Just as importantly, the telomere test marketed to the public, known as the qPCR telomere test, isn’t used in research or medicine. These $100 tests are fine if you’re merely curious—just don’t base health and fitness decisions on your results.

For years, only elite athletes cared about VO2 max, which describes the maximum amount of oxygen that your body can use during exercise.

More recently, however, some experts have suggested that VO2 max can serve as a measure for athletes and non-athletes alike to track the rate at which their bodies are aging.

People with high VO2 max tend not only to be more physically fit but also less likely to develop heart disease, diabetes, cancer, or stroke.24 25 26 27.

In an observational study that followed the health outcomes of 5,107 Danish men over 46 years, men with above-average V02 max during middle age lived an average of five years longer than men with below-average V02 max. Each unit increase in VO2 max was associated with a 45-day increase in longevity. The researchers suggested VO2 max may more accurately predict all-cause mortality than high cholesterol, obesity, high blood pressure, and insulin resistance.28.

You might think of V02 max as a canary and your aging body as a coal mine.

As you age, your chest wall becomes more rigid, the muscles that surround the lungs weaker, and the oxygen-carrying blood vessels calcified and less elastic. The heart also squeezes with less force, max heart rate drops, muscle mass and strength decline, the mitochondria in cells and muscles lose their effectiveness, among other differences.

In addition to raising your risk for many different diseases, these changes can also affect VO2 max, which tends to decline 10 percent per decade starting around age 30.29 30.

In the past, the only way to reliably measure VO2 max was in a fitness lab.

It has been revealed that you would wear a metabolic mask and a heart monitor while you ran or cycled to exhaustion. The mask collected your expired carbon dioxide and monitored how much oxygen you sucked into your lungs. This lab-based testing is still the most accurate way to measure V02 max as well as other key fitness metrics such as:.

Depending on where you live, you might be able to get your VO2 max tested for around $150.

However, if you don’t have access to a VO2 max clinic, three somewhat less accurate options exist.

Sources indicate that wear a heart rate monitor as you walk one mile on a flat surface, such as a treadmill or running track. As soon as you complete the mile, record your heart rate and walk time. Then, plug it into the following formula to calculate your VO2 max:.

132.853 — (0.0769 × Weight) — (0.3877 × Age) + (6.315 × Sex) — (3.2649 × Time) — (0.1565 × Heart rate).

If that feels like too much math, you can also use a free online tool.

Many smartwatches will estimate your VO2 Max for you based on information the watch gathers from your workouts, sex, and age. Compared to in-office testing, smart watches can over- or underestimate V02 max, especially in people who are very out of shape or extremely fit.31.

Because of this, you don’t necessarily want to use your smart watch measurement to determine your current state of health. However, it can help you to see trends. For example, does your VO2 estimate drop after a few weeks of skipping your usual spin class? If so, that’s good information to have.

Fitness performance correlates with longevity. If you’re getting faster at running a certain distance or can go a longer distance than before, you’re getting fitter and increasing your chances of living a long, healthy life.

Sources indicate that one way to test this: the 12-minute run test, also known as the Cooper test. (This is a validated way to estimate VO2 max—and shows about a 90 percent correlation with lab-based measurements.).

Run as fast as you can on a flat surface, such as a treadmill set at a 1 percent incline or running track, for 12 minutes. After 12 minutes, record your distance. Then, plug it into one of the following formulas to calculate your VO2 max.

In lieu of doing math, you can also use a free online calculator.

Try to think of the information you gather about your body as just that—information.

It’s not a moral judgment of who you are as a person.

Just as importantly, it’s not a permanent situation.

It has been revealed that you have options. However, most people make two big mistakes when it comes to longevity-related lifestyle changes.

It’s the simple, boring, “I’ve heard this a million times before” health practices that, when done consistently, add up to a long, healthy life.

We’re talking about things like….

And that’s just a partial list.

According to thousands of studies, people who practice these and other high-impact strategies not only live longer, but also live better. They’re stronger, happier, and less likely to spend their later years disabled or in pain.

(If you’d like to see where you stand when it comes to big impact health and longevity strategies, check out our FREE Longevity Assessment.).

However, when it comes to health, fitness, and longevity, many people pursue options with minimal impact (at best). They reach for the latest, trendy supplement rather than taking steps to quit smoking, as just one example.

Recent findings suggest that here’s the thing: Big rock strategies require changes in behavior. If daily physical activity were as easy as popping a pill, walkers and cyclists would clog up the streets in your neighborhood.

(It’s precisely this reason why so many people need the support of a certified health coach who has undergone training in the science of behavior change.).

The data gathered from biomarker aging tests can give you a sense of control.

Data, in isolation, doesn’t lead to a longer life.

Gathering data without changing your behavior is like checking your reflection in the mirror, seeing spinach wedged between your incisors, and leaving it there.

You need to remove the spinach for the mirror check to be worthwhile.

If you don’t use your bio data to inform behavior change, you’re wasting your money and time.

Consider your biomarker data as a baseline or starting point.

Then, use it to assess whether various lifestyle changes or medical interventions are moving you closer to your goal of living a longer, healthier life.

The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins.

Sources indicate that picture this: you're settling into a private suite at 35,000 feet somewhere over the American heartland. The door clicks shut. There's a full-flat bed, a sliding privacy door, a personal minibar, and a cabin crew member who just handed you a glass of something sparkling before you've even thought to ask. This is Delta One Suites on the Airbus A350-900 — one of the best domestic business class products flying today — and you're on your way from Fresh York to Los Angeles for 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles. Let that sink in for a moment. The same seat on the same flight regularly retails for **$2,500 to $6,000 in cash**. At the low end of that range, your 50,000 points are delivering **5 cents per point (CPP)**. At the high end — during peak travel seasons or last-minute premium bookings — you're looking at **12 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards programs consider 1–2 CPP a "good" redemption. You're potentially doing six times better than that. The ChooseFI community is built on a foundational principle: the gap between what something *costs* and what you *pay* is where wealth is built. That principle applies to points redemptions just as powerfully as it applies to index fund expense ratios. When the market (Delta's dynamic pricing engine) says $4,000 and your award chart says 50,000 points, you've just found a pricing inefficiency — and exploiting it intelligently is exactly what savvy travel rewards strategy is all about. What makes this redemption especially compelling is the *product*. Delta One Suites on the A350-900 isn't a legacy business class seat in name only. The sliding door gives you genuine privacy. The fully flat bed means you arrive in LA rested instead of stiff. The suite design is genuinely luxurious — the kind of experience that, for most people, lives permanently in the "someday, maybe" category. Travel rewards exist to move that experience from "someday" to your actual calendar. For a couple traveling together, this redemption scales elegantly: 100,000 points gets two people into private suites on one of America's most competitive premium routes. That's a combined retail value potentially north of $10,000 — for points you may have earned simply by paying your regular monthly expenses on the right credit cards. This is what the system looks like when it works.

Sources indicate that here's the insight that changes everything: Delta prices its own award seats dynamically, which means when you search Delta.com for a SkyMiles redemption, you're at the mercy of an algorithm that reads demand, load factors, and booking timing. A Delta One Suite that costs 50,000 SkyMiles one week might jump to 120,000 or even 250,000 SkyMiles the next. It's unpredictable, often punishing, and fundamentally unfair to the loyal customer who saved up miles expecting consistency.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

It has been revealed that virgin Atlantic is a Delta SkyTeam partner, which means Flying Club members can book seats on Delta-operated flights using their Virgin Atlantic miles. But critically — and this is the entire mechanism — Virgin Atlantic prices Delta award seats on a fixed award chart, not Delta's dynamic pricing system. That chart at the moment prices Delta One (business class) on transcon routes like JFK–LAX at 50,000 miles one-way. No matter what Delta's algorithm is doing that day, your Virgin Atlantic redemption rate stays fixed.

This is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

The points you need to fund this redemption are almost certainly already sitting in currencies you have or can easily earn:.

For a redemption this valuable, the 1:1 instant transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are your primary path. You transfer exactly what you need, the miles appear in your Flying Club account immediately, and you book. No waiting, no uncertainty.

Virgin Atlantic has a reputation for imposing high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights — and that reputation is well-earned. But here's the critical nuance: surcharges do NOT apply to partner awards. When you book a Delta-operated flight through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you pay only the standard carrier-imposed taxes and fees, which are minimal on domestic U.S. routes. On JFK–LAX, expect to pay roughly $5–$15 in taxes. That's it. The surcharge concern that makes some people avoid Virgin Atlantic entirely simply doesn't apply here.

Recent findings suggest that flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every three years, and your miles will remain intact indefinitely. This is a very traveler-friendly policy compared to programs with hard expiration dates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Sources indicate that hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

I’m working my way through all of them.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, mentioned it this way:.

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

It has been revealed that I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Of course that’s going to feel rough!

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:.

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

Recent findings suggest that after multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

Industry observers note that and it’s vital to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

Sources indicate that you know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

According to recent reports, try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌.

Recent findings suggest that and if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

Your on-ramp doesn’t have to be forever.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

#172888. Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2492 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance.
  • How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.
  • Sources indicate that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a new fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Sources indicate that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a new fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my significant shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

After finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

According to recent reports, “I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev said, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

Sources indicate that “Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he mentioned. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

“There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the intends because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

According to recent reports, “That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that plan. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

Recent findings suggest that sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

Recent findings suggest that “It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

And for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Sources indicate that physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

Industry observers note that “To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

“You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It has been revealed that it worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

“I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before massive races.”.

The day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

“When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

According to recent reports, “I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

That feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

Recent findings suggest that “It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

According to recent reports, thankfully for him, time went by swiftly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

Industry observers note that after that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

Recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

In a recent development, starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a fresh world’s best time, the specter of the Big Island tempered his elation.

Sources indicate that “It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

One of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his new, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev quickly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a big difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of latest cooling strategy.

“It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

“So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

According to recent reports, when you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

“We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he said, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev quickly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

In a recent development, “I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

It has been revealed that “My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

For now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev says he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

Sources indicate that “Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

Sources indicate that “He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

#172887. Breaking: The Cervélo Soloist—The Race-Inspired Road Bike That Makes Sense for the Way Most Riders Actually Ride

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1328 w)
📖 Baca
