This redemption was designed — structurally, if not intentionally — for families pursuing financial independence. Here's why it fits the ChooseFI worldview so perfectly.

Industry observers note that the ideal user is a family of three to six people who want a high-quality, genuinely relaxing vacation without the mental overhead of per-meal, per-drink, per-activity budgeting. The all-inclusive format eliminates the "should we splurge on dinner?" anxiety that can undercut vacation enjoyment. You've already "paid" with points. Just enjoy.

You need a minimum of 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For a realistic 5-night family trip, initiative for 125,000 points — or 100,000 if you hold the World of Hyatt card and qualify for the 5th night free benefit. This is very achievable if you've been accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards through normal household spending on a Sapphire card.

This redemption is also excellent for couples celebrating anniversaries or honeymoons (use Zilara for the adults-only experience), parents of young children who want a vacation where the kids are engaged so the adults can actually relax, and travelers who want a warm-weather, beach vacation without the complexity of international award flight bookings.

This is NOT the right fit if you prefer boutique, off-the-beaten-path travel over resort-style vacations, you're a solo traveler (the per-person value scales poorly), or you're chasing ultra-premium redemptions like business class flights or city luxury hotels. The Hyatt portfolio has those too — but this specific sweet spot is about maximum family value, not maximum luxury status.

In a recent development, this redemption earns an **Easy** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. The ChooseFI community members who struggle with it usually hit one of two friction points, and both are easily solved. **The Earning Side: Very Easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers 1:1 to World of Hyatt instantly. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you already have access to the best transfer path. Earning 125,000 Chase UR points for a 5-night trip is a reasonable 12–18 month project for a household running normal expenses through rewards cards. **The Booking Side: Easy, With One Catch.** The Hyatt website is clean and the points booking process is straightforward. The one challenge is **peak date availability** — spring break and holiday weeks book up fast at the most popular Ziva properties. The fix is simple: use the 395-day booking window. Set a phone reminder 13 months before your target trip and search the day availability opens. **The Transfer Confidence Hurdle.** Some beginners are nervous about transferring points to Hyatt before they have a confirmed booking. The practical risk is real — if you transfer and then can't find availability, those points are stranded in Hyatt (though they're still useful for future bookings). The solution: always **confirm availability before transferring**. Hyatt lets you select dates and see the points cost before you're asked to pay. Get to that confirmation screen first, then transfer. If you can navigate a hotel booking website and move money between financial accounts, you can execute this redemption. Start with a low-stakes search on hyatt.com today — just to get comfortable with how award availability looks.

Check the same dates at the cash rate to calculate your cents per point value. If the cash rate is $600 per night and the award rate is 25,000 points, you are getting 2.4 cents per point. For all-inclusives, values above 2 cents per point are common and 3 or more cents per point is typical during peak season.

Transfer the required points from your Chase account to World of Hyatt. Transfers are instant. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, you can transfer directly. Freedom and Ink Cash points can be pooled to a Sapphire card first.

Sources indicate that complete the booking using your World of Hyatt points. Select the standard room type on points — all-inclusive benefits apply to all room categories. Add any special requests for your family (crib, connecting rooms, dietary needs) in the booking notes.

Industry observers note that if you have World of Hyatt Globalist status (earned at 60 nights or through the Globalist challenge), you unlock suite upgrades (subject to availability), late checkout, and other premium benefits. Even without elite status, the all-inclusive base experience is exceptional — every meal, drink, and activity is covered.

Industry observers note that A 7-night stay at a Hyatt Ziva or Zilara typically costs 175,000 to 245,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 to 35,000 per night depending on the property and season). This covers the room, all meals, unlimited drinks, activities, and entertainment for the duration of your stay.

Sources indicate that at Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) properties, children typically stay and eat free when sharing a room with parents. Policies vary by property and the child's age — generally children under 12 are included at no additional cost. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only (18+). Check the specific property's policy when booking.

Transferring to Hyatt for an all-inclusive typically delivers 2 to 4 cents per point — roughly double the portal value. For a $600-per-night all-inclusive, the portal would cost 40,000 to 48,000 Chase points per night, while a direct Hyatt transfer costs only 25,000 points.

Most Hyatt all-inclusive award stays include resort fees in the points rate, but you may owe taxes and some incidental charges. According to recent reports, hyatt all-inclusive resorts represent the single best hotel redemption for families in the travel rewards ecosystem. The combination of a premium resort experience, all meals and drinks included, and 2 to 4 cents per point value makes this a sweet spot that is hard to beat. A family of four can enjoy a week-long beach vacation at a Hyatt Ziva for 175,000 transferable Chase points — a stay that would cost $4,000 to $7,000 in cash. For the ChooseFI community, this is the redemption that makes points tangible: your kids are splashing in the pool, you are enjoying a beachfront dinner, and the entire experience was covered by your Chase credit card rewards. Transfer to Hyatt, book early for peak dates, and give your family the vacation you have been optimizing for.

Black Friday feels better when you can approach it with mindfulness in mind. After all, having sales and discounts constantly waved in your digital face can make it all too tempting to snap up one of everything and in every color. But if you can release urgency and bring intention into equation, Black Friday becomes an opportunity to take inventory of what you already have and thoughtfully fill any obvious gaps or perhaps finally purchase that product you’ve been eyeing for awhile.

Sources indicate that among some of our most coveted sales picks this Black Friday are a luxury (and top-performing) yoga mat, two latest takes on yoga dressing, a naturally supportive prop, and a smart ring for the meditative among us. And the best part? These items are on our list because we find them to be worthwhile investments. Each just happens to be on sale.

If your practice could use a bit of extra support, you might want to invest in a bolster. If you’ve been looking for a sustainable option that brings more structure than a regular pillow you might grab at home, this cork bolster from Yoloha might be your perfect fit—particularly at its right now discounted price. The natural, recycled cork bolster (yes, it’s also stuffed with cork) is comfortable, substantial, and easy to clean. It’s a durable yoga prop that’s designed to last, no matter how many Savasanas and Reclining Bound Angles it supports.

According to recent reports, A form-fitting yet breathable bodysuit is more of an activewear want than a need. Which is why snagging one on sale makes a lot of sense. Lululemon’s Align Cami Bodysuit is stylish and comfortable, carrying you from coffee to yoga to a long walk with ease. Also, practicing in a skin-skimming bodysuit is surprisingly comfortable, with the single piece conforming to your body sans the distracting rolling or tucking that can come with separates. And as noted, it’s a piece that goes beyond your mat. Seriously, just add a hoodie and it’s an instant outfit.

Sources indicate that this top-rated yoga mat might be a go-to for many yogis, but the price tag likely provides pause for others. That makes it an ideal candidate for your Black Friday considerations. Liforme’s sleek, smooth, and instantly recognizable mats are known for their functionality and grip, with the eco-polyurethane surface keeping you in place even during the sweatiest of hot yoga classes.

The brand’s annual Black Friday sale features up to 40 percent off, with an extra 15 percent discount when you purchase two yoga mats and an extra 25 percent off when you purchase three or more.

Sometimes a pair of tight yoga leggings doesn’t feel like the coziest option for class. For those in the market for a loose, wide-legged option, Athleta’s Dream Drape Mid-Rise Pant is soft and flowy, making it a viable option for your yoga practice and your daily lounge session. Choose from one of three colors, and a multitude of fits, all of which are currently on sale.

The Pulse Mindfulness Ring is sort of an anti-smart ring. All it does is pulse at random or dictated intervals; you get to decide what that pulse means. You can invite the pulse to serve as a reminder to breathe more deeply, focus, relax your shoulders, or whatever other intention fits your needs. After testing the ring for a month, I can attest to the lightweight little accessory’s power to elicit calm.

#172855. The 7 Best Garmin Watches for Cyclists: Editor-Tested Picks for Training, Recovery, and Everyday Wear

The 7 Best Garmin Watches for Cyclists: Editor-Tested Picks for Training, Recovery, and Everyday Wear

📅 25 Mar 2022 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that cyclists, myself included, are often data driven.
  • Sources indicate that many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that cyclists, myself included, are often data driven. Even for cyclists that aren’t particularly motivated to optimize their performance there’s a belief that if a ride, run, hike, or any activity isn’t on Strava, it didn’t happen. Tracking your rides is easy to do with a head unit, but the tracking is limited to just the time spent on your bike.

Sources indicate that many riders and multisport athletes just don’t need a dedicated bike computer—especially with how smart smartwatches have become over the last few years. Smartwatches offer many of the same features that you find on bike computers, but smartwatches can also track sleep, heart rate, and activities you do off the bike. I have a few friends who even track mowing their lawn to make sure they don’t lose out on the activity for the day. With so many smartwatches out there, it can be hard to pick which one to choose, but time and again we go back to Garmin as the benchmark for tracking tech.

Tracking three back-to-back activities can be an annoyance for data-hungry triathletes. However, the Forerunner 970’s “Triathlon” mode gives multisport athletes the freedom to change between workouts without ending their activity. You only need to tap the lap button at the start and end of each transition. However, the 970 is a great option for folks who aren’t also swimming and running on their bike rides.

Recent findings suggest that while I’m not a triathlete, I’ve been testing the 970 for a couple of weeks during road rides, commutes, and my daily routine; my overall impression is quite positive. This is a performance-optimized smartwatch for performance-minded athletes. It can track and measure seemingly every data point across an enormous range of sports and activities. Specifically related to cycling, the Forerunner 970 has preset profiles for: Road, mountain biking, gravel, commuting, touring, e-biking, eMTB riding, indoor, cyclocross, and BMX. If none of those options meet your niche, you can also create your own.

According to recent reports, the variety and specificity of data you can track with the Forerunner 970 is mind-boggling. If you want to measure or see something related to riding, you probably can—although finding it in the array of options is sometimes the hardest part. And like Garmin’s head units, that’s the watch’s biggest downside. Garmin packs so many options into its devices that it can be difficult to navigate within the screens. Luckily, the Garmin Connect app is (mostly) easy to use, and changes made in the app instantly push to the phone.

A feature I like on the 970 is the ability to “Lap by Location”. With this turned on, your watch will automatically start a upcoming lap each time you pass through that GPS location again. That means no more forgetting to tap “Lap” when you’re deep in the red zone with one lap to go in an event. This makes the 970 perfect for cyclocross, criterium, and XC mountain bike racers seeking to track in-race performance data at a granular level.

Sources indicate that the Venu 4’s sleek, not-too-techy profile allows you to maximize your smartwatch mileage, both during workouts and in daily life. It prioritizes general smartwatch functionality, but there’s still plenty of processing power. That makes the Venu great for all-day wear, both on and off the bike.

In a recent development, senior Art Director, Colin McSherry, has tested the Venu 4 against his trusty Forerunner. He notes the Venu‘s solid 12-day battery life is closer to 8 to 10 days when heavily using route navigation for cycling, running, and hiking. He also stated, “I found the navigation a bit simpler and easier to use compared to the Garmin Forerunner 970 due to fewer physical buttons.”.

On the bike, starting and tracking a workout is easy. McSherry noted that, “GPS does take a few seconds to register, but usually picks up as you are taking your first few pedal strokes.” Compared to his Wahoo Elemnt, he found the GPS data was very close. “So if I forgot my computer or wanted to get away from staring at a screen while on a ride, it’s a great way to track basic metrics,” he said.

Sources indicate that garmin released the Fēnix 9 this fall, but we still love the Fēnix 8—and there are some great deals on the watch right now. The 8 Pro is Garmin’s flagship model in its class-leading Fēnix lineup. This watch is packed with virtually every feature you could want to measure and manage your outdoor adventures. The Fēnix 8 Pro includes it all in a rugged design featuring dive-rated buttons, a crisp AMOLED display (or MicroLED for an extra $400), and a titanium bezel. The device connects via ANT+ or Bluetooth to third-party sensors and supports a wide range of activity profiles.

Industry observers note that however, the Fēnix 8 Pro’s biggest upgrade is the included inReach satellite/LTE connectivity. (You previously needed a separate Garmin inReach device for that.) For backcountry adventurers, the ability to message, call, share location, or trigger SOS from your wrist is a must-have feature. All that capability comes at a cost—in both price and battery life. Garmin claims up to 15 days of battery life (in smartwatch mode) for the 47mm model and 27 days for the 51mm version. However, those numbers drop when LTE or satellite features are active.

Jason Griffin, Senior Health and Fitness Editor, is currently testing the 8 Pro. He mentioned, “It’s smarter than I expected a watch could be,” and notes that “answering calls through the watch is super easy, and tracking both rides and runs is intuitive.” He added, “The flashlight was great to find things in the middle of the night while I was holding my sleeping toddler.”.

While the Forerunner 265 is an older model, we find it strikes a good balance between Garmin’s budget-minded watches and its thousand-dollar devices. The 265’s accuracy is top-tier for its price, and this model has a far more readable display than its predecessor, thanks to a bright OLED screen—a near-critical feature if you don’t want to take your hands off your grips for too long to check your mileage.

It has been revealed that if you have smaller wrists (or prefer a more compact watch), the Forerunner 265S is a great choice. It’s lighter, slimmer, and even offers longer battery life.

According to recent reports, garmin’s new Forerunner 70 isn’t really an enhancement of its long-running Forerunner 55 entry-level model: the 70 is an entirely new device. The new model has a larger display, tons more features, and (most importantly for cyclists) many more bicycle profile options.

The Forerunner 70 is designed to be a great running watch, and its features and data logging abilities are best for off-bike activities. However, the 70 is still a good option for fitness-minded riders or cyclists needing to log their rides and basic training data. So, while the 70 cannot connect to your power meter or smart trainer, it still features solid GPS tracking, a heart rate monitor, and it can follow pre-planned courses.

Buying Tip: If you need to track power, spend the extra $50 and upgrade to the Forerunner 170 model.

In a recent development, garmin released the Enduro 4 this fall and we are right now testing it to see how it compares to the Enduro 3. The Enduro 3 is still a great option from Garmin and is on sale right now. The Enduro 3 is what happens when you take the top-shelf performance of the Fēnix and optimize it for maximum battery life. It’s a high-caliber solar watch that can last a staggering 36 days in smartwatch mode and up to 150 hours in GPS mode. It’s perfect for long bikepacking outings to places lacking spots to recharge.

At 51mm, the watch face is large but surprisingly unobtrusive. It feels light (63 grams) and comfortable on the wrist, even during long rides. The Enduro also has a sleeker profile than many premium smartwatches, with fewer sharp edges and oversized buttons. A feature our tester didn’t know they needed is the built-in flashlight. It works very well and is unexpectedly useful in everyday situations.

While the Velcro strap may not win style points off the bike, it’s incredibly functional. It allows for a perfectly snug fit, unlike traditional watch bands (frequently, one loop is too tight and the next is too loose).

Garmin markets the Forerunner 170 Music as a running watch, but that label doesn’t do it justice. It’s a true multi-sport smartwatch, built to support a wide range of activities—including multiple cycling disciplines—and it connects to ANT+ and Bluetooth sensors for more detailed ride data and notifications.

As the name suggests, it includes 4GB of onboard storage for music. This means you can leave your phone behind and still have your playlist. It also features an altimeter, barometer, compass (ABC sensors), a pulse oximeter, and advanced tracking tools, making it capable in almost any scenario.

It has been revealed that if you participate in various outdoor activities, you may prefer to own a single device to track everything. Whether cycling, running, hiking, paddling, walking the dog, or playing pickleball, a Garmin watch offers powerful, versatile functionality in a streamlined profile that’s always with you.

If you regularly track multiple types of workouts, while many road and gravel riders prefer cycling head units for instant access to maps, routing details, power metrics, and other data, some riders prefer smartwatches for logging ride data.

In a recent development, not needing to learn or own multiple overlapping devices simplifies and declutters your life. And in his excellent story, “The Problem with Modern Cycling Computers Isn’t the Huge Screens,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov argues that many head units are bloated with unnecessary functions.

Sources indicate that mountain bikers who often ride technical trails (bike park riders and enduro racers, for example) are increasingly turning to watches to document rides. With some cycling computers costing upwards of $1,000, you don’t want it dangling off the front of your bar or attached to your top tube in the event of a crash. Additionally, a computer is sometimes an unwanted distraction when trying to concentrate on a challenging descent.

Triathletes and duathlon racers are another group of riders who often prefer smartwatches. Watches allow athletes to transition between segments without needing to change devices or combine files after an event. Similarly, since the discipline involves swapping out muddy bikes in the pits during a race, cyclocross racers often use smartwatches.

A quick spin through Garmin’s website reveals a dizzying lineup of watches—sleek, feature-packed, and often overwhelming to sort through. While nearly all of them include the core functions you’d expect from a sports smartwatch, four series stand out as the best options for cyclists: Forerunner, Enduro, Fēnix, and Venu.

It has been revealed that the Forerunner series is Garmin’s core watch for cyclists and multisport athletes. It includes five models, starting with the $250 Forerunner 70, which covers the basics, and going up to the $750 Forerunner 970, which combines high-end smartwatch features with advanced training and navigation tools.

Recent findings suggest that the Enduro is designed for endurance athletes and offers the longest battery life of any Garmin watch. It includes the premium features of a cycling computer and smartwatch, along with extras such as solar charging and a built-in flashlight—making it a great option for long adventures.

It has been revealed that the Fēnix series shares many advanced features with the Enduro line—activity profiles, multisport tracking, and smartwatch tools—but adds specialized options for adventurers and divers. Fēnix has a slightly shorter battery life than the Enduro, and the watch faces are smaller.

Sources indicate that finally, the Venu is another option. It blends performance training, GPS, and data tracking features with fashion-forward styling. So, it looks good on and off the bike.

In a recent development, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#172854. These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

📅 05 Jul 2019 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4079 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

These 10 Editor-Approved E-MTBs Deliver Real Trail Capability

📅 05 Jul 2019 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking.
  • Today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Autumn is our favorite season for mountain biking. The air is crisp, the dirt is grippy, and we can’t wait to head to the singletrack after work and on weekends for great rides. And more than ever, like many other mountain bikers, we’re choosing E-MTBs for our rides. Electric mountain bikes help you maximize those rides and spend more time on your favorite trails.

Today’s electric mountain bikes use lightweight motors and batteries, making them super capable and amazingly fun on the trail. And while heavier than traditional mountain bikes, these pedal-assist models allow you to cover more miles, ride faster, and tackle challenging climbs.

E-MTBs are engineered for performance on singletrack trails and deep in the woods. And while their low-power motors provide a boost when pedalling, E-MTBs are not electric motorcycles. You still have to pedal an electric mountain bike; you can’t simply twist a throttle and blast down the trail.

According to recent reports, the best E-MTBs blend mountain bike components, suspension, and geometry with electronic technology in a brilliant fashion. Like non-electric mountain bikes, some E-MTBs blur the lines of XC and lightweight trail bikes, while others are burlier and take suspension and geometry cues from the top-performing enduro and downhill racing mountain bikes.

It has been revealed that aventon recently launched the Current, the brand’s first full-suspension E-MTB, and it is a gem! The Current ADV offers incredible value, and it’s trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, remarked, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers. The Current’s motor and interface provide riders with a wide range of tuning options and lots of data.”.

The Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor boasting 750 peak Watts and 110Nm torque. (The Current also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and torque to 120Nm.) Rounding out the ADV are a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

In his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab especially likes the Current’s intuitive and easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data and the ability to tune the motor settings.

Want a carbon frame and electronic drivetrain? The Current EXP is a great package for $5,999.

According to recent reports, specialized’s Turbo motor is a benchmark for electric mountain bike performance. It has plenty of power and torque, and the Morgan Hill, California-based brand has updated, polished, and refined the motor over several years. However, the biggest downside to Specialized E-MTBs has been their very steep starting price. But that has changed.

Specialized’s newest Levo model brings the platform to a more palatable $5,000 price. The Turbo Levo 4 Alloy uses the same motor and battery as the pricier carbon-chassis Expert model but with an aluminum frame, heavier components, and mechanical shifting to save pennies. The brand bolts its 105Nm torque and 810-watt Turbo 3.1 motor to a 150mm-travel, full-suspension aluminum frame and equips the bike with value-packed parts. SRAM brakes, a mechanical drivetrain, and Marzocchi suspension highlight the alloy Levo 4’s component package.

Hardtail mountain bikes are a gateway into the sport for many riders because they’re simple, sturdy, and affordable. Plus, massive, burly full-suspension mountain bikes aren’t for everyone. For some riders, they’re overkill—adding cost and complexity without delivering benefits that match their needs. Hardtail E-MTBs provide pedal assistance for about the same price as full-suspension non-electric mountain bikes.

Industry observers note that when introduced two years ago, the Ramblas impressed me with its great performance and capability for the price—and Aventon’s recent upgrades make it even better on the trail. The revised Ramblas ADV’s trail-forward components include a RockShox Psylo fork with 35mm stanchions, a 1x12 SRAM Eagle drivetrain that can handle most climbs, powerful four-piston SRAM DB6 brakes, and a useful dropper seatpost. The ADV’s tubeless rims and 2.4-inch Maxxis tires are also upgrades. These components are unmatched by any other hardtail E-MTB, especially at this price.

Superlight e-MTBs offer an intriguing compromise: In exchange for a less powerful drive unit, you get a lighter bike that feels and handles more like an analog mountain bike.

With the Turbo Levo R, Specialized asks: What if you didn’t need to compromise?

In a recent development, the Levo R has the same drive unit and battery as the Levo 4, but in a lighter, shorter-travel package with matched 29-inch wheels. It’s around 5 pounds lighter than a standard Levo 4 at the same price. In the top-of-the-line S-Works trim, the DU offers up to 111 Nm of torque and 850 watts of peak power with an 850 or 900Wh battery. The 41.4-pound (18.8 kg) S-Works Ultralight uses a 600Wh battery to save weight. Lower-priced models offer 105 Nm, 810 watts, and an 840Wh battery.

Industry observers note that after spending the better part of a year riding an S-Works Levo R (46.7 lb., size S3), senior test editor Matt Phillips calls it a winning combination for many riders. “It has all the capability and range of a big battery and full-power DU, but in a bike that’s much more flickable, lively, and, frankly, easier to ride than a heavier and bigger-travel e-MTB.” He claims Specialized’s e-MTB hardware, frames, and suspension are the icing on top, and calls the Levo R one of the most entertaining mountain bikes, powered or unpowered, he’s ridden this year.

According to recent reports, the 29-inch-wheeled Cannondale Moterra 4 has a subdued appearance, which makes it a sleeper. Many full-suspension E-MTBs routinely cost more than $10,000. However, Cannondale keeps the Moterra 4 to a more modest $5,500 while still packing a lot of punch for its price.

At the heart of the Moterra is a trusty Bosch Performance Line CX motor mounted on a 150mm-travel aluminum full-suspension frame. And inside the bike’s stout downtube is a 600Wh Bosch battery. Cannondale’s product team made smart component choices—such as the excellent Shimano Cues drivetrain and 160mm-travel SR Suntour Xeron air-sprung fork—that save cost without sacrificing much performance. The Moterra 4 also has a long-travel dropper seatpost, tubeless wheels, and Tektro disc brakes.

If you buy the Moterra 4 through rei.com, you can have it shipped to your nearest REI location for professional assembly with in-store or curbside pickup. You also get one year of free adjustments—or two years if you’re an REI Co-op member.

“I’ve never considered an e-bike a replacement for a traditional bike—until now.” That’s what Matt Phillips stated in his review of the excellent S-Works Turbo Levo 4. The latest version of Specialized’s flagship e-MTB is refined, quiet, fun to ride, and refreshingly free of the common annoyances that plague many e-bikes.

It has been revealed that several standout features set the latest S-Works Turbo Levo 4 apart from the crowded E-MTB segment: a powerful motor delivering 111Nm of torque, a larger 900 Wh battery, and the ability to toggle the pedal-assist cutoff between Class 2 (20mph) and Class 3 (28mph). That extra speed might sound excessive, but it’s a welcome boost when you're riding to or between trails.

In a recent development, though the S-Works Levo 4 is less expensive than its predecessor, it’s still eye-wateringly pricey at $12,500. For better value—relatively speaking—we recommend the Turbo Levo 4 Expert. It offers the same carbon frame, battery, and motor as the pricier model, though with slightly less torque. A 160mm-travel Fox 38 Performance Elite GRIPX2 fork and a Fox Float X Performance Elite shock handle suspension duties, and SRAM’s GX AXS drivetrain handles gear changes.

Salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs, yet it’s packed with value. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Nm of torque) and a 430Wh battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, the Moraine has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

Industry observers note that the frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system used by Pivot), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain with four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the component selection on this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Sources indicate that one advantage of an e-MTB is climbing faster and with less effort, leaving you fresher for the descent. A long-travel bike helps you make the most of that on steep, rough trails. It’s like having a personal chairlift for lapping downhill trails.

Recent findings suggest that cannondale’s Moterra Carbon LT 2 pairs a Bosch Performance Line CX motor and 750Wh battery with 165mm of plush, coil-sprung rear travel and a 170mm fork. Its frame combines a carbon front triangle with an alloy swingarm. Size-specific suspension kinematics tailor the suspension performance to each frame size. The mullet setup pairs a 29-inch front wheel with a 27.5-inch rear, giving you more room to move behind the saddle on steep terrain while keeping the larger front wheel’s rollover advantage. The battery is removable for off-bike charging.

For riders who prioritize steep descents and the refinement and reliability of a Bosch drive unit, the Moterra LT 2 is a strong choice.

It’s no exaggeration to say Avinox reshaped the performance e-MTB market. Developed and rolled out by drone maker DJI before becoming an independent tech giant, Avinox set new benchmarks with the M1: 105 Nm of torque and up to 1,000 watts of peak power. It also matched or exceeded established brands in features, function, and assist performance. Suddenly, longtime players were off the back, some way off the back.

Sources indicate that before they could catch up, Avinox followed the M1 with the more powerful, refined M2S: up to 150 Nm of torque and 1,500 watts of peak power. But power isn’t the whole story. Senior features director Louis Mazzante says the M2S “isn’t the thunderously loud, chassis-shaking hot-rod motor that its power suggests. It is quiet. It’s smooth. It’s refined.” He also praises its feature-packed, easy-to-use app and touch-screen controls, and says the motor’s power is smooth and tractable.

Recent findings suggest that that blend of power, control, and features has made the M2S highly desirable to bike brands. Ari’s Wire Peak 3.0 stands out as an affordable way to get it.

Starting at $4,999, the Wire Peak pairs the M2S with an 800Wh battery in an aluminum frame with 150mm of rear travel and a 160mm fork. This setup delivers up to 150 Nm of torque in Boost mode and 1,300 watts of peak power. The bike also has a four-bar suspension design, 29-inch or mullet wheel compatibility, and independent high/low and long/short geometry adjustments.

Ari delivers each bike directly to the buyer with a rider-specific setup. Buyers can customize the build through the configurator, and Ari will accommodate most off-menu parts and upgrade requests.

After his first rides on his long-term test bike, senior test editor Matt Phillips called the chassis excellent, Ari’s buying process superb, and the drive unit best in class. He states the Wire Peak would be his choice if he were buying an e-MTB today.

Industry observers note that the DRT 1.1 (from REI’s in-house Co-Op Cycles brand) is a good pick if you’re looking for an electric mountain bike to explore mellower trails and ride around town. REI equips the bikes with a dependable Bosch Performance Line mid-drive motor and internal battery.

This hardtail rolls on tubeless-compatible 27.5-inch wheels with 2.6-inch-wide Maxxis Rekon tires for off-road capability. The DRT’s 100mm-travel SR Suntour fork with thru axle isn’t glamorous, but it works. The only notable component missing is a dropper seatpost; it would enhance the bike’s trail capability and help riders feel more confident on challenging terrain.

Recent findings suggest that traditional analog mountain bikes are usually grouped by frame travel. E-MTBs, on the other hand, are categorized by their power. However, more power ≠ more better. Pick the style that suits your riding needs, budget, and local trail access.

⚡️ Full-Power E-MTBs are the most common style and are generally equipped with roughly 750-watt peak power (1 horsepower) and 85 torque, or more. Bosch, Shimano, and Specialized are three commonly used motor brands for these bikes.

⚡️ Lightweight E-MTBs feature motors with less power and torque (50 to 60 Nm) and lower-capacity batteries. As a result, these bikes weigh less than other E-MTBs and ride more like an unassisted mountain bike, but with a little help on the climbs. Lightweight electric mountain bikes are less popular now than a couple of years ago, which means you can score good deals on great riding bikes.

⚡️ High-power e-MTBs are the newest category of electric mountain bikes, and they’re swiftly becoming one of the year’s most talked-about cycling trends. These motors produce more than 1,000 watts of peak power and 110 Nm of torque. Category leader Avinox’s latest unit delivers an incredible 1,500 watts and 150 Nm of torque. Its power and performance have prompted Bosch and Specialized to respond with firmware updates that boost the torque and power of their premium drive units. Even so, the Avinox remains the most powerful drive unit available. But high-power motors aren’t without detractors, or potential consequences. Their use has sparked debate and hand-wringing in the mountain biking community over how much power is too much. Remember: “With great power comes great responsibility.”.

When you’re shopping for an electric mountain bike, you must factor in not only the motor’s power and features, but also the bike’s basic capabilities.

Since electronic mountain bikes are heavier than non-motorized bikes, you’ll want to consider a bike with more suspension travel than you have on your non-motorized bike. The longer your travel, the more cushion you’ll get when you encounter obstacles.

Most full suspension E-MTBs are in the 150- to 160mm travel range, which offers a nice balance of increased comfort and improved control for first-time buyers.

Industry observers note that there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding on trail systems.

Sources indicate that class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows people to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Other countries classify e-bikes differently, and many countries do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Most performance-oriented electric mountain bikes are Class 1. Electric mountain bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Sources indicate that bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. A mid-drive motor will almost always offer more power. Because the extra weight on a mid-mount bike is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors. Mid-mount bikes do tend to be more expensive, but all of our favorite bikes feature this type of motor.

Battery Life, Range, Maintenance, and Safety.

According to recent reports, on top of the motor, you’ll want to consider the battery size and range. More is always better for performance, but a battery with a longer range will also weigh more and cost more.

Industry observers note that as a bike's weight increases, it requires more effort from the rider to handle. This is especially an important consideration for smaller riders; extra weight can also become a bigger challenge at faster speeds, when you need to ride the bike more aggressively.

A lighter bike will offer better handling, but if you sacrifice too much battery capacity to cut weight, you may find yourself pedaling home with no assist if you take a wrong turn.

Like all e-bikes, E-MTBs can be pedaled as a normal bike if the battery dies, so you’ll still be able to get home, but it will require extra effort and possibly more time.

According to recent reports, while we can confidently say a larger battery provides more range, it is difficult to accurately estimate any e-bike's exact range. Many factors impact an e-bike's range: How much boost you’re using (most power systems offer three or four settings), how much you weigh, the terrain you’re riding, how much climbing you’re doing, the air temperature, rolling resistance from the tires, and even how clean and lubricated the drivetrain is.

Don’t take any brand's word on its range claims. Start conservatively as you test your bike’s range. The more you ride, the better you’ll understand how far your batteries can carry you in different conditions. If your bike’s main battery isn’t cutting it, some models let you add an external range booster or swap the internal battery for a fresh one. Be warned: These accessories can be expensive!

Industry observers note that like all batteries, e-bike batteries do lose capacity every time they’re charged and discharged. Unfortunately, that means that the more you ride, the sooner you’ll need to replace your battery. Even so, an e-bike battery should give you years of reliable riding.

Follow your bike's manufacturer’s recommendations for storage, but most batteries will last longer if stored with about a 40-percent charge (but don’t forget to plug your bike in about six hours before riding, to make sure you start your ride with a full charge).

It has been revealed that batteries should also be stored at room temperature whenever possible and not left outside or in an unheated garage in freezing temperatures. Some bike brands, including Specialized, have a setting that will prevent the battery from charging fully. This feature is designed to extend the battery’s life, but you may want to disable the feature if the rides you regularly take use your battery’s full capacity.

If, after a few years, your battery loses enough capacity that you want to replace it, be sure to contact your bike’s manufacturer or local dealer and purchase a certified replacement battery through the brand or its dealer.

Don’t be tempted by cheaper options available online from third-party brands. These third-party batteries are generally not certified by bike brands and may void your bike’s warranty. More importantly, third-party replacement batteries often do not have notable safety features, and, as a result, these batteries have been identified as the cause of several serious fires.

There is presently legislation pending at the state and federal level that will bar the sale of non-certified batteries in the U.S., but they are still available as of this writing.

In a recent development, while a handful of bicycle drivetrain manufacturers exist, almost every e-mountain bike will have either a Shimano or SRAM drivetrain. Both are reputable manufacturers that offer reliable shifting and a wide-ranging gear set. Some drivetrains feature electronic shifting. Such drivetrains offer quick and precise shifting, but they will add cost.

In a recent development, the added power of an e-bike puts more strain on a bike’s drivetrain. You can expect to replace your chain more frequently, but you can get more life out of your components if you back off the pedals when shifting, and ease the chain between gears instead of mashing the shifter and the pedal at the same time.

Industry observers note that given the increased weight of an electronic mountain bike, you’ll want to make sure yours is equipped with hydraulic disc brakes, as most are. These brakes offer lots of stopping power and modulation, which ensures you’ll remain in control regardless of your bike's weight, or how fast you go.

In a recent development, several brands offer hydraulic disc brakes, though again, Shimano and SRAM usually lead the way. For additional power, look for bikes featuring four-piston brakes.

Bicycling has been reviewing bikes and gear for over 50 years, and our recommendations are grounded in decades of real-world experience. Our test team—Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy, Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips, Test Editor Dan Chabonov, and Senior Photographer Trevor Raab—collectively brings 75-plus years of ride-testing knowledge to every product we evaluate.

For this guide to electric mountain bikes, Matt and Tara led the charge, drawing from their deep category expertise and the team’s hands-on testing across a wide range of terrain and conditions. These picks reflect what we’ve learned through thousands of miles of testing: The E-MTBs that deliver the right mix of price, ride quality, trail capability, and pedal-assist performance. Whether you’re climbing faster, riding farther, or just having more fun, these are the best electric mountain bikes you can buy right now.

With expert instruction from pro rider Chaz Turmon, this program features motivating follow-along video sessions and flexible workouts you can do almost anywhere to help you ride faster, train smarter, and watch your numbers climb.

This holistic program covers all the tips and tricks needed to improve your riding technique, master cadence, stack speed and endurance workouts, build strength off the bike, and fine‑tune gear in order to achieve the speed gains you dream about.

Watch as host Alison Tetrick takes you through everything you need to know to ride your first (or fastest) century. Along with other cycling experts, she explains how to find the best gear, build endurance, fuel your body during the ride, and much more.

Cycling is the best way to stay fit as you age. With the help of host Peter Abraham and other experts, you’ll learn everything you need to get started and stay riding into your golden years, including choosing a bike, finding a blueprint, and optimizing recovery.

Whether you’re constantly feeling aches or you want to maximize your performance gains, you need the right bike fit. With this guide, host Jenna Foley and certified bike fitter Jonathan Blyer walk you through the process and offer up DIY tips.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Newly introduced England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, my longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance. Those pedals have been effectively abused on everything from getting bashed through rock gardens to long dusty or muddy days on the gravel bike. A few years ago I got my first road bike and switched to a pair of Shimano SPD-SL pedals. Since then I’ve put that bike (and those pedals) through the wringer.

Industry observers note that I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on. This means my road pedals have seen similar abuse to my mountain bike and gravel pedals. They’re still in great shape, but they could use a little love. Even pedals only used for road riding will start to get gritty over time.

Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the fresh pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.

According to recent reports, after I saw the rollout, it felt like a good time to bring my old generation SPD-SL pedals back to life and while I’m at it, give you a few tips on the process. Here we’ll run through how to service your SPD-SL pedals in under 10 minutes and save you a few hundred dollars in the process.

A quick note on reinstalling the pedals back on the bike: make sure you put the right pedal on the right side and the left pedal on the left side. I know, this sounds obvious. I’ve seen the wrong pedal get forced into the wrong side of the crank too many times, damaging the crank and the pedals to the point that sometimes both need to be replaced. Sometimes pedals are marked with an “L” for left and “R” for right, but you can always double-check to see which way the threads go. Left pedal threads will go up to the left and right pedal threads go up to the right. Then when it is time to reattach the pedals, put some grease on the threads of the crank arm and begin to thread them on by hand instead of starting with the wrench. If you can’t begin to thread the pedal onto the crank threads by hand, double-check the pedal is on the correct side, make sure it’s going into the crank arm straight, and make sure there is no debris in the hole of the crank arm preventing it from threading.

#172851. The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

The Anti-Movement Core Routine Every Runner Needs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that glute bridge post-run.
  • Industry observers note that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a latest study on anti-movement vs.
  • It has been revealed that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

Industry observers note that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a latest study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

It has been revealed that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

Industry observers note that when we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

According to recent reports, why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly vital for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

When running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

Industry observers note that while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

While some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Recent findings suggest that even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

Enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an important role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

Sources indicate that runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

3 Restorative Yoga Poses for When You’re Stressed and Short on Time

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past problems beginning in 1975.
  • In a perfect world we would all have time for a long restorative yoga practice daily.
  • Traditionally, a yoga class or personal practice session begins with active poses followed by a brief restorative pose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past problems beginning in 1975. This article about restorative yoga poses appeared in the September-October 1995 problem of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

In a perfect world we would all have time for a long restorative yoga practice daily. But obligations to work, family, friends, and community often leave us with little time for self-care. It is precisely when we are the most stressed that we need to relax and renew ourselves, and bring some restorative yoga into our busy lives.

Traditionally, a yoga class or personal practice session begins with active poses followed by a brief restorative pose. However, the entire focus of this practice is on supported restorative poses.

To relax deeply in this amount of time, you must have a quiet room, but you can get by with a minimum of props. There are only three poses: Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose, Supported Child’s Pose, and Basic Relaxation Pose. Practice them in the order presented. If you can’t find even 15 minutes, practice Basic Relaxation Pose for five.

It has been revealed that this pose is simple to practice, even when traveling. Just lie on your back and let a nearby wall support your legs. This pose brings the blood and lymph fluid to pool in the abdomen, refreshing the leg muscles and enhancing the health of the circulatory system. In addition, the pose reverses the energy of the legs from moving down and out to the feet, as in our normal stance, to moving down and back to the pelvis. Nothing feels better to tired legs and feet than being elevated.

Sources indicate that setting Up. To begin, sit on the floor with one shoulder near the wall and your thighs parallel to the wall. Roll back as you swing your legs up the wall. Once in position, make sure that your lower back is not rounded and your tailbone and buttocks are not lifting off the floor. If they are, move slightly away from the wall so your lower back is comfortably supported by the floor.

If your chin lifts toward the ceiling, place a standard-fold blanket under your head and neck to support your cervical curve. Make sure your chin is slightly lower than your forehead, but do not force your chin down and flatten the back of your neck.

Sources indicate that keep your legs straight but relaxed. Place your arms out to your sides with the palms turned up. Close your eyes. Place an eyebag over them.

Being There. Take several long, slow breaths. As you do, imagine the fluid in your legs flowing down toward the abdomen. With it, all tension drains out of your legs. They begin to feel lighter and softer. Imagine that your brain is shrinking in size as it moves away from your forehead and sinks toward the back of your head and the floor. Feel your entire spine supported by the floor. The position of the arms creates a feeling of being open and free. Enjoy this feeling.

Coming Back. Practice Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose for five minutes. When ready, remove the eyebag and open your eyes. Rest for a few breaths before bending your knees toward your chest and rolling to one side. Pause again for a few breaths before slowly coming to a sitting position with the help of your arms.

In a recent development, benefits. Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose reduces swelling and fatigue in the legs.

Cautions: Do not practice this inverted pose.

Supported Child’s Pose is the familiar posture of rest and sleep for babies and young children. When you practice this pose, not only will it help to relieve tension in your lower back, but it may evoke a sense of security from your earliest days. This pose is one of introversion, one of curling up and reconnecting with feelings of support and release.

Setting Up. Begin by kneeling on a carpeted floor or blanket with your knees hip-width apart and your bolster in front of you. Use more padding under your knees and shins if you need it. To avoid stress on the ligaments of your outer ankles, point your toes directly backward and not toward each other. Sit back on your heels.

If you experience discomfort in your knees, ankles, or tops of your feet, come up and try one or both of the following adjustments. Place one towel, folded lengthwise, into the bend of your knees to create more space in the knee joints. Place the other towel, rolled lengthwise, under the front of the ankles, and let your feet hang over the roll. Experiment with the thickness of these folded and rolled towels to get them just right for you.

Sit back on your heels again. Separate your knees wide enough to place the bolster between your thighs. To enhance relaxation, hold a sandbag across your lower back as you bend forward. The weight of the bag helps to relax the muscles of your lower back.

It has been revealed that your torso should be completely supported by the bolster and your thighs. Your chest should rest easily on the bolster. Let your tailbone drop toward your heels. This action will lengthen your lower back as you relax. Your buttocks do not have to touch your heels.

If you need more support, try one of the following variations. Come up to a kneeling position and place a long-roll blanket on your heels and sit back, or come to a kneeling position and significantly raise the height of your torso support by adding one or more single-fold blankets. If you have difficulty breathing, push the bolster forward so it only supports your breastbone and lets your belly hang free.

It has been revealed that turn your head to one side and bring your chin slightly toward your chest. Turn it to the opposite side halfway through the practice of Supported Child’s Pose. If the side head position is uncomfortable, rest on your forehead and slightly tuck your chin toward your chest. Make sure you can breathe easily regardless of your head position.

It has been revealed that place your arms so they reach either back toward your feet or forward around the edges of the bolster. The position of the arms is unimportant; it is important that you are comfortable. Close your eyes.

Industry observers note that being There. Take several slow breaths. As you do, let your shoulders move away from the ears. Let your belly relax and feel supported. The counter-pressure of the bolster on the belly may feel especially good if you have menstrual cramps.

Coming Back. Practice Supported Child’s Pose for three minutes. Be sure that you spend equal time with your head turned in both directions. Open your eyes. Reach back with one hand and slide the sandbag off your back and to one side. Place your palms on the floor, under your shoulders. Press your hands into the floor, inhale, and sit up slowly onto your heels. Rest for a moment. Come to a kneeling position and immediately bring one leg forward, placing your foot on the floor. Press your hands on the forward thigh, and inhale deeply as you come to a standing position. Coming out of the pose in this way prevents discomfort in the knees.

It has been revealed that benefits. Supported Child’s Pose gently stretches the lower back, relieves shoulder tension, and quiets the mind.

Cautions: Do not practice this pose.

Recent findings suggest that this pose is the heart of restorative practice. Relaxing completely, even if it is only for five minutes, is one of the most important skills you can acquire. When you have learned to relax whenever and wherever you need to, you can use this skill in a variety of situations to reduce stress and its accompanying fatigue.

According to recent reports, the less time you think you have for spending a few minutes a day in Basic Relaxation Pose, the more you need to do it. If you do nothing else for your health every day, make time for this pose. Practice it, for example, at an afternoon break at work, when you first come home from work, after a workout session, or whenever you feel depleted, exhausted, or stressed.

Setting Up. In Basic Relaxation Pose you will be lying on your back with your arms out to the sides and your legs comfortably apart. Give yourself enough floor space to spread out comfortably. Before you lie down, position a standard-fold blanket for your head and neck to rest on.

Begin by sitting on the floor. If you have a tendency to get cold, cover your legs with an unfolded blanket. Now turn to one side and lean on your elbow and forearm as you slide onto your side. Then roll onto your back. Coming into the pose in this way is less stressful on your back than leaning back into a reclining position.

Industry observers note that roll the long edge of your standard-fold blanket slightly to support the gentle curve of the neck. Adjust the prop placement so that your neck is comfortable. Your chin should be slightly lower than your forehead. This position quiets the frontal lobes of the brain. If you are using an extra blanket for warmth, now is the time to pull it up to cover your torso and arms. Cover your eyes with an eyebag.

Recent findings suggest that many people can practice this pose lying flat on the floor. If you have tension or pain in your abdomen or lower back, place a long-roll blanket under the backs of your knees before you lie down. Make sure that your legs are relaxed and the knees supported by the long-roll blanket. If your heels do not touch the floor, place a folded blanket or pillow under them. If your lower back discomfort persists, come out of the pose by following the instructions under Coming Back (below). Resume your practice of Basic Relaxation Pose when you feel ready.

Once you have established yourself, observe the position of your body. Your arms and legs should be equidistant from an imaginary line drawn from the tip of your nose to exactly midway between the feet. Most people practice with the palms turned upwards, but if this is not comfortable, turn them down and let the elbows relax. The most important thing is that you feel completely at ease and supported by the props and the floor. If you need to sit up to adjust props and lie down again, follow the instructions for Coming Back and Setting Up.

In a recent development, being There. Swallow and relax your lower jaw. Soften your upper eyelids and look down toward the lower lids as you close your eyes. Let your cheeks feel hollow and loose beneath the cheekbones. Release the root of your tongue. Your fingers will curl naturally as your hands relax. Let your legs roll outward. Allow the entire back of your body to feel at ease and in complete contact with the floor and the props.

Your arms and legs will feel longer and longer, as well as heavier. Feel the large muscles of the legs, buttocks, and trunk drop away from the bones. Now feel the smaller muscles of your arms, neck, and head as they seem to move away from the bones. Let the bones themselves feel heavy and the skin loose, all over your body. Notice that the abdominal organs seem to nestle gently back into your body. Savor the silence.

Sources indicate that the Centering Breath. As you continue to rest, notice when you begin to feel lighter. This is a signal that your body has relaxed and that you can begin the Centering Breath: a long inhalation followed by a long exhalation, followed by several cycles of normal breathing.

According to recent reports, begin by slowly inviting the inhalation to move more deeply into your body. Do this by lifting your ribs slightly and spreading your lungs. Let the air come to you. As you inhale, imagine that the breath breathes you. Follow the inhalation with a soft focus on the exhalation. Feel your diaphragm, lungs, ribs, and muscles of respiration contracting to press the breath out in a steady and focused stream. When your exhalation is finished, breathe several normal cycles of inhalation and exhalation.

Then inhale slowly and deeply once again. At the fullness of inhalation, pause slightly before melting the inhalation into an equally long and steady exhalation. The inhalation is the receptive part of the breath; the exhalation is the active part. Once again, take several normal cycles of breath.

Once you have established the rhythm of the long breaths, pay particular attention to the quality of these breaths. What is their texture? Is the beginning of inhalation as soft as the end of inhalation? Is the end of exhalation as smooth as the beginning? With each cycle, allow your breath to become more and more refined, like the texture of fine silk.

Industry observers note that remember, never strain or force the breath. If at any time you feel even slightly agitated or out of breath, simply return to normal breathing. Once you feel calm, resume the cycle of long, slow inhalation and exhalation, followed by several normal breaths.

The success of the Centering Breath is not measured by how much air you can take in or let out. So go slowly, gently, and be present with the process. If you feel fatigued, anxious, or light-headed during practice, it is an indication that you have practiced long enough. Let your breathing return to normal, and, in the future, take longer breaks of normal breathing between each round of long inhalation and long exhalation. Do not practice the Centering Breath if you have a fever, a bad cold, sinusitis, or more serious respiratory diseases, such as pneumonia.

In a recent development, repeat the Centering Breath for up to 10 rounds. Be sure to leave some time for normal breathing before coming out of the pose.

Coming Back. Remain in Basic Relaxation Pose for five to 20 minutes. To come out of the pose, bend one knee and roll onto your side. Let the eyebag fall off by itself. Gradually open your eyes. Rest in this position for a few breaths. To sit up, press the floor with the elbow of your lower arm and the palm of the hand of your upper arm. Sit quietly for several breaths before standing up and resuming your normal activities.

Sources indicate that benefits. Basic Relaxation Pose lowers blood pressure and heart rate, releases muscular tension, reduces fatigue, improves sleep, enhances immune response, and helps to manage chronic pain.

Recent findings suggest that cycling radar entirely changed my bike rides. After a speeding pickup passed dangerously close to me on a ride in June 2025, I installed a radar system on my road bike. Since getting a radar, I have ridden over 7,500 miles on paved and gravel roads, and I’ve had a radar mounted on my bike for almost all of them—I cannot imagine riding without it. It’s the best safety upgrade I’ve made in more than three decades of riding and something every road and gravel rider should try.

For Black Friday, Garmin—the market leader in cycling radar—has its two top-performing Varia radar systems on sale. This includes the benchmark RTL515 and the new RearVue 820 released earlier this year. Both are exceptional radar units, and our top-tested models—but which one is best for you, or as a holiday gift for a cyclist in your life?

SHOP MORE GARMIN DEALS SHOP MORE GEAR DEALS.

Garmin Black Friday Radar Deals.

Above: Test Editor Dan Chabanov digs into all of the details in this video.

All cycling radar systems work essentially the same. The radar unit emits pulses of electromagnetic radio waves that bounce off vehicles approaching from behind before returning to the device. Using the reflected beams, the device calculates and tracks vehicles’ distance, direction, and relative speed, and sends that tracking data to your cycling computer. The head unit then provides an audible warning and graphically displays vehicles’ relative location and speed, giving you time to react accordingly. Most devices also integrate the radar with an LED taillight to alert drivers to your presence.

What separates good radar units from bad ones is the proprietary algorithms each brand uses to tune sensitivity and detection for their respective devices. A good radar consistently provides clear warnings of approaching vehicles, but bad ones can provide frequent false alarms, or worse, fail to warn of an approaching vehicle.

In the year and a half since I started using a radar light on my rides, I’ve ridden a dozen radar systems from nine brands. Several work well and I use them on my bikes, and a few of them were duds. However, of all of the cycling radars we’ve tried, none are as consistently reliable as Garmin’s Varia models.

According to recent reports, picking the Varia model that’s best for you (or a rider whose safety you care about) depends on a few factors. Both are excellent units, but why overpay for tech you can’t use or don’t need on your rides?

The RTL515 is the benchmark cycling radar system, and we judge all others against it. The 515 works more reliably than any other radar we tested—Other systems might have longer battery life, weigh less, or pack a brighter light, but none are as well-rounded or as easy to use as this Garmin. It detects vehicles up to 153 yards away, and its 65-lumen flash is visible to drivers from 1.2 miles.

The 515 packs up to 8 hours of battery life per charge, and weighs 72 grams (without a mount). It connects to most cycling computers featuring Bluetooth or ANT+ compatibility, but Garmin’s Varia radar phone app is also stellar. If you ride with your phone on your bar, it can serve as a display, and it can deliver audio notifications through headphones even if you’re not listening to music or a podcast.

In a recent development, garmin’s newest cycling radar improves on the Varia RTL515’s greatness. Compared to the 515, the RearVue 820 has more battery life (up to 15 hours), a brighter flashing light (100 lumens), and greater vehicle-detection range (up to 191 yards). Plus, the 820 adds a brake-light feature that increases rear light intensity as you slow.

Crucially, the RearVue 820 incorporates features found on no other radars (from Garmin or any other brand). While other radars often drop vehicles when they slow down behind you, the 820 tracks vehicles traveling at your same speed; it’s a handy feature you don’t know you need until you try it. Additionally, if you use a Garmin Edge X40- or X50-series computer, the radar tracks a vehicle that changes lanes behind you. It also shows icons to indicate each vehicle’s size (small, medium, or large).

The RCT715 is basically the RTL515 with a rear-facing camera. However, it is larger, heavier, and has a shorter battery life than the 515. It’s so heavy (148 grams) that it requires a proprietary mount. The camera also greatly reduces battery life—in continuous video mode, it might not last through long rides. However, the 715 is worth considering for bike commuters, riders who advocate for better cycling infrastructure, or those who want peace of mind.

Sources indicate that in 1977, the Vantage was the first Brooks shoe to top our charts. The running renaissance began several years prior, when Frank Shorter won the 1972 Olympic marathon in Munich. Two years later, the shoe industry would be changed forever with the introduction of ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) foam, which was lighter, softer, and had more rebound than the rubbers used in midsoles around that time. Our editors knew Brooks had a winner when we tested the Vantage.

According to recent reports, almost half a century later, the brand is still dazzling us with its innovations and earning prizes in the 2026 Runner’s World Shoe Awards. And to think the manufacturer started out more than a hundred years ago manufacturing ballet slippers and bath shoes.

In a recent development, since the 1970s, Brooks has solely focused on upping the ante in shoe tech. The Vantage also introduced the varus wedge, which was basically a medial post used to help with instability caused by overpronation. Now the varus wedge is dated and has been replaced with Brooks’s “GuideRails” system. EVA is also being phased out with improved foams that are bouncier and even softer.
