Sources indicate that brooks has categorized its shoes to help runners choose the best pair that fits their running style and preferred experience. I’ve been a Brooks die-hard since my high school days. For the past 20 years, I’ve been keeping tabs on product updates and saying goodbye to discontinued lineups (taps for the PureProject minimalist list). Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

One helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Sources indicate that through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

Industry observers note that runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

At the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

In a recent development, for runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Sources indicate that before the Adrenaline GTS rolled out in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

Recent findings suggest that in 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Sources indicate that now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Guide rails offer unobtrusive support for both overpronators and neutral runners.

Our lab tests show that DNA Loft remains Brooks’s softest midsole material.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

The most responsive expression of Brooks’s DNA foam debuted on the Hyperion Tempo.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

In a recent development, we always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

  • Sources indicate that so when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant. The two bottles bounced loosely against my chest, with water leaking down my shirt throughout the run. It was not a flattering look. Every step came with its own sloshing soundtrack. I spent so much time adjusting the thing (despite an across-the-chest strap) that I barely enjoyed my run.

Sources indicate that so when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from. During a Reddit AMA hosted by BBC Sport, the Scottish middle-distance star, who casually broke the mile world record in July with a 3:42.66 finish, shared his thoughts on the growing popularity of running vests.

"I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr said, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.

For context, we're talking about a world-record holder, Olympic medalist, and world champion in the 1500 meters. He knows a thing or two about logging miles. And while 12 miles might look quite different on his watch than mine, I don't think his suggestion was particularly outrageous.

And because everything is contested on the internet, plenty of people disagree.

Runner @natalie.the.capn shared Kerr's comments on Threads and explained that she wears a hydration belt on every outing so she has somewhere to keep her phone, particularly in case of an emergency. "Funny how men rarely think of that," she wrote.

According to recent reports, I do understand her concern. I'm a guy, so I'm definitely not going to pretend I have the same safety considerations that women often face while exercising alone. I also bring my phone everywhere, usually carrying it in my hand because iPhones only get bigger and the pockets on most of my running shorts haven't kept up.

She also pointed out that some of her routes take her six miles or more between places where she can get water, which is an entirely different experience from mine.

I live in New York City, where Central Park has plenty of water fountains (that work ... most of the time) and there's usually a deli within walking distance to snag a Gatorade. I can see why Kerr's approach makes sense here, especially for shorter runs. I've also tried handheld bottles and waist straps, and neither has been particularly enjoyable. Between the bouncing, adjusting, and occasional hand cramps, I'd love to carry as little as possible in my hands.

That changes a lot during marathon training, something I've put myself through four times now, when I'm out for considerably longer and need water to wash down those pasty gels. Aside from the hydration aspect, stopping to buy something, pausing my watch, and interrupting my stride halfway through a long run is a vibe killer.

In a recent development, and I'm certainly not arguing against being prepared. I learned the hard way that sunscreen deserved a permanent spot in my prerun routine after years of neglecting it ended with some casual skin cancer surgery.

In a recent development, the Threads debate, naturally, has brought out some pretty different opinions. One commenter, siding with Kerr, wrote, "Yeah im gonna listen to the guy who runs for a living but thanks." Others pointed out that beginners, slower runners, and people training in hot weather could have very different hydration needs.

They're definitely right about that. Twelve miles is a long way for plenty of runners, no matter what their experience level, and access to water, weather, pace, and individual needs all change the equation. Kerr even acknowledged that people have different reasons for carrying gear, something that seems to have gotten a little lost as his comments made their way around social media.

Sources indicate that I still think he has a fair point about how much equipment we sometimes convince ourselves we need on a run. That said, if your vest makes your runs more comfortable or gives you peace of mind, by all means wear it. For me, I'll be keeping my phone close and bringing an appropriate amount of water when I need it.

As for my hydration vest, it's been collecting dust ever since that first outing, and I haven't missed it one bit.

6 Myths About Max Heart Rate Cyclists Need to Stop Believing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1497 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that to dial in your training, it’s vital to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides.
  • It has been revealed that the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr.
  • Over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that to dial in your training, it’s vital to know how to calculate your max heart rate because understanding this metric will help you stay within to right intensity on your rides. The catch? The most common formula for calculating max heart rate is not very accurate.

It has been revealed that the formula, which is 220 minus your age, was developed by Dr. William Haskell and Dr. Samuel Fox in 1970, and it wasn’t necessarily validated by research and involved data from a wide mix of people, including those with heart disease and smokers. As a result, the formula tends to overestimate max heart rate for younger people and underestimate it for older adults.

Over the years, researchers have found other, slightly more accurate max heart rate calculations, like the Tanaka equation: 208 minus (0.7 x age). However, it’s still a rudimentary system—like, “might as well use an abacus as a bike computer” rudimentary, claims Cherie Miner, M.D., a sports medicine specialist in Birmingham, Alabama. “It’s been the standard for years, but there are a lot of variables that can throw off your max heart rate.” Some of those variables: how fit you are, how hot it is, and how much stress you’re under.

Because of these variables, there are also a lot of myths surrounding max heart rate. Here, we debunk some of the most common ones so you can get to know your heart, and use your metrics to train efficiently.

Industry observers note that you’ve got to admit: This is equally horrifying and comical. But you can rest easy because it won’t actually happen.

It has been revealed that “Most people have one to two minutes at their max heart rate—highly-trained athletes may have more,” Miner indicates. Expect to see your performance suffer very swiftly if you try and maintain your max heart rate for more than just a short burst. Fortunately, years of evolving to survive prevents us from actually killing ourselves.

The old-school formulas assume that it is the same, but Golich says it’s much more nuanced than that. Max heart rate is largely untrainable and determined by genetics—some of us have hearts tuned like humming birds’ while others have the slow-and-steady type.

Industry observers note that although not perfectly accurate, age-based formulas give athletes an easy and accessible way to find a rough baseline of their max without undergoing rigorous (or sometimes dangerous, in the case of a sedentary person) testing. That mentioned, The American College of Sports Medicine suggests age-based formulas with a lower standard deviation, for example, the Gelish equation: 207 minus (0.7 x age) or Tanaka: 208 minus (0.7 x age).

No matter which way you calculate it, your max heart rate is not an indication of performance, Golich notes. “If your max is 200, and someone else’s is 190, it doesn’t mean one of you is the better athlete.” In fact, Golich has worked with numerous talented athletes at both ends of the spectrum.

Industry observers note that it’s good to remember that everyone’s max heart rate does drop as they age—but again, that doesn’t mean you’re losing fitness. Regular training and good nutrition will affect performance more than the fact that your max heart rate is now slightly lower than it was three years ago.

Recent findings suggest that in reality, it’s not your max heart rate that determines your fitness level. Being able to hold your max heart rate for longer and longer sessions is what’s key.

Heart rate is a reaction to work being done, not a measurement of actual work. For example, Golich indicates that if you ratchet yourself up to 200 watts (wattage measures your cycling power) for three minutes, for the first minute, your heart may tick along at 170 beats per minute (bpm). By minute two it may be at 180 bpm, and by minute three you could be pushing 189. But you’re doing the same amount of work the whole time: 200 watts.

If you were to ride for three minutes with the intention of maintaining the same heart rate, things would look different. Say you ramped up to 180 bpm to start—you might ride at 200 watts for the first minute, but you’d likely have to drop your watts to sustain that heart rate for minutes two and three.

Golich notes he prefers to have his clients train with power meters or using rate of perceived exertion (RPE)—a personal appraisal of how hard you feel you’re working—rather than heart rate.

“There are a lot of grey areas with heart rate,” he says, adding that being overheated, under-fueled, or even just hopped up on caffeine will throw your heart rate numbers off for the day.

Sources indicate that furthermore, the number displayed by your heart rate monitor or the screen on a gym treadmill may not be accurate. Sure, using a computer is certainly more accurate than the 220-minus-age formula, but Golich adds that because these devices take measurements every few seconds, they’re probably not dead-on.

If you really want to know your true max heart rate, an EKG is one way to go or a cardiopulmonary exercise test for even more accurate measurements, both of which require a visit to your doc or a lab.

It has been revealed that also, if you think that unless you’re hitting your max heart rate on every ride, you’re not working hard enough, here’s your license to chill. Max heart rate workouts should be done sparingly, Miner indicates, since the ultra-high intensity can lead to injuries, extreme fatigue, and other symptoms of overtraining.

In a recent development, plus, there’s merit to working in many different heart rate zones—from increasing your base fitness with low-intensity sessions to pushing the boundaries at your lactate threshold, and even tipping into some anaerobic work. If you only have two speeds—hard and harder—you’re doing yourself a disservice.

Recent findings suggest that heart attacks, while rare, happen to athletes at all different workloads. Even so, cardiologist James Beckerman, M.D., notes you’re slightly more at risk when working at very high intensities.

“This is likely related to a combination of high heart rate, higher blood pressure with exercise (which is normal), and higher levels of catecholamines (hormones produced by the adrenal glands),” he says. “For people without heart disease, exercising at higher intensity is generally safe.”.

If you’re someone with heart disease or who has exhibited risk factors, however, it’s a good idea to talk to your doctor about safe heart rate ranges for exercise and even get a stress test, he notes.

In a recent development, you’re not mistaken—your max heart rate for cycling really may be different than your max for another sport. Again, this is indicative of how variable heart rate is, Golich states.

Recent findings suggest that activities that are load bearing—like running—will generally push your heart rate higher, because you have to do more work to overcome gravity. Cycling, because it has the mechanical assistance of the bike, will generally produce a lower max heart rate. And swimming, which happens in a pool with zero-impact, may be lower still—since the water is keeping you cool, Golich states, heat will be less of a factor in raising your heart rate.

According to recent reports, what exactly is heart rate reserve? According to Miner, heart rate reserve is the difference between maximum heart rate and resting heart rate.

According to recent reports, your heart rate reserve can actually be a good measurement of how fit you are overall. “A higher heart rate reserve indicates better physical fitness,” she indicates. That’s because, unlike maximum heart rate, a lower resting heart rate is associated with better fitness. “If your resting heart rate is lower, then your heart rate reserve will be higher,” Miner says.

Recent findings suggest that tamanna K. Singh, M.D., is a board-certified adult clinical and sports cardiologist and RRCA-certified run coach. She earned her medical degree from Boston University School of Medicine and completed her Internal Medicine Residency at Boston Medical Center. She completed her Cardiovascular Medicine fellowship at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, Latest York, New York and her specialty training in Sports Cardiology at Massachusetts General Hospital. She is at the moment the codirector of the Sports Cardiology Center at Cleveland Clinic in Cleveland, Ohio and assistant professor of medicine at the Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine of Case Western Reserve University. To date, she has held several council roles with the American College of Cardiology (ACC). As a sports cardiologist, Dr. Singh provides cardiovascular care for professional, competitive, and recreational athletes and describes herself as an advocate for safe participation in sports. Media and print contributions include the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Time Magazine, and others. Outside of her profession, she enjoys running marathons, hitting the weights in the gym, playing sous-chef to her wonderful husband while cooking plant-based meals, and playing with her four beautiful dogs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If leaving isn’t an option—just kidding, we know you probably want to be there—there are ways to find grounding and calm within your own being.
  • Industry observers note that these yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva).

In a recent development, certain seasons come with a lot, and we mean a lot, of socializing. On the one hand, this means a chance to spend quality time with family and friends, which is always a win. But if you deal with any amount of social anxiety, gatherings can also come with stress and general overwhelm.

If leaving isn’t an option—just kidding, we know you probably want to be there—there are ways to find grounding and calm within your own being. You can practice breathwork, take a walk, even excuse yourself and enjoy a yoga pose or two for a minute. Or, if you resonate with the asanas on this list, perhaps five!

Industry observers note that these yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible. Escape for a few moments to try one of the more involved poses or enjoy a super subtle modification mid-party!

Holiday gatherings tend to involve a fair amount of standing around—which is where your casual Tree Pose (Vrksasana) comes in. Popping one foot up—whether against your upper or lower leg or, more stealthily, your ankle—can be done at literally any time: while you’re doing the dishes, chatting with loved ones, or experiencing a lull in activity. The reminder that you’re in control of your sense of balance can help you feel steadier on your own two feet in all ways.

Recent findings suggest that social gatherings can feel all over the place, making grounding of all kinds welcome. Sinking into Squat (Malasana) calls for strength and stability. And though households all over the world perform chores and even eat meals in this pose, if you need some privacy to find stillness in a deep squat, we’re sure that your family will understand if you disappear for a minute or two.

According to recent reports, folding forward can provide a sense of tremendous release and relief. Hinging at your hips in Standing Forward Bend (Uttanasana) and allowing your head and upper body to hang heavy—sometimes referred to as Rag Doll—serves as a subtle inversion, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and encouraging calm. Plus, this pose is normal enough to fold into at any point. Just tell your people that you need a quick stretch.

Sources indicate that finding strength within yourself can make chilling out a little easier. Pressing up—or jumping back—into Plank Pose activates your core, arms, and legs, then asks you to pause. Turning your focus toward this physical task, whether for a few breaths or a full minute, can help snap you out of an anxious spin and get you back into a celebratory state.

Sometimes, the best thing you can do is retreat to a spare bedroom (or the couch or the floor) and lie down for a while. Savasana can certainly provide some calming release, but for something a little more likely to get you out of your head and into your body, try Reclining Bound Angle Pose. It’s a subtle stretch that rejuvenates without being daunting—sort of like a best-case-scenario social engagement.

#172840. This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success.
  • Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World.
  • Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success. Go out too hard and you may struggle to hold on. Run too conservatively and you might miss your goal finish.

Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World. One workout he recommends for building this skill is a fartlek he learned from fellow run coach Brad Hudson, his coauthor on the book, Run Faster from the 5K to the Marathon: How to Be Your Own Best Coach.

Moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them. The goal? Building both aerobic fitness and a greater sense of pace control.

This workout helps improve your ability to settle into the right effort earlier, as well as enhance your capacity to hold those paces for longer—a perfect session for both optimizing your weekly speed run and helping you run your fastest race.

After an easy running warmup, you’ll run five faster segments, separated by an easy jog of the same duration.

Industry observers note that the base workout uses three target paces: 5K pace for the one-minute segments, 10K pace for the two-minute segments, and half-marathon pace for the three-minute segment. If you don’t know your race paces, you can also go off of rate of perceived exertion (RPE), with 10 equaling all-out effort. You should still be able to have a conversation around 4 RPE.

Fitzgerald says the workout should feel “fun hard,” meaning the faster running should feel challenging, but you shouldn’t finish the workout feeling like you just went all out in a race. Each surge is relatively short, so focus on hitting your intended effort rather than pushing as hard as you can.

More experienced, higher-volume runners can extend the pyramid to 1-2-3-2-1-2-3-2-1, again jogging for the same duration after each faster segment. This version includes 17 minutes of faster running and 17 minutes of recovery jogging, compared to just nine minutes of each in the original version.

In Fitzgerald’s experience, many runners tend to think of their effort in two broad categories: slow and fast, but this workout challenges that by demanding more care in differentiating between faster paces.

The one-minute 5K pace efforts should be faster than the two-minute 10K pace efforts, which should be faster than the three-minute half-marathon effort, explains Fitzgerald. The differences between these three paces are small—often just a few seconds per mile—so learning to recognize what each one feels like can help you become a more efficient and more confident runner.

Before each segment, think about the effort you’re trying to find. For the first one-minute interval, Fitzgerald suggests literally imagining that you’re starting a 5K race. You wouldn’t want to sprint the opening minute of that race and flame out, so resist that urge here, too.

In a recent development, try to settle into the right pace by feel, then use your watch to check and adjust. Over time, you’ll grow more attuned to the connection between how you feel and how fast you’re moving. “Your watch can’t [run the workout] for you,” Fitzgerald indicates. “It can tell you how fast you’re going. It can’t tell you how fast you should go.”.

Learning to run by feel translates to race day, when you want to hit your goal pace. Your body’s response to the conditions and the effort helps you decide how to proceed through each mile, slowing down or speeding up.

According to recent reports, this workout doesn’t ask you to spend a long time at any single pace. Instead, it gives you short exposures to several intensities within one session.

Hudson, who’s coached multiple Olympians and world-class athletes, tells Runner’s World that moving through a range of paces during a single workout helps with not only pace control, but also running economy or the energy required to run at a given speed.

According to recent reports, additionally, Hudson explains the continuous nature of the fartlek session gives it an aerobic emphasis because you never actually stop running throughout the entirety of the workout. “The faster portions [of the workout] increase oxygen demand, but as you go longer in a workout, the more it becomes aerobic, no matter what,” he indicates. “If you’re keeping the running continuous, the aerobic energy systems just keep going up and up and up.”.

In a recent development, fitzgerald agrees, although he also notes athletes get some anaerobic stress during the shorter, faster efforts. Think of it as a way to work on several aspects of your fitness at once, rather than a session designed to train just one. Plus, switching between paces can make the workout more mentally engaging than returning to the same effort over and over again.

The first time you try the workout, you might overshoot a target pace or find it difficult to feel the difference between efforts. That’s okay. Fitzgerald claims trial and error is an important part of developing the skill.

When you repeat the session, look for signs that your pacing is becoming more controlled: You start each segment closer to your intended effort, settle into a steadier rhythm, and maintain a clear difference between your 5K, 10K, and half marathon paces. You may also find it easier to keep your recovery jogs consistent.

The point is, you don’t need to nail every second of this workout. Learn from your mistakes, adjust when necessary, and remember Fitzgerald’s advice: “Progress over perfection.”.

It may be tempting to think of the easy jogs simply as passing time between hard segments. But both coaches emphasize the value of continuous running and implore runners not to lose focus during the recovery intervals.

According to recent reports, fitzgerald says teaching your body to recover from a faster effort while still moving presents a unique challenge. Your muscles must learn how to continue producing the energy needed to keep you running efficiently while your body works to recover from the harder interval at the same time. This adaptation translates directly to race day when you have to settle back into race pace after surging to pass another runner or gliding a little too fast down a hill.

Industry observers note that the key is paying attention to how your recovery intervals feel. If you have to slow them down more and more to prepare for the next segment, Fitzgerald says that may be a sign you’re pushing the faster portions too hard.

The beauty of this workout is if you realize you’ve gone out too quickly, you can easily adjust so you can still complete the workout. If you overcooked one of your speedier segments, Fitzgerald suggests tacking on another minute or so to the easy jog until you breathe easier and lower your heart rate—then adjust your effort level on the next interval.

Because the workout touches several intensity levels, Fitzgerald recommends it during base training or in the off-season. It can help runners maintain well-rounded fitness before they begin building toward a more specific goal.

It can also work as the de facto speed workout during a lighter training week or serve as a secondary quality workout during half-marathon or marathon training. In this case, the session offers a chance to maintain some faster running while the biggest emphasis remains on your long runs and race-specific efforts.

It has been revealed that hudson uses the workout as a key tool in returning to training post-marathon. After a week off, he generally has his athletes begin with easy running. Then, he adds this workout as a way to reintroduce different intensity levels and prepare his athletes for more demanding work ahead.

Whenever you use it, keep its purpose in mind: It’s designed to help you practice changing gears and build general fitness, and using it to support key workouts specifically tailored to your next race makes it even more effective.

Sources indicate that matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

#172839. Triathlon as the Fresh Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2968 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Triathlon as the Fresh Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities.
  • In a recent development, what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon?
  • From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities. (Photo: Courtesy Alexa and Branden Scheel, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson, Hannah Bradbury, Hilary Topper, and Kyla Lupo).

In a recent development, what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon? You could throw up your hands in defeat and frustration over the bro culture and inclusion challenges, vowing to train in solitude like a spandex-clad, multisport monk. Or … you could start your own tri club, team, group ride, or clinic.

From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.

When Altitude Multisport Club, a tri club in Denver, Colorado, was founded in 2010, the board consisted of all men.

In a recent development, “While friendly, it had a very ‘bro’ vibe and club events were rarely organized by leadership and club meetings were salesy,” notes Erin Trail, Altitude Multisport Club’s former president and current volunteer. “What did it for me was a no-drop group ride that the current president and coaching director were on. I had done three Ironman races, and they dropped ME. I knew the route and was fine, but I thought: ‘What if I was a new person? What kind of experience would this be?’”.

Since the president was term-limited, Trail was able to step up as president in 2016 to change the atmosphere to a friendlier, more inclusive one.

“That first year was very hard. I decided to make the club more inclusive and friendly to beginners and women, eliminating sales or conflict of interest issues and improving communications,” Trail indicates. “I lost a LOT of club friends because I wanted to make things different. Half my board quit because they didn’t want to be held accountable. But in my first year as president, membership grew from 50 to 150 members!”.

Today, Altitude Multisport Club features winter Sunday pool swims with a coach and travel camps to Moab and a local state park in addition to regular training and racing activities.

In a recent development, “My second term as president was much better, with a diverse board that I handpicked. We added a family membership so households, including kids, could join at a group rate,” Trail says. “And we made it clear that the environment is welcoming, organized, and a safe space to learn for everyone.”.

“A LOT of skinny white men. That’s what I saw in triathlon. I didn’t see enough women, and I really didn’t see anyone who was bigger. I realized that if I wanted to see more folks that looked like me, I had to be the coach that made triathlon a place for all folks, regardless of size, shape, color, or anything else,” claims Kyla Lupo, who took things into her own hands, getting certified as a coach, learning everything she could, and starting her team, Go Major!, with just one athlete and “a bunch of friends pretending to be my team.” Since then, Go Big! has grown to 22 athletes.

“Our team makes a point to let folks know that they are already loved, exactly as they are. Team Go Big! stands for a radical level of body inclusivity, both in sport and the world,” Kyla says. “On Team Go Big!, we work to overcome our fear and doubts while getting fit and ready for the start line. Anyone can tri in the body they have right now.”.

It has been revealed that social connection is crucial to the Go Big! community and takes the form of weekly team meetings where members from around the country learn, share their goals, ask for support, and expect accountability.

In a recent development, “We are from all over the country, but there’s a Tuesday morning virtual trainer ride to further connect us. And of course we get to party together at races,” Lupo indicates.

Disruptors: Alexa and Branden Scheel.

Recent findings suggest that people often join tri clubs to find community, only to discover that they are a small fish in a massive sea. When you’re one of hundreds of athletes, you and your journey can get lost in the mix.

Industry observers note that “My husband, Branden, and I were part of two different teams like that. We felt like ‘just another membership,’” Alexa Scheel indicates.

According to recent reports, so she and Branden pursued certifications from USA Triathlon and began building the kind of team they actually wanted to be part of. In 2023, the Scheels introduced Branden Scheel Racing, which focuses on athlete relationships and connection. Despite being a team with athletes around the world, the Scheels strive to make their team feel like family and make each athlete feel seen.

“If we don’t personally know something about each of the team members, we’ve grown too significant, which is why we sit between 100 to 150 members. We are committed to keeping this team on the smaller side,” Scheel claims. The beating heart of the team is its Facebook group, where athletes connect through monthly games and seminars, get answers to their most pressing questions, and find encouragement.

“On our team, every athlete stays until the last athlete completes their event because EVERYONE deserves to have someone cheering them on at the finish line. We’ve even had 15 people stay at the finish line for the midnight finish of Ironman Arizona for one of our athletes,” Scheel indicates. “Having a tri family on and off course to cheer for you and celebrate one of the best days of your life is a huge part of our team culture.”.

Disruptors: Jaclyn Fahey, Tara Hofmayer, and Sami Saad.

In a recent development, fifteen years ago, Jaclyn Fahey started a tri team through a bike store. As it evolved, Fahey recognized the need for a more affordable Long Island-based team, and Landshark Endurance was born.

“It began as a pizza-and-beer team with a triathlon problem, but Tara and Sami have helped take the lead. Because both are speech therapists and have the gift of gab, they’ve attracted a lot more members,” Fahey states. The open-level, co-ed multisport team supports members of all backgrounds with educational clinics and workshops, group workouts, and of course, social events that revolve around pizza and beer.

“By sharing our passion and experiences, we hope to show young athletes that success isn’t always measured by winning, but by perseverance, sportsmanship, and the courage to try,” Fahey notes. “You don’t have to be the fastest or the strongest. You just have to show up for yourself, put in the effort, and enjoy the journey. At the end of the day, the greatest part isn’t always crossing the finish line – it’s the people who help you get there.”.

It has been revealed that “I’m non-binary, and when I visit online triathlon groups and ask if there are any fellow non-binary athletes, it’s not uncommon that transphobes will flood the comments. I can only speak for myself, but the fear of discrimination, or being attacked verbally or worse, can be the most intimidating thing for non-binary and trans triathletes about tri clubs,” states Ruth Carter, a lawyer and triathlete. “There’s so much misinformation out there about trans women and non-binary athletes, as well as assumptions that are not supported by research.”.

When Carter couldn’t find a triclub that promoted equal participation and respect, they created Mutants & Masochists, a tri club that believes in equal participation, recognition, and respect for all triathletes, and advocates for non-binary and trans triathletes.

“We’re just getting started, but I hope the club is a place where trans people can connect, both online and in real life,” Carter says.

In 2023, Hannah Bradbury was training to break an open-water swim record when she was rushed to the ER for an emergency surgery to remove her gallbladder.

“My first thought when I woke up was, ‘When can I get back in the water?’ The answer was six weeks at least,” indicates Bradbury, who had already lost half of her thyroid to cancer in 2017. In an attempt to be part of sport in a way that cancer or a freak surgery couldn’t disrupt, Bradbury created Chicago’s North Avenue Swim and Triathlon Yo (NASTY) Instagram account to post about swimming until she could get back in the water. She also introduced book clubs and threw happy hours to create space for people to be more than just athletes, from cancer survivors to diabetic athletes striving to stay in sport on their own terms.

“Tri and swim clubs are great at training people. They’re not always great at holding onto people when they’re injured, sick, slow, starting over, or just burned out. I wanted to build a club that could hold everyone, from those winning the Chicago Triathlon to anyone rebuilding from injuries, or battling setbacks and the identity crises nobody warns you about when you’re sidelined,” notes Bradbury, who faced another cancer scare in 2023. “While I waited on the biopsy, my friends kept me distracted by doing a 100-mile ride with me, covered in glitter, that we called the ride Centuslay.”.

Fortunately, the biopsy came back negative, and the women’s century became an official NASTY tradition every fall.

Recent findings suggest that “Before NASTY I had a hard time making real friends with people who don’t just ask, ‘How was your swim?’ Through NASTY, I met friends who ask how they can show up for me,” Bradbury claims. “NASTY has grown to over 340 members, and through this community, people have found jobs through a swim or a random happy hour, and even fallen in love. Sport has become an accessory to our friendships, not the glue.”.

Recent findings suggest that “When I first got into triathlon in 2010, I was fortunate to have a warm, welcoming entry point into the sport. My goal with the T2 community is to pay it forward so others can also ease into the sport, learn to love it, and stay connected for the long haul,” says Bryan Mewes, who opened T2 Triathlon & Cycling, a triathlon-focused bike shop in Long Beach, California, in 2023. “The biggest hurdle for beginners is usually being overwhelmed by gear. That and the open-water swim. Once they realize that the shop is a space where they can comfortably ask questions and our group is built on encouragement rather than competition, that anxiety disappears fast.”.

According to recent reports, mewes explains that while it’s easy to say “everyone is welcome,” making sure someone is paired up with a partner at their pace or ensuring no one gets left behind takes actual effort that T2’s committed to making. Beyond the group rides, weekly runs, and bay swims, T2 brings people together off the course and keeps the vibe low-key and welcoming by hosting family dinners at local restaurants, beach days after races, and even a movie club.

“Some people only do our social events, while others only join our rides. What matters is that they participate in their way and see themselves as part of the community. That’s the core of T2. Training is just the anchor,” Mewes says.

Disruptors: Ruth Marie Oliver and Team Rocket’s Race Directors and Officers.

Team Rocket Tri Club (TRTC) is on a mission to promote a fit and healthy lifestyle. Every month, the club organizes a themed, post-brick social, and throughout the year, it hosts various races, from a beginner-friendly pool swim to a duathlon and sprint triathlons.

Industry observers note that during the summer months, TRTC hosts Tuesday night bricks featuring a multitude of pace groups, ensuring no rider is left behind and everyone has buddies to ride with. And in the winter, the focus is on swim clinics and winter trail running.

“Our club president, Ruth Marie Oliver, has done amazing things, including growing our membership to over 300 people,” claims Cynthia Mitchell, race director of TRTC’s Heel and Crank Duathlon.

To up the fun factor, TRTC has its own well-traveled bike box that members can borrow, adding their own sticker to its travel history and essentially bringing the whole team along for that athlete’s adventure. There’s also a TRTC hat that is at the moment “on tour.” It’s been spotted everywhere from Leeds, Alabama, to the head of Bob Babbit in Kona during the Ironman World Championship this year.

Disruptors: Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson.

In 2019, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson relaunched TriBabes WI, a women’s-only, USAT-certified team, to provide a community for women of all abilities and ages to train together.

“Some women join us purely to have the chance to work out with others for one, two, or all three sports. No matter what the sport or goal, we support each other without all the egos,” Merten claims. TriBabesWI makes aspects of triathlon like climbing hills, changing tires, nutrition, and making a race proposal less daunting through the clinics it offers. For TriBabe’s annual team triathlon, athletes can ride with a buddy for the bike portion.

It has been revealed that team offerings aren’t limited to the swim-bike-run. There are team hikes, skiing and snowshoeing in the winter, and opportunities to volunteer and shake a cowbell for others.

“We’ve donated our time and efforts to Breakthrough T1D, USAT triathlon events in Milwaukee, Ironman Wisconsin, and naturally Girls on the Run,” Merten claims.

“When I was new to this sport, I went for a bike ride with a triathlon group and got dropped within moments,” notes Topper, an author and coach who started WeREndurance in 2017. “If you’re just starting out, don’t look like everyone else, or just feel different from everyone, many clubs can feel elitist, especially when you get dropped. WeREndurance is nothing like that. It’s inclusive and diverse.”.

Recent findings suggest that as the group’s triathletes grew older and more injury-prone, however, WeREndurance membership began to drop, so Topper proposed transitioning from a strictly triathlon group to a lifestyle group. Now, WeREndurance members who live locally in Long Beach, New York, can participate in monthly hikes and quarterly races, as well as pool parties, holiday parties, diner breakfasts, and even a psychic night. Members who live out of state can stay connected through monthly meditation sessions, a book club, and monthly/bi-monthly educational webinars.

“These types of activities welcome everyone, including those who are injured or on the sidelines. This builds bonds and social connections,” Topper explains. “As you get older, you realize that sport is not only about being on the podium. It’s about community and having fun with your peers. The social aspect becomes just as notable as training and racing.”.

Disruptors: Brian Masayon, David Bahia, and Kristoffer Crisostomo.

In 2017, Masayon, Crisostomo, Bahia, and six of their friends formed a “silly” club to make training fun, and in doing so, others began taking notice.

“People started reaching out, asking how to join the team. I replied that there was no team. After the 20th inquiry or so, the nine of us decided to open 3P TRI to the public as a fun, drama-free group. That was in October 2017. By the end of the year, we had over 120 members join,” Masayon states. As word spread, the nonprofit tri club’s inclusive vibe attracted members from Canada, Australia, the Philippines, and Mexico.

While Ironman race entries cost athletes between $900 and $1,200, 3P TRI has removed the financial barrier entirely, offering clinics and free 140.6-mile races that are fully supported by the team.

Industry observers note that “There is no timing chip, so members are not pressured to prove how fast or slow they are. Instead, they train and then enjoy race day with their teammates,” Masayon notes. For 3P’s 140.6 triathlon, members come from different states to volunteer and help their teammates finish.

Industry observers note that “People are intimidated by tri clubs because they have this impression of triathletes as being fast, quick, and strong. Our members, however, come in all shapes and sizes, and this becomes an inspiration to many people,” Masayon adds. “Nobody talks about speed and ability. We don’t play the comparison game.”.

Five years ago, a group of New Jersey moms tried a mud run. They had so much fun that one run turned into a road race, followed by group bike rides, and finally dipping their nail-less toes into triathlons, despite the level of intimidation.

According to recent reports, “At a 5K, you’ll see everyone from Boston qualifiers to families participating together, sometimes with little kids in tow. Triathlons can seem like a different world from road or obstacle races. They require training and preparation across three disciplines, and the level of athleticism on display can be intimidating. Sometimes it feels like there are no actual beginners, just really accomplished athletes with super fancy bikes,” says Merino, adding that if someone shows up to ride with a mountain bike, they probably know it’s not the fastest option and don’t necessarily need unsolicited advice about upgrading. The same goes for swim form, running technique, or anything else. “If someone asks for pointers, we absolutely help them! Otherwise, the most encouraging thing we can do may be simply making them feel like they belong.”.

Sources indicate that “That’s what Team Thunderclap is all about. We might not have the fanciest gear or be the fastest people, but we show up, give it everything we’ve got, and probably laugh a whole lot along the way,” Merino says. “At the end of the day, most of us aren’t competing for Olympic medals. We’re ordinary people doing extraordinary things in our spare time.”.

Zwift’s Dedicated Indoor Bike Makes Your Winter Riding Better—and Protects Your Road Bike

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future.
  • It has been revealed that when I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future. It’s easy to use and reliable. It did exactly what I needed it to do—turn my bike into a trainer for offseason training.

It has been revealed that when I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use. More than that, every shop team I’ve worked with would use the Wahoo Kickr Core as their trainer of choice. Then I was introduced to the Zwift Ride and realized I was not done buying trainers just yet.

Sources indicate that as the shop’s service manager, I got firsthand experience assessing bikes after a season of sitting on the trainer; let alone season after season, year after year. The level of maintenance needed for those bikes was initially shocking to me as well as to the customer. Most of us are aware we need to do maintenance on our bikes that we ride outside, but it’s easy to forget about our unsung hero—our trainer bike sitting in the basement constantly covered in sweat, spilled drink mix, and getting the watts cranked into it day in and day out.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a better way than just throwing your bike on the trainer for your offseason. The Zwift Ride V2 with the Wahoo Kickr Core is now my top recommended way to use a bike trainer. It’s easy to see why.

Industry observers note that for those who have multiple riders in one house, this may be one of the biggest benefits. When I had my bike set up on the Kickr Core it was harder for my wife to just hop on the trainer. Since my old trainer bike was carbon, even a simple saddle adjustment required a torque wrench. I’ve even gone so far as to change out stems to change the reach too—not the hardest thing to do, but by no means convenient. On the Zwift Ride, most fit adjustments are super easy and take just seconds.

According to recent reports, the Zwift Ride 2 I’ve been on even has multiple crank length options set up in the cranks, so you just swap the pedals to a different hole in the crank to change the effective crank length. Taking out one more friction point between me and being able to start my trainer ride means I’m even more likely to get my winter trainer miles in.

In a recent development, the other day I was a few minutes into my warmup and I needed to adjust my reach a bit. I pulled the integrated 6mm Allen key out from its place under the top tube, easily adjusted the reach at the handlebars, tightened everything down, and reinstalled the tool all without interrupting my cadence. Having the tool I need to adjust just about anything on the bike is a latest level of convenience I was not used to.

As Matt Phillips pointed out in his Zwift Ride 2 review, “Mechanically, the Ride is almost primitive.” For clarity, this is by no means a negative—when it comes to a trainer bike, mechanically primitive but extremely functional is a best-case scenario. This bike has a chain that goes from the chainring, through a chain tensioner, around the Zwift Cog attached to the Wahoo Kickr, and back up to the chainring. There’s no derailleur, no front tire that needs air, no brakes to knock out of alignment. The handlebars don’t even turn, so there’s no headset to replace in the spring because it was sitting in a pool with sweat all winter.

On the other side, you’re saving your daily driver from a lot of unseen mechanical damage. As the snow thaws out on the roads, road riders are ready to get back in the saddle under the sun, but if you use your bike on the trainer all winter, it may need A LOT of love before it’s road-worthy.

Industry observers note that A bike that sits on the trainer all winter collects significant corrosion in headset and bottom bracket bearings. The sweat that comes off your head drops straight onto your headset and sweat from your body (and any of those sticky drink mixes) drop straight down toward the bottom bracket. Then we get to the drivetrain. I’ve had bikes come in around March that need full drivetrain replacement: chainrings, cassette, and chain after a good season of indoor miles. Finally, we get to the handlebar—at a minimum you should replace that bar tape after a season riding on the trainer. This also gives you a chance to get the handlebar looked at to make sure all that corrosion (sweat) hasn’t eaten into the them.

I’ve seen service tickets range anywhere from $100 to almost a thousand dollars just to get a bike off the trainer and ready to ride outside. For some people one season of trainer riding on the Zwift Ride 2 could be more cost-effective than using your road bike on a trainer.

In a recent development, before an activity becomes a habit people are good at finding reasons not to do something. It doesn’t take long to setup a bike on the Wahoo Kickr Core, but even that little bit of set up time to pop your bike on the trainer is one more hurdle for you not to ride today. If you have to swap your cassette over from your bike to the trainer—you can almost forget about it.

Industry observers note that it doesn’t just go for getting your bike on the trainer. This week in Pennsylvania we’re having a stretch of perfect riding weather—relatively low humidity, sunny, and temperatures between 55 degrees and 60 degrees. Next week’s forecast calls for colder temperatures and rain, also known as great indoor-riding weather. But this week, if I have a window of time to ride, I want to be able to just hop on my bike and go; I don’t want to have to take the bike off the trainer and reinstall my cassette before I can even start pedaling outside. With a dedicated trainer setup, I can just take my bike off the hook on the wall and roll away. Next week, when the weather goes south, I can just hop back on the trainer.

It has been revealed that the Zwift Ride makes it easier to do things like use power-ups, steer the avatar, and toggle through screens, but those features are just an added bonus compared to the other reasons to pick one up. It is a burly, simple, near-flawless machine for riding on the trainer. It’s stable when putting out your max watts. The built-in tool makes it easy to accommodate different riders—including adjusting the reach. Even the bottle cages are designed to fit almost any bottle. The bike’s handlebar tray fits an iPad or other tablet well, but I pair it with a rolling trainer table if I’m using my laptop. You can buy the Zwift Ride itself, or as a package deal with Wahoo’s excellent Kickr Core 2, which gives you everything you need for a stress-free indoor riding season.

According to recent reports, jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#172837. Time Off Feet Will Change How You Think About Recovery

Time Off Feet Will Change How You Think About Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress.
  • Now, as a Latest York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training prepares.
  • Recent findings suggest that while time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress. Absolutely not, was his answer. “It’s not as if he would have assigned me a specific time off feet metric,” Inman says, “but my feet needed to rest, and being a waitress was too much time on feet for someone racing the way I did.”.

Now, as a Latest York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training prepares. For example, a nurse who is “always on her feet,” can’t have runs that overload her so much that she couldn’t keep training or working after a race, Inman claims.

Recent findings suggest that while time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way. “We do have an old saying, ‘Never stand when you can sit and never sit when you can lie down,’” indicates Will Baldwin, USATF and VDOT-certified running coach. Like any generalization, though, that rule isn’t very helpful.

Additionally, despite the many ways runners dig into their metrics and researchers look at small running form and running shoe discrepancies, there is little hard science regarding how much time off your feet you need and how you should best spend that time.

“Instead, you want to use comfort as your paradigm or framework on whether your recovery method is working for you,” says Jim Jastifer, MD, a fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon specializing in foot and ankle reconstruction with OSMC Orthopedic and Sports Medicine Center in Indiana.

🏃🏻‍♀️The Runner’s World Guide to Recovery is your home for a smarter—from managing soreness and fatigue to easing back into running after a race, offseason, or injury.

Industry observers note that in fact, “be comfortable” and “do what makes you happy” may be the best metrics for recovery, according to Jastifer. That’s because it’s not just your feet that need a break—so does your brain.

It has been revealed that are joy and time off feet really related? Turns out, they are. Kara Goucher, distance runner extraordinaire and cohost with Des Linden of the running podcast Nobody Asked Us, has her own way of making sure she gives herself enough time off feet.

Sources indicate that “I love playing Sudoku!” Goucher remarked on the pod, and she considers her game playing part of her rest and recovery. “It’s time off feet that really does calm my mind and it’s so much better for my brain and mental health than doom scrolling on my phone! It's time to reset my body and my mind.”.

In fact, according to the experts, your goal around recovery and time off feet should be to become self-aware of what your body needs, what your feet need (which may be different than what your larger muscles and soft tissues need), and what your brain needs.

According to recent reports, your feet may actually be the best way to determine how to spend your recovery time; your wearable likely doesn’t correlate its opinion of your recovery to the stress that your feet feel, Jastifer notes. “If your Garmin says you’re ready to run, but your feet hurt, you should listen to your feet,” he adds.

Sources indicate that “Someone who is running 70/80/100 miles a week isn’t going to recover more by going for a walk,” notes Baldwin. This is precisely why Inman’s coach didn’t want her, a professional runner at the time, to add waitressing on top of her training schedule.

“Instead, I try to get my athletes to do low-level movement, such as time on the bike.” For his own time off feet, Baldwin saves his favorite highlights to watch during these sessions so he has less mental taxation.

Industry observers note that “Swelling and pain are really the only two reasons you absolutely need to stay off your feet,” claims Baldwin. However, you’ll need to be aware of the difference between swelling due to injury and swelling that occurs simply because fluid has gone to your feet because of extensive motion.

It has been revealed that “Keeping your feet in motion can actually help swelling,” states Jastifer. Walking can stimulate the movement of blood and lymph (a fluid that carries nutrients to your blood and tissues), which can help recovery, but only if your feet aren’t fighting injury. Signs of injury include pain and discoloration.

Of course, you don’t always have to walk—or do anything with impact—to move your feet. Making circles, rolling a ball under them, or stretching them can reduce the swelling. Again, though, if you feel pain, stop and go to a doctor before you run again.

Percell Dugger, Runna run coach, suggests that you always consider rest and recovery within the context of your training plan, and, if your feet hurt, balance that vital metric against the intensity and effort of a planned workout, even if it’s active recovery.

“In practice and by observation everyone recovers differently,” Inman states. “So, you want to be responsive to whether your feet are telling you they need to rest. If so, maybe get in a pool or get on a bike.”.

Even though there is no clear time or method for recovery, the most crucial thing to do between runs is sleep and eat, advises Kristine Sweezey, PT, DPT, CSCS, a physical therapist in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and Charlotte, North Carolina.

It has been revealed that jastifer agrees, adding that rest, cross-training, and time off feet are not at all the same as sleeping. “They serve different functions,” he adds. Without sleep and proper nutrition, athletes cannot actually begin to recover. Moreover, any tricks or tools you use outside of sleep and proper fueling won’t add anything to the recovery equation without a commitment to the basics.

Between sleep, time on feet, and time off feet, the experts recommend that you add foot strengthening to your routine. Because improving the abilities of your intrinsic foot muscles will help your feet cope with long and hard miles on the road. So, what are your intrinsic foot muscles? The small muscles that connect within your foot, but not to areas outside of it, such as your Achilles. The muscles in your toes and arch are intrinsic.

Industry observers note that “By analogy, we have all the same muscles in our feet that we have in our hands, and while they aren’t significant from a force standpoint, they help regulate the force proprioception in ankle stability and are part of a neuromuscular feedback loop so you don’t have to think about how your feet land which will provide you with stability,” Jastifer states. “If you have foot pain, it might be from these muscles.”.

Sweezey agrees and states you should do all the toe scrunches and toe lifts that you can. “I keep a lacrosse ball under my desk to roll around with my feet,” she says. “It helps decrease the soreness and flushes things out.”.

In a recent development, finally, when you are ready to get back on the road with your revived feet—whether it’s been a day or a week—make sure you don’t pair two long runs or speed workouts back-to-back, indicates Dugger. “Progressive loading is better than high spikes and a dive.” If you and your feet (and your brain) need a break, don’t push too much on your next run.

Recent findings suggest that donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly nearly free (taxes and fees only) — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

In a recent development, “All you need is a pair of shoes to start running” isn’t exactly truthful. If you hate your toenails and heels, by all means, wear Converse high-tops. A good pair of running shoes will spare your digits and the skin on your feet—but that doesn’t mean you have to drop cash on expensive trainers.

Cheap running shoes, models less than $130, are a respectable choice for beginners and vets wanting to save. From plush to moderately cushioned, we’ve listed affordable running shoes on this list that’ll help you save up for more run gear, like a fancy GPS watch or that next destination race.

To find the best shoes under $130, we performed comprehensive research on top-rated trainers by well-known brands, and called in shoes for our shoe program testers and staff to evaluate. These shoes were vetted by scrutinizing fit, ride, and comfort. To give you both options, we included our premium recommendation for each shoe from our Best Running Shoes buying guide, just in case you want to spend some extra cash.

🏃 For even more choices, head to The Best Running Shoes of 2026.

We also spoke with Footwear Buyer Jon Notary, who works at the local running store Aardvark Sports Shop in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. Notary provides insight on what you’re compromising on when buying cheap shoes, and gives advice on what to look for when you’re out shopping for your next pair.

Buying an affordable trainer doesn’t necessarily mean subpar features. Brands will sometimes incorporate “old” technology into these shoes, like midsole foams, to mitigate a high price. But you are sacrificing some premium specs, like plush cushioning and more durable materials.

Though not as plush or responsive as, say, the more expensive 1080 or 880, the 680 still encapsulates New Balance’s soft-cushioned feel, absorbing shock and promoting comfort on every run.

Sources indicate that its Fresh Foam midsole provides a supportive, plush, lightweight ride, making the 680v9 an excellent choice as an everyday trainer that can handle base-building mileage. A breathable, cozy upper makes this a comfy running shoe and great for casual wear, as well.

The shoe is also great for long runs thanks to its PureGel tech and FF Blast midsole; you’ll have a soft ride that absorbs impact.

The FloatZig 2 looks bulky with its unconventional, zigzag midsole rim around the shoe. But we found it surprisingly lightweight during testing. Its soft cushioning—that midsole isn’t just for looks—provided a supportive bed for testers’ feet.

In a recent development, “What I found most enjoyable about this shoe was how lightweight and balanced it is,” said tester Mike Parmer. “The fit and comfort allowed longer training runs and no sore feet or toes. This shoe is one of the better shoes I have tested recently and would compare equally to Hoka.”.

The Superfloat+ midsole promotes high energy return, giving a much-needed boost when the road feels long.

👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Shock Absorption Shoe → Upcoming Balance 1080v15 (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at reebok.com | Shop Women’s at reebok.com.

Anta proves you can have premium cushioning on a budget. The PG7 3 has an incredibly plush feel, making the shoe versatile for easy runs, long runs, and casual wear. The cushioning stays soft and also supportive, allowing you to run hard and fast.

In my runs in the PG7 3, I’ve found the ride and feel comparable to the Saucony Triumph and Brooks Glycerin.

“Budget shoes always feel cheap,” remarked Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “There’s an undeniable compromise you have to make to pay less. And that stinks. In this case, the PG7 doesn’t really feel like it’s holding anything back. It’s comfortable, cushioned, and supportive. It’s going to work as a daily driver for a lot of runners.”.

According to recent reports, though the C202 7 costs the most on this list, it’s more than worth the $130 price. Compared to racing shoes that are upward of $200, the C202 7 has a full-length carbon-fiber plate sandwiched in its midsole of DAN cushioning, a TPU supercritical foam.

It has been revealed that the shoe feels snappy and responsive. And it has good traction too. Furrer tested the shoe during a rainy 5K in San Antonio, Texas. While other competitors wiped out on slick turns, Furrer stayed vertical cutting corners and accelerating on waterlogged sidewalks and muddy dividers.

According to recent reports, 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Racing Marathons Shoe → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s).

It has been revealed that trail running demands a lot from your shoes. Between the hard-charging descents and scraping against rough rocks, the last thing you want is a cheap, flimsy shoe that won’t hold up. The Saucony Excursion TR17 has Versarun, which absorbs impact and provides comfy cushioning over trail debris.

One knock is the shoe is quite heavy, and it runs a little small and narrow, so consider sizing up and trying on the wide version.

All models of the Excursion TR17 have 4.5mm lugs to keep you on your toes when things get dicey.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

In a recent development, according to Notary, the two main sacrifices you make when buying cheaper running shoes are comfort and longevity. That doesn’t mean you’re stuck with choosing uncomfortable shoes when you’re searching for cheaper pairs. It just means you have to do the extra, er, footwork, when considering more affordable shoes.

Notary notes the materials are not as premium or as durable. “That being said, the industry does benefit from what I call the technology trickle-down; many of the materials on lower priced models were once used on a ‘fancier’ one.” For example, the Brooks Launch 12 has DNA Flash v2 foam which was used in its Hyperion Elite super shoes.

It has been revealed that “A lower cost shoe will use older foams and fabrics, possibly less outsole, or no outsole, and less involved construction techniques. All of those realities typically lead to less overall comfort than what else is currently available,” notes Notary. A cheaper shoe will be comfortable, it just won’t have the same max plush and support of a top-shelf trainer.

Industry observers note that notary claims comfort is king. “If it feels heavy, stiff, and firm in the store, don’t expect that to change. Conversely, if it feels hyper-light, super flexible, and marshmallowy soft, there is a good chance it won’t be as durable.”.

Perhaps you’re leaning toward one end of the spectrum of cushioning or somewhere in the middle. The best way to find if a cheap shoe—or any running shoe—is right for you is to try it on first and go for a test run in the store. Some shoe stores allow you to run on the sidewalk or on a treadmill to see if the shoe’s a good fit.

In a recent development, cheap running shoes have a shorter shelf life. “Because the materials are less premium they typically break down faster even when they’re not being worn,” says Notary. “This isn’t always true and is somewhat of a generalization, but higher grade materials generally offer more durability. If we’re considering mileage, a lower-cost shoe typically yields fewer miles.”.

Notary adds, however, that some of the most expensive running shoes on the market right now, i.e., super shoes or shoes with a carbon plate, also have a shorter mileage life, which is another thing to put in perspective.

We took pains not to include discounted models on this list but shouldn’t be overlooked when buying running shoes. In some cases, the differences between last season and the current season are unnoticeable.

When the Price Is Too Good to Be True.

Industry observers note that beware of dupes on sites like Amazon. A usually expensive model slapped with a too-good-to-be-true price tag is probably just that. The model in question likely isn’t the shoe promised, is poorly made, and could cause injury due to poor quality materials. Check the seller to see it’s from the actual brand (and make sure it’s not someone posing as a well-known brand).

For models by lesser known brands, Notary gives us some pointers when choosing running shoes. “Things to look for are a rubber outsole and a removable footbed/liner,” he indicates. “These are two quick check aspects of a viable running shoe. Also, look for fewer sewn overlays on the upper, more will only cause problems with flexibility and add excessive weight to the shoe.”.

Will cheap running shoes make me run slower?

In general, a cheaper shoe will not have as much pop or energy return as a more expensive one which in theory should make it slower. Lower cost shoes will likely lack plating or supercritical foams found in today’s ‘fastest’ shoes. However, a lot depends on how comfortably the shoe moves with you. Some of the ‘fastest’ shoes on the market today don’t agree with my body’s mechanics, and I find them slower than more conventional shoes in my rotation.

Are cheap running shoes a good choice for new runners?

In my world, any shoe that gets someone running is a good choice. That said, a well-fitting, comfortable technical running shoe will have a much better chance of keeping a upcoming runner in the sport.

It’s a shame that with so much great and relatively affordable product available, many people start the sport in the wrong shoe and quit, never knowing a different reality exists for them. Unfortunately the ‘running shoe’ category is a bit of a catch-all, and there are plenty of shoes categorized as ‘running’ that have no place being labeled as such.

How old can a past shoe model be for it to be ok to run in?

Industry observers note that unworn shoes will definitely lose some cushioning after about two to five years due to oxidization, which hardens the midsole foam. Glue also weakens over time, increasing the risk of delamination in shoes that have been sitting around a while, primarily between the upper and the midsole and the midsole and the outsole. They can be used, sure, but they won’t have the typical 300 to 500 mile range of usability nor the comfort of a ‘fresher’ pair.

Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon.
