It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that nothing sucks harder on a run than an uncomfortable, unsupportive (or too supportive) sports bra that digs, chafes, causes pools of sweat to collect, and generally makes you curse the day you hit puberty. Luckily, we’re looking out for you. Our team was as rigorous with bras as we are with running shoes, treadmills, and other gear as we evaluated them. We focused chiefly on comfort, breathability, durability, the potential to chafe, bounce control, and ease of laundering.

And yes, we look at bras with and without pads, because anyone who has ever wrestled with those flimsy things can tell you that while they may hide the headlights, there are times when you’d rather light them on fire than deal with them before lacing up and hitting your run.

Recent findings suggest that the best sports bras for running work with your cup and band size, what level of support you require, and how you like it to fit on your frame. We chose a range of adjustable high-impact bras, traditional pullover sports bras, bras with pockets, bras that are budget-friendly, and bras made for different size and shape breasts.

It has been revealed that our testers span all experience levels, paces, ages, and body types, with sizes ranging from 28 to 40 bands and A to F cups. Over the past year, we’ve tested more than 45 different sports bras to see how they held us and how they held up. We wore these bras for running plus low- to high-intensity workouts like yoga and HIIT, evaluating each for comfort, breathability, mobility, and—of course—support.

We sorted our picks into three categories: adjustable bras (hook-and-eye closures, zip fronts, Velcro, or adjustable straps), pullover bras (no adjusting required, though maybe some contorting), and pocket bras, which we also rank on storage space and how packing affects mobility and support.

We update this roundup regularly, but inventory changes fast—some colors and sizes may run low.

Sources indicate that there are few bras that you try on and feel comfortable straight out of the bag, but the Run Times Bra manages. It’s a comfortably compressive, encapsulated, adjustable bra that is designed to take you for long miles. It has sweat-wicking fabric that prevents pooling under the breasts, and the mesh panel at the top allows for additional breathability. On a long run, that extra breeze makes a huge difference in comfort and chafing prevention.

According to recent reports, our tester took this out on a 35-mile climbing trail run through the Adirondack Mountains and through the heat and the rain. The bra performed beautifully, even under a long-sleeve tee and tech jacket. It didn’t get swampy, nor did the shirt start to stick to it, as can happen when sweat and water soak a T-shirt.

It’s especially great for women who have lost a significant amount of breast volume due to weight loss or breastfeeding because of how the additional Lycra material encapsulates and hugs each breast. Where some bras may make these breasts feel almost “folded,” the Run Times Bra simply supports and cradles your breasts in an anatomically comfortable way.

According to recent reports, old Navy has long been a favorite of ours for its inexpensive athletic wear, and now, that also includes sports bras. The PowerSoft bra hits well outside of its weight class in both features and performance, starting with a front zipper that spares you the post-run wrestle of a sweaty pullover. Adjustable cross-back straps let you fix the fit through your shoulders and torso, and the brand’s namesake PowerSoft fabric is buttery soft with moisture-wicking that holds up when you’re hitting those hot runs.

The size range is where Old Navy really highlights up the competition: broader than what many premium brands offer. At $40 full price—and often marked down below $25—it’s impossible to overlook.

And not for anything, this is one of the bras we tested with a zipper that isn’t a sensory nightmare for our autistic testers.

In a recent development, the construction of this bra makes it among the best I’ve ever worn. The uniqueness of that construction? A dual adjustable strap in the back that allows you to dial in your fit. If you need more support up top, you can clasp it closer together. Need a bit more band space? The lower hooks are there for you. This is a bra designed for women who may have volume in different spots across their ribs and chest. And it works beautifully.

The construction also makes for a more comfortable experience. I have a pretty severe rib flare thanks to pregnancy and a short waist, and the ability to tighten the bra more up on top and less on the bottom makes it comfier than most other bras I’ve tested.

However, if you have pronounced lat muscles, you may notice a bit of rubbing during pull-ups because of where the shoulder straps fall. But that nitpicky aspect doesn’t take away from it being an all-around winner.

Runderwear Power Running Bra Review.

In a recent development, the Shadowlite is very sensory friendly. The flat-locked seams are coated and stitched in a way that they don’t rub or interfere with your run. It’s also not a traditional encapsulation bra, nor is it a traditional pullover compression bra. Instead, it’s a combination of the two. Instead of the sewn-in lifting panel squeezing the breasts together and in, it lifts them together without the squish.

Recent findings suggest that “The bra gave me a very secure feeling without restricting my breathing—I forgot I was wearing it, which is always the best possible outcome,” stated Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá. “The band has ribbing on the inside that I found helpful in keeping the bra in place—no feeling of rotation on the run. I usually try to get two runs out of a bra, if I can, before washing. I was able to do three with this bra.”.

In a recent development, the gel-cushioned straps on this sports bra ensure you won’t get raw markings from all-day wear and intense activities. The Spot Comfort is also extremely breathable and moisture-wicking—mesh on the adjustable straps and front panel promotes ventilation.

Industry observers note that the bra is lined with molded cups for non-underwire support, and the back hook-and-eye closure makes it easy to take the bra off. One thing to consider: size up. We found the fit a little too snug, even on the loosest hook-and-eye setting. It’s also H-back-only, which may not be everyone’s preference when wearing a sports bra. This one launders like a dream—seriously. For the price, it doesn’t pill, it doesn’t stretch out, and we don’t always follow our own laundering advice and just throw it in with everything and call it good.

In a recent development, the Energy’s foam cups, which go up to size DDD, offer comfortable and secure support while also providing a flattering fit that doesn’t squish the chest down. In the back, we appreciate the crisscross straps’ fun design as well as their functionality—once adjusted, the straps stay in place for a no-budge run.

Industry observers note that some of our testers reported that the Energy runs small, so it may be best to order a size up to ensure the bra is a good fit or try it on in person. This bra also has three points of adjustment: the chest band as well as both sets of cross straps.

Recent findings suggest that the bra that underwent 2,000-plus miles of ultrarunning is buttery soft and has plenty of lift. Tested during lululemon’s Further campaign, in which 10 women runners ran an ultra over the course of six days, the Go Further Bra is a high-impact pullover that can carry you through thousands of miles—and it doesn’t have to be in one go.

The bra is made of lululemon’s Ultralu fabric, which feels yoga legging smooth. Support Code technology in the cups changes the stiffness of the cups to prevent your breasts from bouncing as you run. You can see the tech when the bra is on a flat surface; instead of the conical domes you see on an encapsulation bra, the cups pucker and look slightly sunken in.

According to recent reports, our tester, who wears a 32B and tested the Go Further in a small, had her doubts when she saw the bra lying flat on her desk. She changed her mind after running in the Go Further. “From the look of her, I was convinced that she would never fit, and that she’s made for much bigger boobs than mine,” she says. “And was I wrong! She fits like a glove and is easy to put on and take off. She doesn’t deprive me of air but is completely supportive on my runs.”.

Sources indicate that you’ve probably seen influencer ads for this all over your social media feeds. Running Girl’s ad budget is thriving, but thankfully, your budget will be too, if you grab this one. The bra is comfortably high-impact with no squish. Instead, the molded cups lift and separate your breasts doing more holding than straight compression.

The bra is featherlight and breathable but be forewarned, there’s a lot of cup to these cups. I get that it’s an aesthetics thing, but it is wild seeing yourself in a sports bra that adds to your breasts. If you’re not opposed to more boobs than ever on a run (and honestly, it looked good to me!), and you want a simple, affordable bra, this is a great option.

This extremely reasonably priced back-pocket bra is one of my top picks from my sports bras with pocket testing. The phone pocket is easy to reach, and, unlike other pocket bras, there isn’t an overload of material along the back strap design. That does mean the pocket is shallower than similar models, and I find myself reaching back to make sure my phone is still there (I haven’t lost it yet, but it’s something to keep in mind).

This bra is available in a ridiculous array of fun colors, has an easy-to-wear shape, and features a well-fitted design with good coverage and comfort for most cup sizes. For those of us wearing wired headphones, you can thread the cords through a bonded eyelet above the pocket, and the bra stays quite odor resistant even after sweaty workout sessions.

To determine your sports bra size, Lawson uses this system of measuring:.

Sources indicate that but this equation isn’t doctrine. There is no industry standard for bra sizing; not every brand follows the same conventions of measurement. Some brands, for instance, instruct customers to add 4 or 5 inches to the band measurement to determine band size.

Sources indicate that “I’ve been creating, evaluating, revising, critiquing sports bra fit charts for decades for brands large and small,” Lawson says. “Because our bodies and breasts are so diverse, it’s virtually impossible for any brand to create the perfect sizing scheme and fit chart that works for 100 percent of women.” But Lawson calls this “a blessing,” comparing sports bras to jeans. Imagine if every size 10 jean had a standardized fit. That would alienate curvier, thinner, shorter, or taller individuals. “It can take trial and error to find your perfect jeans fit match, but once you do it can be a life-changer.” And the same goes for sports bras.

She offers some tips to navigate the Wild West of bra sizing.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to support, there are two basic sports bra designs: compression and encapsulation. Compression is when strong elastic materials are used to compress your chest. Encapsulation is when each breast is supported separately in its own cup. According to Lawson, many women with larger breasts prefer encapsulation because they find it more comfortable. “It’s not smooshing everything together, trapping moisture between the breasts,” she says. That being said, some encapsulation bras, such as the SheFit, Janji, and lululemon Run Times, also offer degrees of compression inside the encapsulation, which serve as both impact protection and an additional layer of support and protection for larger-busted people or those who have lost volume.

In a recent development, regardless of the type of chest design, an adjustable waistband and shoulder straps help improve overall support when you have larger breasts. More padded straps won’t necessarily translate to a more comfortable fit, Lawson claims. Putting in more foam may initially feel more comfortable, but it won’t decrease pressure. “The one thing that will decrease strap pressure is a wider strap. If you make the strap twice as wide, it doesn’t quite cut the shoulder pressure in half, but it’ll take it almost down to half.”.

It has been revealed that some of my favorite racing shorts are pocketless, which isn’t a substantial deal—when your sports bra has pockets. Some brands offer bras with side pockets and front pockets for housing keys or gels. There are bras with back pockets for storing your smartphone as well. A thing to note with bra storage is that you could be sacrificing support if you weigh down your bra with items.

Some people believe that storing your phone in your bra can increase your breast cancer risk. “There is no conclusive data to suggest that cell phones are linked to cancer,” notes Diana Medgyesy, MD, a medical oncologist at UCHealth. However, she adds that “this is an evolving field since cell phone technology and the use of cell phones are changing rapidly,” so use your own discretion on whether or not to run with your phone in your bra.

Sources indicate that when it comes to finding the best sports bra for you, patience and some trial and error are key. “Be prepared to become a sleuth,” Lawson says. “Be prepared to do a little work to understand your own body/breasts and then a lot of work to sleuth out brands whose fit philosophies and metrics match your needs and preferences.

“Most of us are willing to try a dozen or more running shoe brands/styles/sizes to get the best product match for our feet and workouts—give your sports bra quest the same effort and attention to detail.”.

One population of runners we don’t want to leave out is those who have had lumpectomies, mastectomies, or other breast surgeries. That’s why we spoke with breast surgeon and runner Deborah M. Capko, MD, FACS, from Memorial Sloan Kettering in New York City. She claims that “it’s all about compression” for women who have had breast surgery. For up to a year after surgery, you could be dealing with swelling and discomfort during your runs. Having a compressive bra like a SheFit or lululemon Run Times bra can help.

Capko says underwires are a no-go, but keeping your post-op breasts “stable and highly supported” can cut down on that swelling and pain. We also spoke with a few runners who have run postmastectomy and lumpectomy, and they agree. When it comes to preferred bra design, they suggested clasp or zip over pullover because a pullover is harder to deal with and far less comfortable.

What is the best sports bra type for running?

Ideally, you want a bra that has a medium or high level of support, a secure, but not too tight band, and straps that sit just before the acromion bone (the boney protuberance at the top of your shoulder.

What Makes a Sports Bra High Impact?

It has been revealed that high-impact sports bras are made to decrease breast movement while you’re performing high-impact activities. They usually use some sort of compression, encapsulated cups, molded cups, supportive fabrics, wider bands, and adjustable straps or closures or combination of these to create a secure fit.

A running sports bra should feel supportive and pretty darn snug without making you feel like you can’t breathe. The band should sit nicely around your torso, under your breasts, and the cups should fully contain your breasts. The straps shouldn’t slip, and if you’re noticing slipping of any area during your run, it either needs adjustment or you need a upcoming size.

Getting a bra with flat-locked seams like those on this list, with well-fitting straps and the correct cup size is the most important thing. Having good, moisture-wicking fabric allows it to dry faster to prevent friction. Before you head out on a long run, do a shorter workout first to try to notice potential hot spots.

How Often Should You Wash Your Sports Bra?

You can wear your bra several times before washing, but be sure to wash it at least every couple of runs. Because you’re sweating in the sports bra during running, which is a high-intensity activity, your bra can develop bacteria buildup (gross).

According to recent reports, most sports bras can be tossed into the washing machine, but read the garment label just in case. Refrain from adding in fabric softener, since that can degrade the material and interfere with its breathability and moisture-wicking properties.

Air-drying is strongly recommended, although you can put the bra in the dryer on a tumble setting. Heat from your machine can degrade the bra’s structure as well.

How long does a sports bra last?

It has been revealed that like a running shoe, sports bra shelf life is dependent on the wearer. While it’s recommended you retire your sports bra once or twice a year, we get it—you’ve formed an attachment. But there are telltale signs that it’s time to say goodbye. If the straps are overstretched, the band is loose or causes friction when it never used to, the cups have lost shape, or there’s a hole in the fabric, time for a latest bra.

Another sign to go shopping: your body has changed and the bra doesn’t fit like it used to. It’s worth buying a fresh sports bra that gives you proper support instead of willing an old bra to give you support it can no longer provide.

Bra manufacturers have a real concern creating a full range of sizes for high-impact sports bras. It is rare to find a bra that goes above a 42DDD. SheFit manages, and a few select other brands, but in general, bras with band sizes above 42 and cup sizes above DDD are hard to come by. This is an error in the industry that makes it difficult for people in larger bodies to achieve their running and fitness goals comfortably. Plus-size runners are wildly underrepresented across the span of gear. Running and running gear should be accessible for all, no matter the size of body you live in.

Runner’s World began covering all things running in 1966, but the first sports bra, the Jogbra, wasn’t invented until a decade later. Sports bras are as necessary as a pair of running shoes. Since their invention, they continue to undergo changes in design and tech.

According to recent reports, we researched the history of the sports bra and combed through the products available on the market today. We spoke with designers, brand representatives, and experts in the field, including LaJean Lawson, PhD.

Known as Dr. Sports Bra in her field, Lawson has two graduate degrees in sports bra science and is the principal at Creative Fitness Solutions in Portland, Oregon.

Additional interviewing and research was done by Senior Features Editor Pavlína Černá, Deputy Health & Fitness Editor Mallory Creveling, and Director of Hype Aly Ellis.

Fortunately, you don't have to make the trip to Indiana to catch the action. Here's when everything starts, where the races are being held, and how to watch from home.

Division II runners will have to wait a little longer, with their national championship scheduled for Friday, December 4.

#172831. Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3038 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there’s no shortage of latest cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable.
  • Our editors bring different perspectives to testing.
  • According to recent reports, our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s no shortage of latest cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

Our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

According to recent reports, our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+.

According to recent reports, I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

That mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

It has been revealed that when I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates promptly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

It has been revealed that I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex Pliers Wrench (86 03 180).

Knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

Industry observers note that these aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

Despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

Peak Design Mobile Crossbody Multi-Strap.

In a recent development, as a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

It has been revealed that its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them promptly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

Spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

Industry observers note that I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

The main concern I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

In a recent development, back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

According to recent reports, now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

According to recent reports, so far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Vittoria Corsa Pro Control Tan, 700x42c.

Launched in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls rapidly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT TR.

According to recent reports, I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

Sources indicate that in nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit complications. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

Pearl Izumi Pi PRO/BLACK Mesh Jersey.

Recent findings suggest that at $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

The fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common issue I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

Sources indicate that I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

Sources indicate that it’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

The wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

Heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

Sources indicate that the sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

Q36.5 Dottore Pro Long Sleeve Jersey.

The Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

It has been revealed that I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

The Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full revision to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

Recent findings suggest that same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a big reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an upgrade to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

Industry observers note that but even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing showed the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

The Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

The straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

It is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 revealed to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

Industry observers note that other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

Industry observers note that one of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

#172830. Industry News: 3 Subtle Breathing Exercises You Can Do at the Dinner Table

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (619 w)

Industry News: 3 Subtle Breathing Exercises You Can Do at the Dinner Table

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are certain occasions that call for covert calm.
  • Industry observers note that your breath is a powerful tool.
  • Industry observers note that if you’re already dealing with low-level overwhelm, drawing attention to yourself and your nerves is likely the last thing you want to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are certain occasions that call for covert calm. You know what I mean. Those times when you’re incredibly stressed, uncomfortable, or anxious but can’t really extricate yourself from the situation. Take, for example, the occasion dinner. If the thought of a large gathering and non-stop (as well as unfiltered) conversation fills you with even a slight sense of unease, subtle breathing exercises might just be your latest favorite mindfulness practice.

Industry observers note that your breath is a powerful tool. Practicing breathwork, even the quiet kind, can affect your physiological, mental, and emotional state, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and easing your entire being out of panic mode. Known as pranayama in yoga, breathwork is a broad category, allowing you to find the breathing that resonates with you and return to it whenever signs of stress arise.

Industry observers note that if you’re already dealing with low-level overwhelm, drawing attention to yourself and your nerves is likely the last thing you want to do. So, rather than jumping up from the table for a quick yoga pose or engaging in a liberating round of lion’s breath, subtle breathing exercises invite you to remain in your chair, appearing engaged as you regulate your nervous system.

Start with a count of 3 or 5 rounds of each of these breaths and see how you feel. If the tension is still palpable, take as many as you need to self-soothe. And if you forget any of the below in your situation, simply lengthen your exhalations.

Also known as diaphragmatic breathing, belly breathing invites you to take your deepest breath possible. At it’s core, this breathing exercise is about (surprise!) inhaling into your belly. This is, of course, anatomically incorrect. But think of the larger goal here, which is to direct your inhalations toward your belly without exaggerating the movement in your ribs. The results is the diaphragm lowers and creates space to breathe into your actual lungs.

Belly breathing also gets your breath out of your upper chest, which is the sort of shallow, stunted breathing that often accompanies anxiety. Slowing and deepening your breath signals safety, reminding your animal self that this is not a moment for fight, flight, or freeze—even if it feels like one.

Industry observers note that sometimes evening things out is the answer. Box breathing involves a simple pattern of inhaling for a count of four, holding for a count of four, exhaling for a count of four, and holding for a count of four, thus (figuratively) creating a sort of square shape with your breath. If four is too short of a count for your natural breathing, you can change your number to five, six, or beyond, so long as each part of the breath (inhalation, exhalation, and holds) remains even.

Turning even part of your attention away from the group and toward your own breath gives you a break from the noise while demonstrating the power of your own body and mind. Box breathing is often used for focus, so don’t be surprised if you return to the conversation with more interest and alertness.

The simplest option on this list, equal breathing is all about matching your inhalations to your exhalations. This is a practice of balance, so track the count of a deep inhalation, and if it feels okay in your body, apply it to your exhalation. It’s also the most adaptable, so feel free to vary the count slightly. You don’t want to stress yourself out, after all.

In addition to providing the aforementioned benefits of breathwork, redirecting your focus places your entire being in neutral, enabling you to consider your current circumstance with more clarity and calm.

U.S. Women Could Be Upgraded to World Half Marathon Gold After Kenyan Runner’s EPO Ban

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that on Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) declared that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance.
  • The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain already had plenty to celebrate after earning the United States its first women's team medal at September's World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. But nearly two months after finishing with silver, the American trio could soon have gold added to their résumés.

Sources indicate that on Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) declared that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance. The decision officially disqualifies her second-place finish at the September 20 event, where her silver medal helped Kenya secure the women's team title. But with Loleo's result now thrown out, Kenya's team score has to be recalculated. Countries are ranked by the combined finishing times of their three fastest athletes, and Loleo’s removal means Kenya must now count Lilian Kasait Rengeruk, who finished 34th in 1:10:36, potentially lifting the U.S. to first place in the team standings.

The Kenyan women originally led with a combined 3:17:33, ahead of the Americans' 3:19:51. But removing Loleo's 1:06:05 pushes Kenya's total to 3:22:04, leaving the U.S. in first place by two minutes and 13 seconds. Kenya would drop to second and Ethiopia would remain third, although World Athletics has yet to officially confirm the updated results.

Hurley recently acknowledged the uncertainty in a comment on Citius Mag's Instagram, noting that nobody can know exactly how the race would've unfolded without Loleo. Still, she admitted, "it would've been so cool to celebrate gold 🥹.".

According to recent reports, loleo's sample was collected during an out-of-competition test on September 6 ahead of the championships, two weeks prior to the competition. She initially told investigators she couldn't explain the positive result, mentioning an injection she'd received for an injury, but later admitted to the violation on October 30, which earned her a one-year reduction from the standard four-year suspension.

It has been revealed that loleo wasn't the only major Kenyan distance runner to receive a final decision Thursday. Peres Jepchirchir, the reigning world marathon champion and 2021 Olympic gold medalist, was also handed a three-year ban following an EPO finding.

“The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go,” AIU chief executive Brett Clothier noted in a statement.

“The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.”.

According to recent reports, jepchirchir, who had been provisionally suspended in October, has accepted the disqualification of her results dating back to July 17, including her August victory at the Sydney Marathon. Fellow Kenyan Irine Cheptai is expected to inherit that title.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone.
  • In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.
  • Before we dive into the science, an notable clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone. At the opposite end of the spectrum, swimming in very warm water can also crater your comfort and results. That’s why we were psyched to test the EZ Hydro-Glide Cap, a one-of-a-kind attempt to boost swimming performance and safety using wearable technology designed to enhance thermoregulation.

In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.

Before we dive into the science, an notable clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap. More on that below.

But first, kudos to EZ Gains, a popular outside-the-box triathlon retailer, for attacking a problem that numerous triathletes experience – significant discomfort when swimming in very cold and very warm water. We’ve learned a lot in recent years about thermoregulation, and any improvements in this area could help many athletes, including friends of mine who’ve quit the sport after repeated unpleasant swims.

It has been revealed that EZ Gains’ approach is based on credible science. The firm notes that your head plays an outsized role in your body’s response to ambient temperatures, given the extensive network of blood vessels and nerves just beneath your scalp. This rings true, as does the contention that regulating the temperature difference between the water and your head – both the initial gap and the ongoing variance – can mitigate the downsides of extreme heat and cold.

According to recent reports, we use insulated neoprene caps for chilly swims, after all. What if a single, more sophisticated solution helped us thrive in both polar and equatorial waters?

EZ Gains’ answer is a honeycombed high-tech foam and hard plastic wedge that sits at the top of your forehead under an (included) standard swim cap. Before putting it on, you can place one or two small thermal packs (also included) inside the hollow center of the wedge. These packs – and an additional thin heating strip – provide a cooling or warming effect as needed. In warm water, you can use a frozen pack or two to cool your forehead, which is meant to keep your core temp down and reduce heat fatigue.

In a recent development, you’re also supposed to use frozen packs when swimming in frigid water – say 60 degrees F or less – according to EZ Gains. The idea is to pre-condition your head to the chilly temps you’re about to encounter. This may sound counterintuitive, but EZ Gains says the pre-cooling technique can prevent cold shock, a serious autonomic response that elevates your heart rate and can cause panic and even cardiac arrest. The packs can also be heated for a touch of warmth when facing cool-but-not-arctic conditions.

For more preparation for swimming in cold water, read: How to Acclimate and Prepare for Cold-Water Triathlons.

Industry observers note that to evaluate the system, I tested it in various bodies of water over the course of five months, from midsummer to late autumn. My primary locations were indoor and outdoor pools in Boulder, Colorado, and our local reservoir. Water temperatures ranged from 84 degrees F all the way down to 50 degrees F. All of my swims were 45-90 minutes long, more than enough to mimic race conditions and assess how well the device limits heat and cold stress.

Recent findings suggest that the TLDR from my testing: Some new technologies sound great on paper but don’t pan out in real life. Sadly, this device is one of those. On two of its three core value propositions, the Hydro-Glide fell short. I’ll tackle them one by one.

Industry observers note that first, EZ Gains says the cap will reduce heat fatigue and related complications – anxiety, increased heart rate, dehydration, and confusion – when using the frozen packs. I did notice a cooling sensation in the early parts of my summer swims, typically lasting 10-15 minutes. But while I appreciated the initial cooling, I didn’t discern a material difference in fatigue, judgment, or heart rate after an hour, even during my most intense workouts.

Sources indicate that second, the cap is supposed to prevent the instant discomfort and cold shock that many people experience when diving into frigid water. Perhaps I’m less sensitive than other athletes (my long-suffering wife might have an opinion on this), but using slightly thawed ice packs to pre-cool my head (as instructed) didn’t eliminate the ice cream headaches.

In my experience, this kind of pain starts in my face and forehead, neither of which are protected by the device. It’s possible that the Hydro-Glide would help other swimmers, since physiological reactions vary widely, but I’d speculate that too much of your face, forehead, and neck remain exposed for the cold to be significantly neutralized.

Third, EZ Gains says the cap will protect your head when another swimmer clobbers you, which seems legit in the case of head-on impacts. A friend in my Masters group sustained a concussion last year when another swimmer swerved into her during a backstroke set. While I didn’t do any head-banging to test this claim, it’s reasonable to believe the Hydro-Glide’s foam would’ve absorbed that blow. Since the wedge doesn’t cover the sides or back of your head, though, it wouldn’t deflect all-too-common errant elbows or kicks to those areas during a race start.

In a recent development, there are two additional downsides to consider. If you have an XL melon like mine, you may experience discomfort from the pressure of the cone against your head. I did, typically after about 30 minutes. And if you’re even the slightest bit fashion-conscious, you will probably draw the line at looking like a Corythosaurus from Jurassic Park. The first time I revealed up at the pool wearing the Hydro-Glide, several of my masters teammates burst out laughing. Someone compared me to a Conehead.

Which I could possibly live with if the results had been stellar. However, the Hydro-Glide didn’t deliver a meaningful upside for me versus a standard swim cap. While EZ Gains deserves praise for its waaay-out-of-the-box effort to improve swim safety and comfort, this product’s current execution doesn’t justify a $270 investment.

6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics.
  • Industry observers note that research shows just how notable core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine.
  • The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Industry observers note that research shows just how notable core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, says core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

Sources indicate that to help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in Fresh York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

In addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

It has been revealed that even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun new ways, but also engage your brain.

Industry observers note that how to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

Tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir notes. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

How to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

Sources indicate that why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

How to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Sources indicate that why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir notes. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

It has been revealed that why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

Recent findings suggest that how to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir states.

Sources indicate that how to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

Recent findings suggest that why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir says. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

How to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (733 w)

This Mileage Target Can Help You Determine Whether You Built a Strong Enough Base to Start Race Training

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time.
  • Building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too rapidly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off.
  • In a recent development, the hard part of this foundational phase?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Base training involves spending a few weeks running at an easy pace and slowly increasing your mileage over time. It’s a crucial first step in any running journey, designed to help you ease into race-specific training.

Building a sufficient aerobic base helps you avoid the aches and pains that come with ramping up mileage too rapidly, especially if you’ve been running sporadically or took some time off. It also makes running feel more doable, as it bridges the gap between your current routine and your goal training plan.

In a recent development, the hard part of this foundational phase? Figuring out if you’re ready to tackle the first few weeks of a initiative and start race-specific workouts. Thankfully, coaches offer a helpful benchmark to hit, plus they explain how to smoothly transition your base routine to race training, without shocking your system.

Sources indicate that building a strong base before racing any distance helps prevent injuries and improves long-term performance, including improved aerobic capacity, endurance, faster recovery, mental conditioning, and weight and stress management, Jill Becker, a personal trainer and run coach at Life Time in Westminster, CO, previously told Runner’s World. That’s why the phase is necessary for all runners, whether you’re upcoming to the sport or have a Boston qualifying time on the list of goals.

“Even a 5K race relies heavily on aerobic systems for energy production—so the better the aerobic base you have, the faster you can race,” Laura Norris, owner and coach at Laura Norris Running in Boulder, CO, previously told Runner’s World.

Additionally, Norris claims doing these easy miles weeks before your goal training block allows your body to adapt to the mileage first, so you can then add in speedwork leading up to race day with lower risk of injury and burnout. Taking this approach helps you avoid increasing volume and intensity at the same time, which can often lead to overtraining.

Finally, tackling a base phase means you’ll feel more confident heading into, say, a four-miler with faster-paced efforts (like tempo or race pace miles), as you’ll have already run four miles at an easy pace consistently for several weeks.

Recent findings suggest that building a strong base requires covering a certain number of miles consistently over the course of several weeks. Beginners should aim to spend at least 10 weeks on this training block, while intermediate runners can follow a six-week initiative, and more advanced runners typically need about four weeks to set that aerobic foundation, Becker claims.

If you’ve already picked out your training proposal, Norris recommends working up to at least 80 percent of the weekly mileage prescribed in the first week of that plan. For example, our 20-week beginner marathon plan prescribes 12 miles in the first week. That means you’ll want to work up to about 10 miles per week before diving into the plan. If you’re looking to break two hours in the half marathon, which requires running at least 18 miles in the first week of the Runner’s World plan, then you’ll want to work up to about 15 miles.

It has been revealed that if you haven’t identified your training strategy yet, Becker recommends adding at least 10 miles to your current weekly volume. (If you’re currently running 10 miles a week, work up to 20.).

Look for a proposal that builds up to that mileage goal slowly, following the 10 percent rule, which means increasing your mileage by no more than 10 percent each week.

It has been revealed that keep in mind, base training is about setting the foundation for your next training block, and a part of that process should include recovery time. This means making time for rest days and down weeks (in which you reduce your volume to allow for recovery and better performance), as well as staying on top of your nutrition, sleep habits, and cross-training.

She covers a wide range of health and wellness topics, with a primary focus on running performance and nutrition. Monique is passionate about creating content that empowers runners to become the best versions of themselves. As an avid runner and parent, she loves spending time outdoors with her daughter, who often accompanies her on weekend runs as her personal mini run coach.

These Three Offseason Strength Exercises Can Help You Break Through Your Climbing Plateau

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time.
  • For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside.
  • It has been revealed that the workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time. If you’re thinking about winterizing your bike for the season, then it’s the perfect time to start looking at your strength training proposal for the offseason.

For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside. For others it takes form as time on fat bikes, skis, or even a pair of running shoes. Regardless of how your winter activities take shape, be sure to add some strength training to make sure you can hit your 2027 goals.

It has been revealed that the workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training. Each exercise targets a different part of the body to dial in the strength you need when you are trying to power up climbs next year. The workout can be done as a stand-alone set of exercises or it can be added on to your current strength training strategy.

So many cyclists want to just spend time in the saddle for training—that’s great up to a point. Eventually we all need to get off the bike and spend some time strength training to help break through those frustrating plateaus. These three overlooked exercises can help you elevate your climbs for 2027.

Today I had my first hill-focused ride after a few weeks focusing on running and trainer rides. The first steep pitch quickly reminded me how much I use my upper body while getting up a hill on the bike. As I climbed, I felt myself pulling on the handlebar with each pedal stroke while gravity was trying to pull me back. Developing the pull muscles is something that will benefit the whole kinetic chain while climbing. Bent-over rows in particular are a great upper-body exercise for this because they engage multiple muscle groups for one movement pattern. Rows can be done with so many different types of equipment: dumbbells, kettlebells, TRX Suspension Systems, elastic bands, and more. Here’s how I recommend doing them with dumbbells.

One of the reasons I love deadlifts for cyclists is because they are exercises that works almost all the muscles through the kinetic chain in one simple move. As we climb, we are pulling energy through our upper body, driving through the hips, and pushing the power through our legs into the pedals. This exercise trains the muscles through your arms, back, and core, while simultaneously working the muscles throughout your legs. Another reason deadlifts are one of my go-to exercises is that they can be done with several different types of equipment. My favorite equipment for this exercise is a barbell, but deadlifts can be done with dumbbells and kettlebells too.

Recovery Tip: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is very real, and depending on the person, your muscle burn can last for a few days after your training session. Initiative accordingly for your rides following a heavy weight day. Listen to your body and add a recovery ride or off-bike activity if that's what you need.

Your core is what ties everything in your body together, so it is integral to grow your stability and power here. While riding today, I was trying to really be in tune with how I was using my core when climbing. When I was in the saddle I felt like the focus from my core was on stability, allowing for a sound upper body while pushing power through my legs and out of the pedals. My simple go-to core exercise to improve climbing is a plank with cross-body knee taps. This works stability through your core while working the internal obliques through the cross-body motion of the knee tuck. This exercise will really show its gains when you get out of the saddle as the climb pitches up.

A quick note on consistency: strength training will give you the best results when you incorporate it in your initiative week after week. It will offer significantly diminished results if you are sprinkling it in sporadically. If you are able to, try to commit to adding strength training consistently for a four- to six-week block and see how that impacts your rides.

Our strength training program can help get you started with a more in-depth workout blueprint. It’s vital to remember it does not matter where you are in your cycling journey, there are gains to be found from adding some level of strength training to your calendar.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#172823. Latest Update: For Years, Doctors Blamed My Mysterious Symptoms on Running. A Simple Blood Test Proved Them Wrong.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (930 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: For Years, Doctors Blamed My Mysterious Symptoms on Running. A Simple Blood Test Proved Them Wrong.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 concern of Runner’s World.
  • Running and menstruation entered my life around the same time, at age 13.
  • In a recent development, throughout my years on the high school cross-country team, this irregular pattern stuck: I only got about four periods a year and never knew when they would arrive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 concern of Runner’s World.

Running and menstruation entered my life around the same time, at age 13. I got hooked on running the mile, and, swayed by a persistent and impactful track coach, I eventually left soccer behind to join the cross-country team. My first period arrived right before my first track season; however, while the training cycles progressed, my menstrual cycle didn’t—my second period wouldn’t come until five months later.

In a recent development, throughout my years on the high school cross-country team, this irregular pattern stuck: I only got about four periods a year and never knew when they would arrive. I felt confused and left out whenever my teammates asked me for a menstrual pad I had no use for, like my body couldn’t do what it was supposed to do.

According to recent reports, when it came to running, though, my body felt strong, capable of carrying me through interval workouts and lifting heavy weights during weight room sessions. On the track, I felt more equal to my teammates. The training cycle was one I could control.

Industry observers note that at my yearly physical exams, I expressed concern that my periods weren’t occurring monthly, and the feedback was the same every time: I was still young, and sometimes it takes time to become regular. That I accepted. What didn’t sit well with me was what followed: “You’re missing periods because you run a lot. Try eating more.”.

Neither felt like an answer to the problem. My 20-something-mile weeks kept me physically fit and helped me deal with anxiety, especially when my dysfunctional home life felt out of control. Not only did the exam show I kept a healthy weight, I had been putting on muscle mass from deadlifting 200 pounds. But hoping the doctor was right, I took a year off from distance training.

Still, no regular cycle in sight.

In a recent development, at 19, I started seeing a new primary care physician. My doctor was surprised when I recounted my prior experiences. “So you’ve never had any blood tests done?” they asked. I underwent the test and a pelvic ultrasound, and it didn’t take very long to get an answer: The likely culprit was polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

Industry observers note that PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in people assigned female at birth of reproductive age, yet so much about the condition is still unknown, including the cause of PCOS, according to the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. The National Institutes of Health requires only two of the following symptoms for PCOS diagnosis (all of which I’ve experienced): ovulatory dysfunction (irregular, heavy, or missed periods), high androgen levels (often manifesting as excessive body hair or acne), and/or one or more cysts on the ovaries. Besides irregular menstruation, PCOS can cause, for example, infertility and weight gain. Although there isn’t a permanent cure, some patients are able to treat their symptoms by managing their lifestyle: eating well, exercising regularly, and getting enough sleep.

The diagnosis came at a turbulent time in my life. I was swept up in another cycle: emotional abuse stemming from controlling relationships. I escaped this abuse through schoolwork and decided to take extra classes over the summer so I could graduate from college a year early and find my own place.

But I also got back to running, which has always helped me build a sense of agency and played a big role in my postgrad transition—I spent that summer running across the empty campus and habitually relying on a few miles to calm me when faced with chaos. I started taking an herbal supplement that others with PCOS raved about. I moved in with roommates. I found a therapist to help me unpack the trauma I’ve experienced.

And at 21, I finally started to get a regular monthly period.

Every menstruation since has felt like Christmas morning…followed by some gnawing cramps.

According to recent reports, what I am only now starting to understand is just how much my environment affected my mental health and how that in turn impacted my physical health. I recently read research studies linking PCOS and emotional abuse, and that’s when I found what felt like the last missing link.

I still mourn for the runner I was in high school, who felt lost and frustrated without any answers, dealing with conflicting feelings around her body image. I remember lying on cold, uncomfortable tables, intimidated by informational pamphlets—none of which covered hormonal health—all while doctors were delivering confusing medical advice or dismissing my concerns with oversimplified notions. A 2022 health survey found that 29 percent of women and 21 percent of men felt doctors disregarded their worries during visits. I was told my problem existed “because I ran.” In reality, it’s far more complex than what many people are told, and I am just one example.

In a recent development, I’ve since run two half marathons while maintaining regular periods throughout each training cycle. Running was never the problem. On the contrary, the very thing doctors blamed my symptoms on brought me relief all along—and I will never give it up again.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and at the moment competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

  • Sources indicate that you won’t catch me heading out for a run without a hat.
