Editor’s Note, November 20, 2026: There are several markdowns on our list for Black Friday! The hi-vis and reflective Headsweats Cap and Nathan Run Cool Stash Hat are both 25% off. Scroll down for even more hats on sale!

Sources indicate that you won’t catch me heading out for a run without a hat. Unlike headbands, which tend to slip over my eyes or off my head, caps stay put and have a long list of features that optimize your run. The whole point of a hat is to make my runs easier.

When I’m shopping for the perfect hat, it has to check off several boxes:.

The hat completes my race outfit when I’m running any distance from a mile to a marathon. It keeps my hair from getting into my eyes, and sometimes has extra features, like UPF or even a pocket. And with brands making hats with cool patterns, it can also be a vessel for self-expression. They know that wearing a favorite accessory, one that puts the fun in functionality, can get you into the right headspace when you run.

Industry observers note that I started wearing running hats seven years ago. I’m so used to wearing a hat on a run that I feel naked running without one. As I accumulated hats, I started to see some fits and features trumped others. The hats on this list were evaluated with years of experience, research, and hat testing.

On top of my own research, I also had some of our RW staffers test caps and provide feedback.

In a recent development, the caps below all have features that cater to different needs and types of runs. From logging a run on a blistering hot day, going for a workout in the evening, or having a penchant for snacking on pickles during training, know this: there’s a hat for that.

I’ve also added some beanies for the colder months. When testing beanies, I paid attention to fit, comfort, and warmth. It’s not true that you’ll catch cold if your head isn’t covered, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t wear a hat to keep your cool.

The Ciele FSTCap wins Best Overall as a cap-wearing runner because of its no-fuss, flexible design. The brim isn’t rigid, allowing it to sit comfortably on your head, and it doesn’t flop out of shape. It’s lightweight and breathable, with fast-drying, anti-odor mesh panels.

But its best feature is the adjustable bungee cord closure. I’ve worn several iterations of Ciele FSTCap at races, and the simplicity of the hat gives me peace of mind before racing because the toggle doesn’t require much dexterity when my arms feel like Jell-O during a marathon when I have to loosen or tighten the cord. It’s machine-washable, too.

This hat is Best Budget, but it’s also Best Visibility. The entire rim of this Headsweats’s Hat has reflective trim for visibility in low light, making a car’s lights heighten your bobbing cap’s outline when you’re running on the shoulder at dusk or dawn, or even nighttime. This feature is fantastic if you feel the neon colors are a little too loud to your liking. The black version isn’t a bad choice, thanks to the reflective rim.

Industry observers note that the hat is a great tool when you’re an early riser or night owl, and the knit shell is soft and breathable. I do have one main critique: it looks cheaply made. I can get over the knit material wearing fast—proper care, like machine washing and air-drying only, should add to the cap’s longevity. Maybe it’s the lack of patterns or even mesh panels or overlays besides the logo on the side. While this hat doesn’t win fashion contests, it definitely fulfills its purpose for running safely by staying visible.

Industry observers note that the Ponyflo Alex Active was tested by me and editor Monique LeBrun, who said we should add this hat to our guide for runners who specifically wear high hairstyles. The positioning of the pony opening allows you to run without your visor comically almost covering your eyes if your hair is half-braided high. Runners like me will appreciate how the positioning makes my hair stop just above my back so it’s not whipping my back when I run.

The hat comes in a variety of colors and there’s even an edition with a longer, wider brim for more sun coverage; though both LeBrun and I felt like we were about to spend a day out gardening wearing them. We felt the brim on the Alex Active sufficed, but the option is there.

Recent findings suggest that even though the Ciele FSTCap is my racing hat of choice, we’re giving the best racing hat accolade to the Rnnr Pacer Hat. Our testers loved how feather-light the Pacer is and how its perforated panels provide ultimate ventilation.

My one knock would be the buckle, but we didn’t find ourselves struggling to adjust the closure.

“I suppose the best thing I can say about this hat is that never once did I have to adjust it midrun,” said RW News Director Andrew Daniels, who tested the whimsically graphic Jungalow version.

Industry observers note that our other Pacer tester, News Editor Theo Kahler, chose to wear the less loud, mostly black Bolt iteration. He appreciated how the hat wasn’t bulky or stiff. “It didn’t give me headaches like some hats do,” he said. But he had one complaint: “On the inside, it claims ‘Party pace wins the race.’ I don’t really know what that means and could personally do without that.” And as Scroogy as the comment may have sounded, I got a kick out of that.

A pocket in a hat is hard to find, so I was glad to stumble across Nathan’s Run Cool Stash. The hidden pocket can doubly serve as storage space for ice, a key, or even an ID card. The pocket is drop-in below and above; I can tuck in my ID card in both flaps, or clip on a running light. It’s a close stretch against your head so items won’t bounce in the compartment as you run. It’s perfect for my key fob when I park my car by a trail, and can’t store it in my pocket-free shorts.

One caveat: you can only stash on one side of the hat, so if you’re feeling the heat on your right side, I guess you’ll have to wear the cap backwards to cool that side down.

All hail the hard-brimmed trucker hat—only Oiselle does theirs with a twist. The firm brim folds in half down the center, making it easy to downsize into a little triangle and stash into your pocket if you want the sun to hit your face (or maybe have that hat rim forehead imprint fade before you head to work in the morning).

Industry observers note that this was the only hat I packed when I stayed in Sydney for a week leading up to the marathon. The interior sweatband’s mantra “Go fast, take chances” was the positive energy I needed running a race on the opposite side of the world. The wide-holed mesh back also kept my head cool as the race went on and the day got warmer.

Industry observers note that A small drawback is how funky the hat can get after a couple wears. The hat is hand-wash only, which explains why an old Runner Trucker’s toggle broke after a machine wash. The hat is mighty on the run, but delicate during a wash cycle.

Industry observers note that I’m going on five years running in my Pickle Peeps hat and have had several compliments over the years whenever I wore it. The all-over print of smiling, shades-wearing dills, gherkins, and cornichons helps me take my races not too seriously. And I’ll absolutely use this hat as an unvoiced request to have the pickle that comes with your sandwich during a postrun brunch.

I loved this hat so much, I called a Barnes & Noble in Dallas, Texas, to find it and please mail it back when I realized I returned home without my Pickle Peeps in tow. But it’s not just this hat: bananas, ice cream, flying pigs, pizza slices—I have a Sprints hat for every craving and every mood.

My only critique is the Velcro closure. It’s ruined running shirts, scarves, and whatever else is in my laundry basket or accessories pile. Sprints has snapbacks, but they don’t come in an extensive pattern collection. Sometimes I have to safety-pin the closure when the humidity puffs out my hair.

The Varsity Runner’s Hat brings to mind snowy winters on campus when I went to college in Latest England. The hat stays put when I head out on windy winter runs, and functions as an out-and-about beanie when I’m not running. The 100-percent merino wool material helps with thermoregulation and sweat-wicking.

The Creek Run Beanie’s waffle knit texture screams cozy, but you can also wear it when you’re actually running (as its name suggests), or skiing if that’s also your thing during the winter. This hat is stretchy but it does run small.

Industry observers note that the Skida Alpine is a stretchy, toasty hat that doesn’t overheat your head. Senior Editor Cat Bowen appreciated how the hat was sensory-friendly; its material feels super smooth, and it requires no tugging or micro-adjusting.

Fit can sometimes be tricky when the hat you’re interested in is unisex, or the over-confidently phrased “one size fits all.” You want the hat to be secure around your head so it doesn’t fly off on windy runs, but not too tight that you get a headache.

If the hat comes in multiple sizes, peruse the site’s fit instructions to match. If it’s the dreaded OSFA, check the type of adjustability and material to make sure it stretches and it can expand—or tighten—around your crown.

In a recent development, concerning caps, you have plenty of options to consider in terms of adjustability and closures. Velcro allows you to easily adjust without fumbling with toggles or buckles and straps, but the material isn’t stretchy and can lose its adhesiveness. Buckles/snaps stay put but can be a pain to troubleshoot and aren’t always easy to adjust midrun.

My personal favorite is the bungee toggle, but they don’t always lock in place and the cord can overstretch over time.

I’m the owner of several hats and no matter how much I rotate or wash them, they eventually get funky. Besides retiring old hats or soaking them in vinegar and baking soda, one thing that doesn’t draw flies to my head postrun is perforated panels or mesh on my cap.

Material is also key, especially when it comes to beanies. Instead of the inevitable sauna your head would be subjected to running in a rigid, cotton-canvas trucker hat, technical running caps are made of nylon and polyester, and beanies are made of polyester and merino wool, which evaporate moisture by drying fast.

Any ol’ running hat, IMHO, is better than none, but there are hats with extra features to look for if you want a hat more tailored to your needs. Some hats come with UPF to block UVB and UVA rays. Reflective detail is something to consider if your runs are mostly in low light. Pockets are great for storing small items, like a key or even a photo ID if you’re okay with running with a noticeable rectangle on the side of your head. I sure am.

How do I measure my head to get my hat size?

According to recent reports, the circumference around your head, above your eyebrows and ears is the measurement you seek. You can use a tape measure, or string and ruler if you don’t have measuring tape, to find your circumference. Then, check the brand’s sizing, if provided, to find your fit.

Does running in a cap make you warmer?

Sources indicate that this depends on the thinness of the material and the breathability features—is it mesh, perforated? Some caps like the Nathan Cool Stash Hat can store cold packs or ice in a pocket. An easy way to keep your head cool is to dunk your hat in cold water before heading out on a run. And to keep your head warm? Go with a hat made of merino wool, which naturally insulates.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

In a recent development, cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Tech Report: 20-Minute Seated Yoga to Help You Find Some Stillness

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This 2o-minute yoga for rest practice, led by adaptive and accessible yoga teacher Rodrigo Souza, asks you to slow your body and quiet your thoughts through simple seated movements.
  • Sources indicate that we live in a culture that teaches us to keep moving.
  • Recent findings suggest that I struggle with this, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This 2o-minute yoga for rest practice, led by adaptive and accessible yoga teacher Rodrigo Souza, asks you to slow your body and quiet your thoughts through simple seated movements. Think of it as yoga for stillness, and no, that’s not an oxymoron.

Sources indicate that we live in a culture that teaches us to keep moving. To produce, compete, consume, achieve, and constantly reach for what comes next. So much of our attention is placed in an imagined future that it can be easy to forget how to inhabit the life that is already here. Our bodies are present, but our minds are often somewhere else.

Recent findings suggest that I struggle with this, too. My mind moves very fast. It wants to create, teach, write, travel, and participate in everything life has to offer. But I live in a body with a disability, and my body moves at a very different rhythm. Sometimes finding the balance between what my mind wants and what my body needs is one of the hardest parts of my practice.

Yoga continues to teach me that listening is also a form of action. There are moments when I need to stop being the teacher, the creator, or the person trying to be of service and become my own teacher instead. I have to notice what my body is asking for and offer myself the same compassion I would offer one of my students.

Rest can be difficult because many of us have learned to associate our worth with what we accomplish. Stillness can feel almost uncomfortable. But yoga reminds us that we do not need to earn our right to pause. Rest is not the absence of practice. Sometimes rest is the practice.

When we become still, we begin to notice what constant movement can hide: the breath moving through us, the release of the body being supported, the sensations of the present moment, the simple experience of being alive. We return from the imagined future to the body that has been here all along.

It has been revealed that the following yoga practice is an invitation to return to stillness without guilt. To listen before forcing. To receive support instead of always pushing forward. To remember that there are moments when the most loving thing we can do is simply stop.

Sources indicate that we do not always need to be becoming something. Sometimes yoga asks us to stay here long enough to realize that this moment, this breath, and this body are already enough.

Sources indicate that welcome to your seated accessible yoga class. This class is about yoga for rest. It’s about yoga for stillness and finding that place within ourselves that is always at peace and rested. Let’s go there.

According to recent reports, as you can see, I am in a wheelchair. I am going to adapt the practice to my body, and I would love if you would adapt it to your body as well. Use your agency. You can visualize the practice or change the movement according to your needs. You will need a sturdy chair.

In a recent development, find a comfortable seat in your chair. Feel the soles of your feet touching the ground or your sit bones touching the chair. Release your shoulders. Go ahead and close your eyes or find a soft gaze, whatever is comfortable for you, in Mountain Pose.

Dive inward, noticing how you feel with compassion. Notice how still and peaceful everything feels. Your mind might be taking you places, and you can gently bring yourself back. You can also notice your breath at this moment. Feel this sense of calmness and tranquility. Notice the temperature of the room. Unclench your jaw. Try to soften the muscle between your eyebrows. Gently open your eyes.

We’re going to start with some mindful movement.

I would love for you to hold your chair frame and start gently rocking in your chair from side to side, shifting your weight between your right and your left sitting bone as you do that.

As you rock, you can extend one arm out to the side as far as is comfortable to you. First your right arm. Then your left arm. Do that another time on each side.

Come back to center and maybe add some hip circles. Then change directions. Always noticing how you feel, always being grounded and moving consciously.

According to recent reports, after energizing your body, bring yourself back to stillness. Soften your shoulders.

According to recent reports, you’re going to bring some mindful eye movement to Mountain Pose. Raise your stare straight ahead at the screen in front of you. And from this place of stillness, you’re going to trace the shape of the screen with your eyes. You can do that by gazing to the four corners of the screen. You can do that 3 times in both directions, never forgetting to breathe.

In a recent development, behind the screen that you’re looking at, there is a wall. Now trace the shape of the wall. Imagine that there is a brush on the tip of your nose that you are going to gently invite some neck movement here, moving 3 times. Then repeat in the opposite direction.

Stay here in Mountain Pose. Don’t go anywhere. Notice how you feel. Maybe place one hand on your heart and another on your belly.

Release both arms at your sides. Lower your right ear toward your right shoulder, and you can use your right hand to hold onto your chair frame for better balance. Spend some time here noticing the stretch along the left side of your body.

While leaning your head toward the right, you can add some movement, reaching your left arm toward the side. You can move your hand from palm facing forward to palm facing backward at the same time as you turn your gaze from the ceiling toward the floor.

Then repeat on the other side, leaning your heard toward the left and reaching your arm to the right and flipping your palm forward and backward.

Sources indicate that bring your body back to center. Reposition yourself in your chair if you need to feel secure to raise your arms. You can instead visualize the side bending movement.

Recent findings suggest that start from your Mountain Pose. Inhale, raise your arms any amount, gaze toward your hands, and hold it here. Exhale, lower your right arm and get hold your chair frame with your right hand as you reach your left arm overhead in a Side Stretch. Inhale and exhale here a couple times.

Raise both arms up again. Then exhale hold your chair frame with your left arm and get into a side bend with your right arm. Come back to center with both arms overhead. And then release. Maybe you give your arms a little shake.

In a recent development, take a moment here. Always bring yourself back to stillness. Notice how you feel.

I adapt Sun Salutations to my beautiful self, so I invite you to adapt it to your beautiful self as well. We’re going to do this 3 times. Try to synchronize your breath and movement as much as you can, always taking a long exhalation.

Sit up tall with your arms at your sides. Inhale, raise your arms any amount.

Exhale, lower your arms and come into a forward fold. You can release your head down or you can keep your spine extended.

Inhale, come back to center as you sit upright.

Exhale, come into Cat Pose by rounding your back.

Inhale, into Cow Pose by arching your back and lifting your chin.

Inhale, raise your arms one more time.

Exhale, hands together in prayer at your chest in anjali mudra.

Sources indicate that that was our Sun Salutation. Repeat that twice more, moving at your own pace. You might need to reposition yourself in your chair.

When you are done, bring some stillness back to your body.

Sources indicate that I would love for you to cross your right leg over your left leg. Press your right foot against the floor and then bring your left elbow against your right thigh. Inhale and come into a gentle twist here, turning toward the right. Gaze over your right shoulder. Get into stillness here. Inhale, exhale.

And release your leg. Now we do the same thing on the opposite side. And release as you bring yourself back to center.

It has been revealed that let’s go back to that space of stillness one last time. You can bring one hand to your heart center and the other to your belly. Relax your shoulders. Close your eyes if it’s comfortable for you. Notice if your mind wanders somewhere and bring it back to stillness, back to that place where there is nothing missing, that place of rest. Stay here in that place of stillness.

Industry observers note that when you’re ready, gently open your eyes. Inhale and raise your arms any amount. Exhale and bring your hands to anjali mudra, prayer hands, a sign of gratitude in front of your heart center. Thank you so much. I would love to remind you that the world might be very busy out there, but there is that place inside you that is always in peace, always in rest, always still, and you have access to that any time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

Sources indicate that recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes. I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

According to recent reports, keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

According to recent reports, this budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Sources indicate that using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

Sources indicate that besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

The bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

It has been revealed that this is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another big plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

Industry observers note that to keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more.

Sources indicate that merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. It follows the familiar design cues of premium exercise bikes — a sturdy frame, heavy flywheel, and whisper-quiet belt-drive system. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

The Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. It connects via Bluetooth to the Echelon Fit app, allowing you to track speed, distance, and calories. If you’re taking a live class, you can also view your ranking on the leaderboard. The app offers over 40 live classes daily and a library of more than 15,000 on-demand sessions. While the bike doesn’t have a built-in screen, its device holder accommodates tablets up to 8 inches wide.

That said, you don’t need the connected features to get a great workout. At its core, this is a solid, well-built exercise bike with a heavy flywheel and 32 resistance levels, manually adjusted with a knob behind the handlebar. The bike features a “one size fits most” design, with adjustable saddle and handlebar positions to suit most adults. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

With Bluetooth and USB connectivity to the Schwinn ConnectTM, Zwift, and MyFitnessPal apps, this stationary bike is a great option for interactive workouts—particularly if you want to work through pre-programmed sessions and track your progress over time. The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

Sources indicate that unlike many of the bikes we've selected that adjust gradually in difficulty at the turn of a knob, this model has 25 preset levels of magnetic resistance, which provides a nice range in difficulty. The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit people from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

Looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

While it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

People love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”.

Industry observers note that just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s important to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

In a recent development, for example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, says Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

According to recent reports, if you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” notes Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

Flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

In a recent development, since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.

#172816. The Real Grand Theft

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (899 w)

The Real Grand Theft

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor-in-chief Chris Foster on why Grand Theft Auto 6 costs more than you think (Photo: Donald Miralle/Getty Images).
  • Everything has a price, and I think the cost of Grand Theft Auto 6 — the much-anticipated sixth installment of one of the most successful video games in history — is far too high.
  • Triathletes know all about expensive things: Tri bikes now start around $3,000 and rise (quickly) up from there; running shoes now routinely crack $200; and now we’ve got $270 swim caps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor-in-chief Chris Foster on why Grand Theft Auto 6 costs more than you think (Photo: Donald Miralle/Getty Images).

Everything has a price, and I think the cost of Grand Theft Auto 6 — the much-anticipated sixth installment of one of the most successful video games in history — is far too high.

And I’m not talking about the cost to your wallet.

Triathletes know all about expensive things: Tri bikes now start around $3,000 and rise (quickly) up from there; running shoes now routinely crack $200; and now we’ve got $270 swim caps. And don’t even get me started on entry fees — the 2026 Hawaii Ironman World Championship, for instance, topped $1,800, granted that’s easily our sport’s crown jewel, but even a newly introduced event like 70.3 Utah still rings in around $500.

And even once you factor in the hard out-of-pocket expenses for equipment, entry fees, pool access, coaching, travel, accommodations, and so on, there’s still that looming cost of your time.

If a midpack triathlete did our most popular 70.3 training strategy, they’d spend about 150 hours of training over the 20-week plan. For our 16-week Olympic-distance plan, a triathlete would rack up about 65 hours of training. That’s a pretty substantial chunk of life, but I know I’m preaching to the choir, as all triathletes know that our sport requires a big time commitment.

However, there’s good news: We know that much of that time can be spent outside; we know that — when done correctly — swimming, biking, and running are very healthy endeavors; and we know that much of that time can be spent with others. To that last point, for better or for worse, even just the act of going to a race forces us to participate within a community.

In a digital world that competes ferociously for our attention (think: social media, TV, AI, and so on), giving your precious and valuable attention — your time — to swimming, biking, running, and triathlon will do more for your physical and mental health than getting hooked and strung out on a screen for hours.

Sources indicate that so it’s here, in the obsession over the release of GTA 6, that as the leader of an outdoor-related title — and within the context of an era of critically dangerous social disconnection and physical isolation — I find myself confused about why the larger culture is celebrating the creation of something that will drain our attention and time like a dystopian plug in the back of a Matrix battery-person’s skull. I just can’t celebrate.

On one hand, a video game centered on crime and violence is probably more of a sign of the times than a cause for rising crime rates in real life. I’ll succumb to a little bit of Qoheleth-level despair recognizing here that “what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.”.

In a recent development, and of course this is an outdoor sports publication, not Morality Weekly, but I still can’t shake another quote from the bestselling book of all time: “The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness.”.

GTA 6’s content notwithstanding, from my position in outdoor/endurance sports, I certainly can’t quite abide when our culture treats the release of a video game like a high holy holiday. Especially when it comes at such a high cost.

Set aside the hard price tag of a gaming console and game (let’s say less than $1k), which is actually relatively low compared to a hobby like triathlon, and keep your eyes fixed on the time cost and quality.

Experts from IGN note that Grand Theft Auto 6 took their editors between 42 and 115 hours to complete the upcoming release. It’s probably a good guess that the average gamer would spend 80ish hours to noodle around in that virtual environment. That’s a lot of “life spend.”.

And unlike many other video games, it’s time spent, well…alone.

Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 has no multiplayer mode as of this writing (though it could come). This means there’s no opportunity to connect with other people — even remotely — during gameplay. You can’t commit crimes alongside your buddies in the living room; you can’t fire at police alongside friends in Sweden, Hong Kong, or France. You’re alone, for 60 hours, stealing cars and shooting people. You interact only with that world and the characters coded into it.

Now I won’t be entirely obtuse here — not everyone can physically train for a triathlon; not everyone has time or safe access to a place where they can spend 65-150 hours outdoors, even if they wanted to.

However, there is a large proportion of people whose time spent playing a video game (alone) will prevent them from being outside (with others) — moving their bodies through nature in some way, shape, or form.

That’s why, rather than relish the empty streets and bike paths that have been reported across major metropolitan areas this week, I’ll be hoping that once the game ends and the credits roll (do video games have credits?), folks will head back outside to get a refund for time better spent.

Tech Report: Our Editors Rode Dozens of E-Bikes. These 12 Are Worth Buying for Commuting, Trails, Cargo, and Tight Budgets

📅 20 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, you wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions.
  • In a recent development, I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in Fresh York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, you wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions. However, whether you’re hunting for deals or seeking out the latest tech, now is the time to buy. With holiday discounts and new e-bikes rolling out to dealers and online retailers, plenty of great commuter, cargo, and e-MTB options are out there—at great prices.

In a recent development, I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in Fresh York City. Plus, I commute daily on an e-bike and ride test dozens of electric bikes each year. Last summer, I even went almost entirely car-free thanks to an electric cargo bike.

Industry observers note that whether you’re choosing your first e-bike, upgrading to a newer model, or adding another electric model to your garage, dozens of great options are available—and our editors and staff have tested many of them. No matter your age, cycling ability, or budget, brands offer electric bikes that meet needs.

In a recent development, tip for E-Bike Buyers: Don’t overpay for an electric bike, but spend what you can comfortably afford. If an e-bike is fun to ride, you’ll use it more often. It’s more cost-effective to buy an e-bike equipped the way you want it upfront than to upgrade it later. Also, remember: you cannot change an electric bike’s motor system if you decide you want more power.

It has been revealed that the Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. Over several years, the Level platform has proven to be reliable and low-maintenance. Plus, its price doesn’t break the bank.

It has been revealed that aventon split the 4th-generation Level into two models. The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. Aventon also added regenerative braking, increasing the bike’s range up to 75 miles. The pricier ADV edition features a mid-drive motor; it bumps up the torque to 100 Nm and range to 110 miles. Both versions come standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

According to recent reports, another feature users will find quite useful is the Level’s connected features. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

BUY LEVEL 4 STEP-THROUGH BUY LEVEL 4 ADV.

The relatively affordable seven-speed model Soltera 2.5 from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat. This makes it an excellent choice for getting around town or quick commutes. It’s even better than the original version, thanks to hydraulic disc brakes. A push of the throttle gets you started; then, the brushless hub motor gently assists your pedaling.

Industry observers note that along with disc brakes, the Soltera features integrated lights and turn signals, and the battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (rather than the bolt-on batteries found on many similarly-priced e-bikes). Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a strikingly light 46-pound package.

Aventon also offers a singlespeed, Soltera 3 ADV with a Gates belt-drive system.

Sources indicate that when buying a low-priced e-bike, a simple, low-cost, easy-to-repair, and reliable model usually beats out complicated designs. Lectric’s XP Lite2 is about as basic as it gets. It has a low-maintenance singlespeed drivetrain, a 300-watt hub motor, and a 375Wh battery. With its compact size, 20x2.5-inch tires, and twist-grip throttle, the XP Lite is perfect for zipping through traffic, commuting to the office, or heading to the gym or bar after work.

The XP Lite2 features only one gear and a 300W motor, so it’s not ideal for very hilly terrain. But with the throttle, you can get over small rises and bridges. Lectric also equips the bike with hydraulic disc brakes and front and rear lights. The XP Lite2 is also great for RVers and campgrounds, since it’s lightweight (about 48 pounds) and folds down to 36x16x27-inch dimensions.

Industry observers note that many “step-through” e-bikes don’t actually have a low step design. This makes it challenging for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, by REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. The CTY is a great choice for older riders, those with reduced mobility, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

Recent findings suggest that REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor that provides smooth pedal-assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem for a comfortable riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for better stopping. For less than the cost of some e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI warranty and service.

It has been revealed that the Current ADV is the priciest bike in this story, but for a good reason. Some electric bikes look a lot like mountain bikes, but that doesn’t mean they are built for real off-road use. Aventon’s new Current is the brand’s first full suspension E-MTB, and it is trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, noted, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor with 750 peak Watts and 110 Nm of torque. (It also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and 120 Nm of torque.) Rounding out the ADV are high-end components like a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

Recent findings suggest that in his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab particularly likes the Current’s easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data as well as the ability to tune the motor settings. If you don’t need rear suspension, check out Aventon’s updated Ramblas ADV hardtail E-MTB.

READ AVENTON CURRENT REVIEWMORE GREAT E-MTBs.

Getting into E-MTB trail riding on a budget is tough. Low-priced electric mountain bikes often aren’t built strong enough for off-road riding (or weigh half a rider’s weight), and trail-capable models typically cost more than $4,000. That’s what makes the TrailRush a standout bike—for less than $2,000, you get a trail-ready hardtail you can take on singletrack and have some fun.

Ride1Up equips the 29-inch-wheeled TrailRush with a Brose mid-drive motor. With 90 Nm of torque, it isn’t as powerful as many new, higher-priced E-MTB motors, but it gets the job done. The TrailRush also comes stock with a dropper seatpost, four-piston disc brakes, and tubeless-compatible rims with Maxxis Minion tires.

According to recent reports, of course, to hit this great price, Ride1Up made some equipment sacrifices. The 504Wh battery isn’t as large as some peers (like the Aventon Ramblas), so you get less ride time between charges. Additionally, the 11-36T cassette and 38T chainring limit your ability to climb steep hills.

Sources indicate that compared to earlier iterations of the Aventure, the third-generation model has a smoother ride and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s upcoming torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found earlier models had too much torque, but this Aventure remedied that fault. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

It has been revealed that the Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-roading, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths, but with this burly bike’s weight and components, it has limited functionality on singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Industry observers note that aventon also offers the Aventure M, a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same massive, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price. Those refinements cost about $1,000 more than the Aventure 3.

Industry observers note that buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have limited mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike technology, but it lets you get out and enjoy some rides without breaking the bank.

I combed through dozens of Amazon listings comparing low-priced electric bikes, and this Heybike stood out for its combination of price and features. Then, I saw someone on the local bike path with one and asked them about the bike. The rider liked it and noted it has been trouble-free (they noted a local bike shop assembled it for them). Heybike’s U.S. support line is available for warranty service or product questions.

Don’t want to purchase from Amazon? Use this exclusive Bicycling discount link for $100 (applied at checkout) off the Cityscape 2.0, plus free shipping.

In a recent development, tern’s cargo bikes are the gold standard for practical features, durability, and ride quality. This reputation makes the brand’s GSD (longtail) and HSD (short-tail) cargo models top picks for bike commuters, families, and riders looking to cut their dependence on automobiles.

The fresh third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

Industry observers note that while it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example of this is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

In a recent development, many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. At the moment priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it boasts an impressive 60-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. (The dual-battery model for $1,799 doubles the range to 120 miles.) This makes the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around and a good option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

“The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

In a recent development, however, to reach a price like this, concessions have to be made somewhere. This results in a somewhat cheap feeling to the bike. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but at times, it feels erratic. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend buying.

Recent findings suggest that plenty of commuter e-bikes cost far less than Specialized’s Turbo Vado SL 2, and they can probably do most of these things. So why spend twice as much as many popular options? I dive into the details in my story, “Stop Wasting Money on Cheap E-Bikes. Here’s Why Spending More Pays Off for Commuters.”.

It has been revealed that the TL;DR: The Turbo Vado SL 2’s excellent ride geometry, silky-smooth motor, low weight, and premium components make riding fun. Together, these features make you want to ride the Vado every day and use it for more than simply getting to work. And thanks to Specialized’s extensive dealer network, you have somewhere to turn when it needs service.

Industry observers note that “Lightweight e-bike” might sound like an oxymoron to some, but a sub-40-pound weight is impressive when many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds. And often, e-bikes this light are pricey. Yet, the Velotric Tempo is only $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight.

Sources indicate that velotric achieves this weight reduction by ditching the bulky suspension fork (suspension forks on lower-priced bikes often don’t work all that well, to be frank), swapping heavy tires for 700x42c gravel tires, and using a smaller battery. Riders who need to carry the bike up any stairs or load it onto a bike rack will appreciate the reduced weight. However, heavier riders may want to test ride the Tempo before purchase, as lower-powered motors can bog down and reduce battery range for bigger-bodied people.

In a recent development, bicycles are my life, and I’m a dedicated e-bike user and enthusiast. I’ve also worked in cycling for over 25 years. For almost six years, I’ve ridden and tested electric bikes as Bicycling’s Deputy Editor—and I use e-bikes for my daily commute. Before joining the staff, I led product development for top bicycle brands.

Industry observers note that our editors test dozens of electric bikes across every cycling category, and we continually receive newly introduced models to evaluate. Our riding involves much more than taking bikes on short spins; we use electric bikes in our daily lives. Commuting, school drop-offs, grocery runs, and daily transportation are only a few of the things we regularly do with e-bikes. We also hit the trails on E-MTB models to test their performance in real-world mountain biking conditions, not simply riding them around town.

In addition to ride-testing, our editors regularly talk to cyclists of all ages and abilities about their riding needs. This helps us craft our list of Best Electric Bikes: e-bikes that will meet your needs on the street, trails, and around the neighborhood. Two of the e-bikes in this story even made the final cut for our 2026 Bike Awards.

Recent findings suggest that electric bike prices range from entry-level models for less than $500 to premium machines costing almost as much as a good used car. However, our years of testing have proven that many of the best and most practical models live squarely in the middle.

It has been revealed that we find that many standout e-bikes are priced between $1,500 and $3,000. These models strike a good balance between reliability and practicality, without requiring you to overspend on features or technology you don’t need. Electric bikes costing less than $1,000 often take shortcuts to achieve this, either by using lower-quality parts or offering limited service after the bike is purchased.

Of course, you can also spend much more on electric bikes. Premium e-bikes typically offer improved motor performance, higher-quality components, lower weight, or more tech features. However, for most general riding purposes, these bikes are overkill—but they‘re certainly fun!

→ Consider how much cargo you’ll need to carry if your riding involves commuting or running errands. Look for a bike with appropriate racks, mount points, and other accessories.

→ For singletrack and trail riding, look for mountain bikes with knobby tires, adjustable suspension, high-quality frames, and low weight.

→ Pay attention to weight. While fat tire e-bikes and cargo bikes offer versatility, many weigh over 90 pounds. If you’ll need to carry your bike up any stairs or lift it onto a bike rack, a lighter option will be a better fit.

→ Bike storage is another consideration. While most e-bikes don’t require excessive space compared to their non-pedal-assisted counterparts, ensure you have access to a power outlet where you initiative to store it for easy charging.

Recent findings suggest that several e-bike brands, Aventon, Ride1Up, and Lectric, performed well in our ride testing and evaluations. These bikes might require some minor assembly at home, such as installing pedals, a seat, and tightening handlebars. We considered how easy bikes were to assemble in our recommendations. Many bike shops will not assemble or otherwise work on e-bikes they do not sell due to liability issues. The direct-to-consumer brands we recommend have dealers nationwide ready to support you.

Established bike companies, such as Specialized and Trek, manufacture e-bikes and have hundreds of dealers across North America. Additionally, REI sells its house-brand Co-op electric bikes (and models from Cannondale and Tern) in its stores.

Recent findings suggest that there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding your bike.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Recent findings suggest that what this means: Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows customers to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Other countries classify electric bikes differently, and many do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Electric bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Sources indicate that bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. Mid-drive e-bikes tend to be more expensive, but are typically more reliable and higher performance. Because the extra weight on a mid-drive motor is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors.

Recent findings suggest that measured in Newton meters (or Nm), torque is a rotational measurement of force—and the number to pay attention to when you want an idea of an e-bike motor’s output. More torque means more power off the line and more boost to your pedaling.

Recent findings suggest that the heavier the bike, the more torque it needs. Lighter road bikes typically have 30 to 40 Nm of torque, and trail and cargo models (generally) have at least 80 Nm. Most commuter bikes fall somewhere in between.

According to recent reports, the size of an e-bike’s battery is measured in watt-hours (or Wh). This measurement represents the energy stored in the battery and how many watts it can deliver each hour. The higher the number, the longer the range, but the faster you go, the faster you drain the battery.

So, if a 504Wh battery paired with a 500W motor gives you one hour of ride time at the highest assist, riding at about half that power will double your range.

Many e-bike brands seamlessly integrate batteries to make the bike look sleeker (and more like a traditional non-assist bike). Most batteries lock to the bike and come with a key that lets you unlock and remove it, which serves multiple purposes: You can remove the battery and charge it off the bike, plus a locked battery deters (and hopefully prevents) a thief from stealing it. An e-bike with the battery removed is safer for hauling on a bike rack and lighter for carrying up steps.

It has been revealed that since e-bikes can maintain higher speeds for longer than standard bikes, you want extra control when riding. Wider tires provide better traction and the freedom to leave the pavement with little penalty, and a suspension fork will help tame some of the rougher roads you might explore. Good disc brakes are a must, too, for slowing a heavy bike at high speed. This is not a place to skimp.

Some e-bikes have an integrated lighting system that turns on when you power up the bike. While this is a great feature, it’s not a deal-breaker if your bike doesn’t come equipped this way. It’s just as easy to attach your own since so many great bike lights are available.

E-bikes need regular maintenance and repair to stay in good working condition. Because they’re heavier and go faster than non-assist bicycles, e-bikes often require more regular service on parts like brakes, tires, and drivetrain components. We recommend having a good relationship with a local bike shop experienced in e-bike repair to keep your equipment running smoothly.

In a recent development, E-bikes use electronics for their motors, batteries, and displays. These parts are often proprietary to bike brands or even specific e-bike models, making replacement more difficult than parts on non-electric bicycles. Make sure to use the correct electronic replacement parts to avoid damaging your e-bike (or it catching fire).

Established brands usually (but not always) have a good supply of these parts for replacement, even for years after a bike goes out of production. Bosch and Shimano are two e-bike motor manufacturers with some of the most compatibility between bikes and stock parts for previous generations of systems.

Sources indicate that look for e-bikes from brands that offer at least a one-year warranty on electronic components (many brands’ warranties are longer) and make items like replacement batteries for your bike. These parts are usually not cheap (sometimes up to half the cost of a new bike), but it’s the difference between having an e-bike that can be repaired or becomes a bicycle-shaped paperweight if something goes wrong.

Industry observers note that following a dramatic increase in fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes, there is a push from local officials, regulatory agencies, and advocacy groups across the U.S. for improved safety certification of e-bikes, batteries, and motor units. In September 2023, a New York City law took effect requiring that any e-bike sold in the city “has been certified by an accredited testing laboratory for compliance with Underwriters Laboratories (UL) standard 2849”.

It has been revealed that however, just because something is marketed as UL 2849 compliant, tested to UL 2849, or even “certified to UL 2849” does not mean it is UL Safety Certified. Ibrahim Jilani, UL’s Global Director of Consumer Technology, notes: “Certification is always earned by a manufacturer and not a given when they undergo a product submittal. The UL Mark, or any authorized certification mark, can only be issued upon successful demonstration of meeting the requirements of the safety standard.” You can find UL’s updated list of products certified to UL 2849 here. You can cross-reference OSHA’s Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories for a deep dive into the topic.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

She Just Qualified for the Olympic Marathon Trials—At Age 48

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roberta Groner had what she calls “a rocky road” for the year leading up to the Newly introduced York City Marathon on November 1.

In her previous three attempts at the marathon, during which she had hoped to run an Olympic Marathon Trials qualifying time (2:37), she had racked up three DNFs in a row.

According to recent reports, she was in great shape for the Valencia Marathon in December 2025, having just run 1:12:21 for the half marathon, and she thought she might be in shape to better her lifetime PR in the marathon, which is 2:29:09, from 2019, when she was 41. Her conservative goal was getting the Trials time.

But a warm day in Spain—about 75 degrees—and a brain lock about translating kilometers into miles caused her to step off the course late in the race. Her coach, Devon Martin, of the Central Park Track Club, still rues that one. “She had no idea she had seven minutes to spare at mile 18,” Martin mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that two weeks later, Groner hopped in the Marathon Project in Arizona. Martin had tried to convince her not to. Sure enough, her legs hadn’t recovered from the hard miles in Valencia, and she dropped out there, too.

Then came Grandma’s Marathon in June in Duluth, Minnesota. Groner felt off. She later realized that her body was adjusting to starting hormone replacement therapy for perimenopause symptoms. Another DNF.

By the time she got to New York City, her hometown race, Groner—a former nurse who is now a full-time coach with Central Park Track Club—was uncharacteristically a basket case.

According to recent reports, “I had to fight some mental demons, especially the week before,” she remarked. “My coach was probably like, ‘Oh, I can't handle her.’”.

Sources indicate that groner ran with the elite women, always a small group in New York, which leaves those who can’t keep pace with the strange sensation of running a big-city marathon alone. She was well behind the leaders, running side-by-side with Steph Bruce for the first 17 miles, before Bruce fell back. Groner spent the next 9 miles with her eyes scanning the distance for any women she could pick off on the way to the finish.

She passed a handful of runners in the final stretch and finished 22nd in 2:35:55, her third Olympic Trials qualifier. She’ll be 50 when the race goes off in St. Louis. Dot McMahan of Michigan, who has qualified for her sixth trials, will be 51.

“I was able to race and compete, which was great,” Groner remarked. “And yeah, it wasn't my fastest Latest York, but I was really happy with the performance. Knowing that my faster days could be done, I still want to race really well. To be able to pass a few people at the end. I’ll give it an A.”.

But are her fastest days really behind her? Groner doesn’t necessarily think so. And she’s not backing off her goals just because she’s in her late 40s.

Recent findings suggest that she had a decade away from running when her three sons—now 23, 20, and 19—were growing up, which makes her feel like a younger runner than she is. When she got back to running, most of her career highlights were after she turned 40. In 2019, she represented Team USA at the World Championships marathon in Doha, Qatar, finishing sixth in extreme heat and humidity. The race started at midnight to avoid the worst of the heat.

Since she’s been in the 45–49 age group, Groner has set 10 American records, at distances from the 3,000 meters to the marathon.

Although she states she takes days off more frequently now, she still routinely hits 90 miles per week. She’ll come into Manhattan several times a week from Latest Jersey to coach and train with the top men and women of the Central Park Track Club, many of whom lined the marathon course to cheer for her.

When Martin hired Groner as a coach at CPTC, Martin made her promise she wouldn’t give up on her running. Coaches can become so absorbed in their athletes’ needs, their own training takes a back seat. But for Groner, coaching others has made her even more coachable and tuned into her own abilities. Having a team full of training partners has been helpful, too.

Martin indicates she’s an inspiration to younger runners all over Fresh York.

It has been revealed that “We always joke, ‘When is this going to end?’” Martin mentioned of Groner’s fast times. “She just keeps surprising, and she has changed women’s running in Latest York City. Women in their 30s and their 40s, they look at running differently now.”.

Recent findings suggest that “She’s just a tough racer,” Martin added. “She’s so mentally strong, and just really believes she’s not done.”.

According to recent reports, sarah Lorge Butler is a writer and editor living in Eugene, Oregon, and her stories about the sport, its trends, and fascinating individuals have appeared in Runner’s World since 2005. She is the author of two popular fitness books, Run Your Butt Off! and Walk Your Butt Off!

Try This Variation of Sun Salutation if You Have a Tight Back or Hamstrings

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past challenges beginning in 1975.
  • Sun Salutations are a means of aligning your breath and movement in a cyclical, graceful way.
  • In a recent development, this Sun Salutation variation provides some opportunities for altering poses for anyone who experiences tightness in the back or hamstrings while retaining the strengthening along with the calming breath and movement of a classic Sun Salutation (Surya Namaskar).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Klaus Nielsen | Pexels).

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past challenges beginning in 1975. This article about a Sun Salutation variation for tight hamstrings poses appeared in the September-October 1990 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Sun Salutations are a means of aligning your breath and movement in a cyclical, graceful way. The series of poses unfolds in a way you can get lost in, creating the type of flow state you’re often after on your mat.

In a recent development, this Sun Salutation variation provides some opportunities for altering poses for anyone who experiences tightness in the back or hamstrings while retaining the strengthening along with the calming breath and movement of a classic Sun Salutation (Surya Namaskar). More specifically, it skips Plank but includes poses such as Chaturanga and the ferocious Upward-Facing Dog (Urdhva Mukha Svanasana), inviting you to further work your arms, legs, and abdominals.

Looking for even more of a challenge? Try hopping or jumping between poses when it makes sense for you.

Begin with your hands by your sides or at heart center in Mountain Pose.

Recent findings suggest that stretch your arms over the head and look slightly toward the sky in Upward Salute. If you want, bring your palms together and press.

Recent findings suggest that keep your knees bent as you bend forward with your arms extended over the head. Feel as if you are lifting your soft frontal body (the abdomen, organs, and lungs) into the shell of your back body (the pelvis, spine, and rib cage) so your spinal muscles do not overwork.

Recent findings suggest that as you hang in Standing Forward Bend, begin to lift your sit bones upward, so the legs begin to straighten a little and your pelvis tips farther forward over your feet. You will feel an increased stretch along the back of the legs as the knees straighten. If you feel strain in the back of the knees or the lower back, keep your knees bent.

On an inhalation, step your left leg back behind you in Low Lunge. Allow your left knee to bend slightly or lower to the floor and make sure that your right knee is directly over your right ankle. If this pose puts too much strain on your lower back or groin, rest your hands on two blocks placed on either side of your forward foot.

Recent findings suggest that exhale to place your hands on the your mat and step back to Downward-Facing Dog. In this version, bring the feet hip-width apart, lifting the sitting bones and keeping the knees bent if needed. Keep the sitting bones lifted as you lower the heels toward the floor.

The most common mistake in the practice of Chaturanga is to bring the shoulders all the way forward over the wrists without bending the elbows. Lowering the chest from this position requires tremendous arm strength and almost invariably results in lowering the belly first and then collapsing the chest onto the floor. Lowering the knees to the floor can help.

On an exhalation, gently lower the knees to the floor and shift the chest forward until it is directly over the hands. Keep the elbows close to the rib cage as they bend, lowering the torso toward the ground without bending through the middle of the spine. If your arm strength is insufficient to prevent the middle of the spine from collapsing, you may want to do Plank Pose instead.

keep the abdomen lifted into the lower back as the chest lowers to just above the floor. Press back through your heels to elongate the spine.

Keeping the knees lightly on the floor, inhale and press the hands into the floor to straighten the arms. As the arms straighten, come onto the tops of the feet and broaden the shoulders, rolling the base of the shoulder blades down and forward in Upward-Facing Dog. Draw the belly back into the body, to support the lumbar spine, and lengthen the abdomen upward toward the chest. This variation creates a less extreme curve in the lumbar spine than the straight-legged version. You can always lower your chest closer to the floor if the backbend feels too extreme.

Move through Downward-Facing Dog, Standing Forward Bend, and Upward Salute, finishing with your hands together at heart center in Mountain Pose.
