#172792. This Is the Minimum Amount of Time You Need After a Half Marathon to Run Your Next Race

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1324 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

This Is the Minimum Amount of Time You Need After a Half Marathon to Run Your Next Race

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race.
  • Sources indicate that but jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results.
  • Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race. You might only get a few chances per year to run a marathon, but you can stack up multiple half marathons, 5Ks, and 10Ks per season, as long as you balance those harder efforts with sufficient recovery time.

Sources indicate that but jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results. Even if you feel ready to race again soon after a half marathon, specifically, you might need more time than you think. So what’s the ideal reset time after 13.1 and when should you be able to line up again?

Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.

In general, it’s a good idea to take two to four weeks off from high-intensity work after a half marathon before racing again, says Laura Norris, a Seattle-based certified personal trainer and run coach with a master’s in applied exercise science.

You should first take three to five days postrace off completely to clear up any muscle damage and let your body fully recover, then stick exclusively to easy running for the rest of that two- to four-week period.

“There’s new research that shows the half marathon stresses the heart pretty decently for two weeks postrace,” Norris claims. While it’s not the same level of stress as a full marathon, it’s still important to take sufficient time to recover before tackling another high-intensity effort.

With that in mind, you can make adjustments to your timeline:.

The harder you push, the longer it takes to recover, so Norris suggests waiting those three to four weeks before racing again if you just ran your fastest half marathon, even if you feel good.

However, you can consider your upcoming race distance and goal: If you’re jumping into a Turkey Trot 5K for fun, for example, you can probably get away with just two weeks of recovery, but wait at least the entire four weeks before gearing up for a full marathon, Norris suggests.

After a race where you feel really beat up, you’re extra sore, mentally drained, or fatigued, it’s a good idea to take those first three to five days off followed by two to four weeks of really easy running, Norris indicates. But that doesn’t mean you jump right into another race.

It has been revealed that in this case, “it might be worth spacing your races at least six to eight weeks apart, maybe even a full training season apart,” she notes. Otherwise, you could enter into a vicious cycle of overtraining, not recovering fully, and entering another race underprepared and beating yourself up again, Norris explains.

It can feel really disappointing to train hard for months for your race and not have results to reflect that work, but it’s important to honor your recovery and health more than performance.

The amount of time you give yourself to recover from a bad race depends on the reason the race went poorly, Norris claims. If you just had a bad day, dealt with a difficult course, or struggled with fueling, you might stick to three to four weeks before another race.

According to recent reports, but if you were dealing with an illness after your event or you undertrained leading into it, then in addition to taking days completely off and a few weeks of easy running, you probably want another few weeks of adding in speed before jumping into another race, Norris suggests. This would give you an opportunity to prepare more for your next race, while allowing your body to heal.

Wait a minimum of six weeks before racing again. “That’s at least two weeks to recover, four weeks to navigate training again, and also a few weeks to make sure that you aren’t impulsively making a decision based on high postrace emotions,” Norris claims.

Norris notes that you have to evaluate how poorly you feel and listen to your gut, too. It’s always a good idea to get pain or potential injury addressed by a physical therapist and navigate your timeline from there.

In a lot of cases, you can use post-half marathon fitness to your advantage to tackle another race and see how much better you can do. “If you want to race in a couple weeks once your legs feel better and you’re not sore, it might not be a bad time to do a 5K,” says Christine Rockey, an exercise physiologist, RRCA-certified run coach, and principal lecturer at Coastal Carolina University.

But there’s a difference between setting your sights on another PR and jumping into a fun family 5K. Here’s how you should prepare in training for your next race, depending on your goal.

Norris suggests slowly ramping back up with about a week of 30-minute easy runs after the three to five days of rest. “They won’t feel great at first, but we just want to get the legs moving now that most of the muscle damage has started to repair,” she notes.

According to recent reports, then, continue with easy running during the following week, but try to aim for about 75 percent of your peak volume during half marathon training. For example, if your peak long run was 14 miles, you might aim to cover 10.

It has been revealed that if you have two more weeks, you can add in some race pace work to sharpen your speed during the first of those two weeks, then give yourself a week to taper. It’s always easier to maintain fitness than it is to build, and you want to avoid being overtrained before your next race, Norris claims.

As you lace up for your next race, keep a realistic goal in mind. It’s always good to be an ambitious runner and gain more race experience, but remember to keep your expectations in check, Rockey says. “I think if you go in thinking the next five races you do are all going to be PRs, I think you’re going to end up disappointed and you might even get so frustrated that you stop running,” she says.

It has been revealed that you have a bit more leeway to do lower volume and run a few short easy runs every other day, for example. Norris says you can coast on 50 percent of your peak half marathon volume and know that you’ll still be fit enough to jump into a last-minute 5K.

It’s important not to go back to a completely sedentary state if you initiative on racing again. “If you were to sit on the sofa [instead of easy running] and do absolutely nothing for three weeks, you would begin to detrain,” Norris adds. “It might not be that serious, but it would probably make the race not feel as good.”.

Sources indicate that plus, going from the couch to another half marathon can lead to aches and pains, Norris adds. “If you go from doing nothing for three weeks to doing 13 miles, that’s a huge jump in single-session load,” she states, pointing to a study published in 2025 that highlights jumping up your single-run volume by more than 10 percent in a 30-day span can increase injury risk.

Keeping up with a couple easy runs in between efforts will help you race your best—even when your best means having the most fun.

You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

Bike lights are a must-have item for anyone commuting or riding road or gravel in the winter months. Even if you already have a light, I’ve found it super useful to own an extra set to have at the office, on my other bikes, or as spares for friends.

Lezyne consistently makes great front and rear lights. While slightly pricier than budget picks found on Amazon or AliExpress, they’re durable, work well, and last several seasons. Plus, we’ve found Lezyne’s advertised runtimes and lumens are much closer to reality than many no-name lights.

Garmin’s Varia RTL515 is our benchmark cycling radar, and its fresh RearVue 820 builds on that great reputation—and it’s on sale for Black Friday. Compared to the 515, the RearVue 820 has more battery life (up to 15 hours), a brighter flashing light (100 lumens), and greater vehicle-detection range (up to 191 yards). Plus, the 820 adds a brake-light feature that increases rear light intensity as you slow.

Industry observers note that crucially, the RearVue 820 incorporates features found on no other radars (from Garmin or any other brand). While other radars often drop vehicles when they slow down behind you, the 820 tracks vehicles traveling at your same speed; it’s a handy feature you don’t know you need until you try it. Additionally, if you use a Garmin Edge X40- or X50-series computer, the radar tracks a vehicle that changes lanes behind you. It also shows icons to indicate each vehicle’s size (small, medium, or large).

Sources indicate that showers Pass makes our best-tested winter gloves, and they’re right now on sale at 19% off. In their review, our test rider remarked, “This knit, waterproof glove has a midweight feel and sufficient insulation when temperatures hover around freezing. Most riders will find the Crosspoints reach its limit at about 30-35 degrees, depending on how hard you’re riding.”.

It has been revealed that the glove traps some body heat, so your fingers may be slightly chilly at first but will warm up within 15 minutes. Better yet, when the mercury climbs, your hands won’t feel hot and sweaty.

Recent findings suggest that gore’s Endure glove is a solid pick for those cold or wet winter rides. The gloves’ Gore-Tex membrane sheds moisture while Primaloft insulation keeps your hands cozy. The Endure features a textured silicone palm—it helps you hold the bar in slippery conditions. Plus, the gloves are touchscreen-compatible, so you can operate your cell phone or head unit without your hands getting cold.

According to recent reports, shoe covers are a bit like gloves for your shoes. Winter socks help keep your feet warmer on cold rides, but they add bulk that can affect shoe fit. So, many cyclists turn to shoe covers and booties to wear over their cycling shoes. Shoe covers also block wind and create an air barrier to insulate your feet. I’m a fan of Capo’s knit shoe covers—they’re perfect for chilly rides when heavy booties are overkill. (Use code “BLACKFRIDAY25” at checkout.).

It has been revealed that electric mini-inflators burst onto the scene a couple of years ago and have promptly become a rider favorite for pumping up your tires at home, at the trailhead, or on rides. Of the inflators we’ve tested, the AS2 Ultra came out on top. With svelte dimensions and a 106-gram weight, the Ultra is small enough to stash in a jersey pocket, flat kit, or bar bag. Plus, it quickly inflates tires of all sizes to pressure. The AS2’s super-accurate gauge also makes it worth considering for your home shop or carrying in a race-day tool kit.

RockBros’ inflator stands out for its consistency and is a favorite of Bicycling editors. It’s compact, lightweight, and has an accurate gauge. In our testing of 15 electric pumps, it inflated a road tire to 65 psi in 45 seconds, and filled five tires before running out of power.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2—Bicycling’s Best Overall Indoor Trainer—is on sale for the lowest price we’ve seen: $399.99. The Core combines excellent performance, great accuracy, and high max resistance in a package perfect for Zwift rides after work, winter training, and even competitive virtual racing.

Indoor training bikes are promptly gaining popularity for their ease of use and low maintenance. With a dedicated indoor setup, you no longer have to wrestle with getting your bike on or off the smart trainer, which also makes it convenient to share with other riders in your family. Plus, you won’t wear out pricey parts. Zwift’s Ride is our favorite: it sets up quickly and adjusts for a wide range of rider heights and fits. It also costs thousands less than its competitors.

Sources indicate that shorter daylight hours and lower temps often mean fewer hours spent riding outside on the road or trail. An indoor trainer helps you maintain your fitness through the winter months while getting your riding fix. Garmin’s Tacx Flux2 is the brand’s mid-range smart trainer; with 2,000 watts of resistance, it simulates gradients up to 16%. The Flux also connects to virtual platforms like Zwift and Rouvy for immersive indoor riding experiences.

Stainless bottles have become popular among cyclists over the past several seasons. They keep water chilled on hot rides and don’t give your water a funny plastic taste. Many gravel and off-road riders love CamelBak’s Stainless Podium, particularly for its open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Stainless also ranked best in our heat testing last summer and performed well in our winter bottle testing.

SUMMER BOTTLE TESTING WINTER BOTTLE TESTING.

With a five-star rating and 8.14 STAR score, the P2R A20 Mips places third in Virginia Tech’s road helmet rankings (and eleventh overall). That ranking is great for any road or gravel helmet—but for a helmet that normally costs only $60, it’s downright amazing.

In a recent development, P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting many corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road. The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it said the A20 fits a little snug near their temples.

TOP 5 RANKED VA TECH ROAD HELMETS.

Recent findings suggest that elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs significantly less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

Sources indicate that this helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis uses the Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

MET’s Trenta 3K Carbon is one of the top five road helmets by Virginia Tech’s helmet lab. It’s also one of the best for racing and high-performance riding, as proven by UAE Team Emirates’s results—Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. Typically priced over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit, but this deal cuts the cost by almost a third.

Arm warmers are among the most versatile pieces of cycling clothing you can own. This magical piece of kit turns your short-sleeve jersey into a long-sleeve in seconds—and you can change back to short sleeves again mid-ride if the temps rise.

Industry observers note that I’ve owned many pairs of arm warmers over the last three decades, and I rarely ride without them on my arms or in my jersey pocket if the temperatures are between 45 and 60 degrees. Pearl Izumi makes some of my favorites, and these Elite Thermal arm warmers are a steal for the price. They’re easy to pull on or off while riding, and they don’t sag.

A quality rain jacket is a must-have item for riders who live anywhere it rains or snows. Rapha’s Core Rain Jacket is a great option for layering over your winter jersey without adding too much bulk. It features a two-way zip to regulate body temperature, reflective hits for riding after dusk or in the early morning, and packs down small if the weather clears mid-ride.

Sources indicate that if you ride in temps below 40 degrees, a good cycling jacket is a great asset. As a Scottish brand, Endura knows a few things about riding in the cold, dark days of winter, and its MT500 Freezing Point jacket is a great option for trail rides and commuting in low temps. It features PrimaLoft Gold insulation and a DWR finish to shed raindrops. Another great feature is the MT500’s underarm zippers; they allow you to cool off and ventilate without unzipping your entire jacket.

In a recent development, the Alpha Air jacket is a splurge-worthy piece of cycling kit. I’ve had one for the last four winters; I reach for it when temperatures will be sub-freezing. It features Polartech Alpha fleece on the chest to keep your core warm and lighter fleece on the arms and lighter, breathable fleece on the back and arms for thermal regulation. If you need an even heavier jacket, Velocio also has the Alpha Zero jacket on sale for Black Friday.

These bibs are pricey, but worth it. When cold weather hits, bib tights ensure you stay warm on rides. Of the many cycling tights available, Velocio makes some of our test editors’ favorites. The Luxe Thermal bibs use Velocio’s proprietary chamois and have cargo pockets on the thighs to carry snacks or your phone. They’re constructed from a compressive thermal fabric with wind-blocking panels to hold in warmth in conditions down to 32 degrees. This makes them perfect for road, gravel, and trail rides on all but the coldest days.

In a recent development, instead of shredding your nice, lightweight road tires on weather-worn winter roads, swap them out for more durable rubber. Vittoria’s Rubino tires are a proven all-season road tire with a smooth, fast-rolling center and siped edges for cornering traction. They’re tubeless-compatible, so you’ll catch fewer flats in the cold, and come in widths from 26mm to 34mm with black or tan sidewalls.

Modern bike computers do much more than display speed and distance. These devices are a critical information hub for many cyclists. Cycling computers can record ride metrics, display real-time performance data, and help you navigate—but that’s only scratching the surface of their capabilities.

A great option is the Hammerhead Karoo. This head unit features a 3.2-inch color touchscreen Gorilla Glass display and up to 35 hours of run time. The Karoo stands out for its mapping and navigation. The navigation, along with its pop-up hill climb feature and ability to sideload apps, makes the Karoo my overall favorite.

It has been revealed that the Edge 550 packs a ton of power and functionality into a small package. This makes it perfect for mountain bikers or road and gravel riders who don’t want a big screen sitting on their handlebar. Unlike the larger Edge 1050 and pricier Edge 850, the 550 model uses a button control interface instead of a touchscreen. This is super handy in winter when you’re wearing gloves, or if your display gets wet from snow or sleet. The Edge 550 gets up to 36 hours of use per charge, and it features LiveTrack, so friends and family always know where you are.

A good torque wrench is a must-have tool for anyone working on high-end, lightweight, or carbon bike parts. We use Topeak’s Torq Stick torque wrenches in our workshop. This model has an adjustment range from 4 to 20 Nm and includes Torx and hex bits in common bike bolt sizes. Topeak also includes an extender, a small ratchet, and a finger bit driver in the plastic protective case.

Sources indicate that POC makes comfortable, well-ventilated helmets for road, gravel, and mountain biking. The Kortal is a trail-style helmet, featuring an adjustable visor, room to stow your glasses or goggles, and plenty of airflow for hot summer trail rides. The straps are also comfortable, something that often bugs me on other lids.

Sources indicate that fresh bar tape is the quickest and most cost-effective way to improve the look, feel, and comfort of any road or gravel bike. I’ve used Fizik tape on several bikes that have come in for testing, and have also bought it for my personal bikes. It has enough cushion, reliable grip, and is easy to wrap. You can’t ask for much more from bar tape.

It has been revealed that while many riders are adding electric mini-inflators to their tool kits, a quality floor pump remains an essential part of every cyclist’s arsenal. They never run out of batteries, pump as many tires as your arms can handle, and are easy to use.

In a recent development, riders and mechanics have trusted Topeak’s JoeBlow pumps for decades—because they work. Although many JoeBlow models are low-cost and utilitarian, the JoeBlow Ace DX is a Cadillac-level floor pump. It features alloy construction with a metal chuck and can inflate tires up to 260 psi, with three different inflation modes: high-volume, standard, or high-pressure.

The 6 Best Folding Treadmills for Runners, Tested by a Treadmill Expert

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The best folding treadmills give you a real running experience without permanently eating up your floor space. I adore having a folding treadmill at home, because, living in a smaller space, I can easily stash it away or bring it out for a go. And this time of year, when there's sleet and snow? I don't want to miss out on a workout.

If you're like me and you want to be able to run a treadmill at home, but you can’t give away valuable space to a huge piece of fitness equipment? We get it. There’s a solution, though: A folding treadmill gives you the ability to pack up and store your ’mill between runs. Their compact size and light weight comes at a cost: They often don’t have as many convenient features we expect from a top-of-the-line model, nor do they offer huge inclines and top speeds. That remarked, most can do the basics effectively when you need them to, then fit in your closet when you’re done. The best folding treadmills, as we see them, offer a range of sizes and prices for casual runners and athletes in training.

The dream of shoving your treadmill under your bed between runs is alive in the Echelon Stride-6. This high-performance mill features a full-size, 20.5- by 60-inch running deck that can hit a max speed of 12.5 mph, but still manages to fold up tight. Personally, I store mine upright against a wall, sometimes hidden behind a curtain. It takes up about as much space as a few snowboards or a couple of winter coats. No, I'm not kidding, it's just that compact.

The Stride-6’s belt features low-response cushioning that creates a ride that feels closer to outdoor road running than treadmill running, which I love when I’m training for road races. Also, as an autistic sensory seeker, sometimes I really enjoy beating the hell out of the deck after a bad day. Are you also a sensory seeker, or have one in your life? If so, this is a solid choice. At full speed, with a 12 percent incline, this machine gives as good as it gets, too.

This treadmill does not have a touchscreen, though. Instead, it syncs directly to a running watch or tablet, for which it has an extra-large holder. The pre-loaded running programs are fine and dandy, but nothing to write home about. Echelon produces a paid workout video library like NordicTrack’s iFit, which you can access via an app, but it’s no different than any other virtual workout platforms without native support on the treadmill.

Let’s talk a little more about the folding mechanism, though, because that’s the reason to buy this treadmill. It is one of only a handful of options that doesn’t require any assembly. Unbox this beauty, unfold it, plug it in, and you’re good. It has an “autofold” feature that makes collapsing the treadmill feel seamless. All that you do is press the foot pedal, and the crossbar and board fold onto the surface of the treadmill. You can then store it flat on the ground or upright, which is a win for anyone who doesn’t have the permanent floor space available.

Also, after testing treadmill after treadmill in my house, I can confidently say my cats prefer the Stride-6, and I have no idea why. They're obsessed and I can't figure it out. It is also the easiest to store, fun to run on, and it's by far the easiest to move around.

According to recent reports, when this treadmill is folded, it practically disappears. Fully folded, it drops to under 11 inches tall, which is easily flat enough to slide under a bed or stand upright in a closet corner. For anyone training for a marathon in an apartment, a spare bedroom, or a shared space, you know the value there. The SwiftFold mechanism handles it in one motion, and there’s no assembly required.

Industry observers note that what I appreciate is that folding this flat usually means compromising on the machine underneath. This one doesn’t. You still get a dual brushless 4.0 HP motor, a 0–12 percent auto-incline, a 12.5 mph top speed, and a 300-lb weight capacity that matches most treadmills in its class. The 51.18 x 18.9-inch deck is a touch narrow for tall runners, and that is, admittedly an matter.But, when you add the real marathon course maps and an AI coach, along with that magical fold? At around $900 to $1,000 it’s a ‘mill that’s hard to say no to.

Urevo CyberMega Treadmill Review.

I will be the first to admit I was incredibly skeptical about this machine. I mean, it folds up to be smaller than your average card table. I have luggage that’s bigger than the G5i. But, I hear the cawing coming because I need to eat crow. It’s surprisingly stable and fun to run on. It’s really pretty smooth. It is more road-like than cushioned, so if you’re expecting pillowy surfaces, you’ll be disappointed. But if you’re worried you’re going to feel the fold seam, or feel super penned in, you won’t.

According to recent reports, no, this is not a treadmill for tall runners. I’m 6-feet tall, and I’m at the tippy top end of the range of someone who should throw miles on this. But, that being said, if you’re shorter than I am, starved for space, and you want a folding treadmill with serious speed and incline, this is a fantastic option. One thing I will note, though: that first fold when you’re folding it isn’t as soft as you’d expect, and it’s kinda loud. But considering the fact that you could store it just about anywhere, and that it takes less than five minutes to set up and assemble? It’s freaking impressive as all get out. Like, truly wild territory, here.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a serious running machine that also happens to fold, then you can’t do better than the NordicTrack Commercial 1750. Both Dengate and I really appreciated the feel of running on this machine, which has he called “Goldilocks” cushioning. The deck is firm enough that you don’t feel like you’re running on rubber but soft enough that it wasn’t as hard on our joints as a road run would be. We were also sold on the quick controls for both speed and incline changes, which are both easy to identify and toggle. I found that it stops a bit more abruptly than other NordicTracks: It’s not “knock you off your feet” fast, but there’s a little learning curve.

In a recent development, the Commercial 1750 has a large running surface, which I appreciate as someone who tends to wander on the ’mill a bit. All NordicTracks come with a trial subscription to iFit, the brand’s virtual workout library, which gives you dozens of programs, like marathon training companions, guided runs, and more. It costs extra after the first 30 days, but I think it’s a distinctive and worthwhile option if you like a guided workout. Of course, you can run on this treadmill without iFit, too.

Industry observers note that on to the folding: The frame is huge–it weighs over 300 pounds–so it needs the hydraulic lift help that gets it to fold. The process could be a hair easier, but the balanced weight makes it fairly simple. Moving the 1750, on the other hand, is tricky. Sure, it technically has wheels so that you can roll it around, but that requires tipping the machine and balancing it while you do. Once you place it, you can fold it, but you’re better off leaving it where it is.

According to recent reports, the Horizon 7.0AT was the easiest treadmill to get started and learn how to use, but its simplicity holds it back from being the outright best. It’s an old-school treadmill with no touchscreen display or video components, and that limits options for programming. That being said, it’s a very affordable option that gets the job done so long as you don’t need a guided workout or on-board entertainment.

The Horizon 7.0 does exactly what you expect and does a great job of it. It has a 20- by 60-inch running deck that’s plenty large enough for the majority of runners. I wish that it felt a little firmer underfoot, but other members of our team did not have the same complaint. The pre-loaded programs are easy to find if you know your way around a treadmill. (Most of the runners I spoke with are “set and forget” or running with program apps—which you can link through your watch or tablet—so it’s not a worry.) The toggles for speed and incline are intuitive and easy to use.

Folding this one is nice and easy, thanks to a hydraulic assist mechanism. Moving it around is pretty easy, too: The wheels line up in a better place than the 1750. It shrinks by nearly 40 percent when folded, which is genuinely impressive when you consider its massive build and huge incline range. One thing to keep in mind, though: That steep incline lifts you fairly high, so I do not recommend it for basement gyms unless you plan on running flat, or you live in a fancy place with 9-foot basement ceilings.

Read Full Horizon 7.0AT Treadmill Review.

I’ve never met a treadmill that folds up smaller than the WalkingPad R2. In keeping with the brand, it’s made for walking, with a top speed of 3.7 mph and speed walking at 7.5 mph. And honestly? It’s so compact that you could reasonably put one of these in your home as a more portable complement to a standard, non-folding treadmill without feeling cramped. Use it as an under-desk treadmill or move it around to wherever you can find some free space.

It’s a fantastic treadmill for anyone who wants to get moving when they’d otherwise be sitting around. It features a smaller deck, super-responsive cushioning, and whisper-quiet motor. You could walk on it during a Zoom call with your microphone unmuted, and people would be hard-pressed to hear it. The cushioning means that you’re not going to wear yourself out while you work, and keeps you from bouncing around so badly that you can’t type.

One little thing I like about this folding treadmill is its smart “automatic mode,” which automatically detects your speed changes depending on where your feet are hitting the deck and adjusts as you go. That alone is worth the cost of the machine.

According to recent reports, folding this treadmill is a cinch, and so is storage, thanks to its low weight and small footprint. Even if you store it in a different room from where you use it, it’s only 55 pounds, so you can just haul it from space to space without any problem.

The team at Runner’s World has been testing all things running for decades. We work year-round on everything from shoes to treadmills. Personally, I have been running for over 20 years, running multiple marathons and ultras, and treadmill training is a huge part of my regimen. And I’ve been professionally reviewing products for nearly a decade.

Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate designed a rigorous testing protocol to measure a number of critical features in each and every treadmill that we test, and I wrote a specific rubric to test folding treadmills based on that protocol. This year alone, I have run on over 40 models, racking up almost 200 miles in the past several months. Dengate, who is “never not running,” has also put in miles on many of these models. With folding treadmills, there are several specific qualities we examine to separate the best from the just ok:.

It has been revealed that having the ability to fold should not make a treadmill any less useful. While it’s impossible for them to maintain all of the features of certain non-folding treadmills, many or most of them are every bit as good. Some are so gozZod that they even appear on many of our guides.

Recent findings suggest that even with a compact folding model, it’s crucial to proposal ahead and measure out the spaces where you plan to use and/or store your treadmill. Keep in mind that you need at least 2 feet of clearance surrounding your treadmill in every direction while you’re running. As someone who has put a Cat-shaped hole in the wall of her basement because I lost my footing, I cannot recommend this enough.

There’s a Right Way to Fold and a Wrong Way to Fold.

Recent findings suggest that this sounds like a no-brainer, but a folding treadmill should become more compact and easy to store when folded. There are a ton that technically have a folding mechanism but are not all that much smaller in their folded form. If the folded treadmill is too tall for a room, or if it doesn’t clear very much floor space, it doesn’t make sense.

A small running platform can prevent you from feeling comfortable at your full running stride, so we generally think that longer is better. (There are exceptions, of course: A walking pad doesn’t need a long belt.) Width is crucial for people with a wider stride or who tend to wander a bit, or those of us who run a bit duck-footed. A narrow belt can feel constricting when you’re running.

Don’t Worry Too Much About Max Speed and Incline.

Recent findings suggest that with folding treadmills especially, you only want as much power as you actually need. A faster max speed requires a bigger motor, which makes for a bigger, heavier treadmill. Most people will be just fine with 10 mph for running, and 3 or 4 mph for walking, so a huge motor isn’t necessary.

It has been revealed that inclines are controlled by a separate motor, so the same rule applies. Most of us don’t want to pretend we’re climbing Everest at the gym, so a 15 percent incline is overkill. It’s nice to have occasionally, but not a dealbreaker to go without.

What are some ways to stay safe on the treadmill while training?

Industry observers note that with the treadmill setting the pace for you, it is important to select a pace that you feel capable of walking or running at, and use the safety equipment provided. Be sure you know where the automatic stop switch is and where the speed adjustment buttons are before starting to run/walk.

Should I adjust my mileage while using a treadmill?

Industry observers note that because treadmill running can be easier than road running, you may need to increase your mileage (or adjust speed and incline) when training on the treadmill to get the same level of workout you get from running outdoors. However, many people find treadmill running far less mentally stimulating, making it difficult to do longer distances indoors.

Is a treadmill a good way for newbie runners or walkers to start?

There are benefits of starting your training on a treadmill. The external pacing of the treadmill allows you to set a desired pace, then not have to think about maintaining it once it’s set. Treadmills are also indoors, which means inclement weather can’t stop you from running. They also can have screens attached, allowing you watch reveals or follow a video workout instead of just listening to music. However, walking outdoors has been shown to be beneficial for mental health with the changes in scenery as you walk, increased vitamin D production from being in the sun, and decreased sensory stimulation with the absence of screens.

Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X Review (2025): Assault’s Best Bike Yet?

📅 15 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines at the moment offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity.
  • Industry observers note that here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike.
  • At Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines at the moment offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity. Popular in the CrossFit community, this fan bike consists of a belt-driven system and a heavy-duty steel frame, making it a great tool to build both endurance and strength.

Industry observers note that here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike. We put it through hours of strenuous cardio workouts to see if it could take on the challenge. In this Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X review, we’ll highlight our results, how well the bike ranked in testing, and how it compares to other fan bikes.

At Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment. We have a product testing team that has put hundreds of machines through the wringer, using them for everything from gentle warm-ups to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workouts. Many of our staff members are home gym owners themselves and use these products nearly every day.

According to recent reports, with the knowledge we’ve gained over the years, we created a proprietary scoring system that we used to rank the AssaultBike ProX in various categories. Not only did we evaluate how the bike performed on its own, but we also compared it with nearly 30 other exercise bikes to see how it stacked up against the competition.

From the founders of the AssaultRunner (one of the best treadmills to train with), the Assault Bike ProX is made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat that helps keep it corrosion-resistant and capable of standing the test of time. It is a top-tier fan bike that can provide a brutal workout for any athlete.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to its tough and durable frame, it incorporates a belt-driven system for a quiet, smooth training experience. It also requires less upkeep than chain-driven systems, which should come as a relief to busy individuals who can’t be bothered with complicated maintenance protocols.

At the time of writing, the Assault Bike ProX costs $899. Fortunately, there is also an option to finance it at around $82 a month through Affirm. For comparison, the Assault Bike ProX is more expensive than the AssaultBike Classic at $699 but cheaper than the Concept2 BikeErg, which costs around $1,100.

The Assault Bike ProX also provides free shipping, which is a big deal for equipment this size. Buying an air bike from another brand could set you back another $100 in shipping costs.

All of the above considered, we’ve rated this bike 4 out of 5 stars for its shipping rate, finance options, and value.

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX weighs 125 pounds, has a max user weight of 330 pounds, and boasts a heavy-duty steel frame with a corrosion-resistant black powder coating finish. We love this type of frame and finish because it means less maintenance over time.

It’s also similar to what you would see with the Rogue Echo Bike, which has a black powder coating and almost looks like it was built from scraps of a heavy-duty squat rack! But the Assault Bike ProX isn’t as bulky as the Rogue Echo Bike, making it more compatible with small spaces, which our product testers enjoyed. For comparison, the ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high, while the Echo Bike is 55 inches long, 29.5 inches wide, and 52.25 inches high.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX provides a wide padded seat that can adjust to 11 different heights and six different directions either forward or backward. These adjustments were the same on the Assault Bike Pro, which the ProX replaces. The rubber handles on the ProX help you maintain your grip and keep your hands comfortable throughout the workout as well.

According to recent reports, this fan bike also comes with footpegs at the base of the handlebars for you to place your feet. This gives you the option to do an upper body-only workout, which is great for injury recovery or arm day.

Based on the quality and construction of the Assault Bike ProX, we rated it 5 out of 5 stars.

According to recent reports, we gave the AssaultBike Pro X 5 out of 5 stars for delivery and assembly because of how straightforward it was to build. The bikes arrived at our testing facility 75 percent built, so all we had to do was attach the LCD console, pedals, handlebars, seat post, and saddle. Assault Fitness provides all the tools needed to build your air bike, and it should take roughly 35 to 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, when testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a smoother and quieter ride than what we’ve experienced with other air bikes, like the Titan Fan Bike or the AssaultBike Classic. This is predominantly thanks to the belt-driven system. A belt-driven system requires less maintenance than a chain-driven system, but it is also harder to use. When you pedal, the steel fan wheel generates resistance based on your effort. The harder you pedal, the more resistance is applied.

Sources indicate that however, once you stop pedaling, the fan wheel will stop moving, requiring more effort to get it started again. This might be tough if you’re not prepared for a high-intensity workout. Due to this, we gave the Assault Bike ProX a 4 out of 5-star rating for performance.

The Assault Bike ProX’s LCD monitor provides seven built-in training programs and a competition mode for those ready to take on the challenge. Through the Assault Fitness App, which we’ll review below, there is also an option to follow instructor-led programs or create customized workouts.

All in all, we give it a 3 out of 5 star rating in this category. The included workouts aren’t as robust as what you’d see in a more interactive bike like the Peloton. However, we do appreciate having them and think they can be valuable for people who may not know where to start.

While the AssaultBike Classic was only compatible with the Polar T34 heart rate chest strap, the Assault Bike ProX is compatible with other brands, like Garmin. You can link a heart rate monitor through the bike’s Bluetooth features. However, you need to purchase a compatible one separately, which is why we only rated it 4 out of 5 stars here (though to be fair, this is common for most exercise bikes).

The Assault Bike ProX comes with a five-inch by eight-inch monitor, which is a common size amongst other fan bikes. This high-quality LCD monitor is powered by four AA batteries, which Assault includes with your purchase. The console is great for tracking stats such as calories, distance, heart rate, speed, watts, and RPM. It also connects to the Assault Fitness App.

Our product testers loved that it could track power output in addition to distance and speed, which is a great measure of energy expenditure to quantify workout intensity. The Rogue Echo Bike monitor doesn’t provide feedback such as watts and RPM on its monitor, which gives the Assault Bike ProX the edge.

All things considered, we’ve given this bike 5 out of 5 stars for its display and tracking capabilities.

When testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a ton of conveniences. First, the air bike requires no electric outlet, and we loved being able to use it anywhere. This feature is also a welcome benefit for commercial CrossFit gym owners, as you don’t have to worry about your members tripping over power cords.

In a recent development, other conveniences include a device holder and a water bottle holder. Some fan bikes like the Titan Fan Bike also include these conveniences. Others, like the Rogue Echo Bike, don’t (though they are available to purchase separately). We always appreciate it when a brand throws in little extras like this. They allow you to have all your workout essentials within reach. Plus, you don’t have to worry about potentially placing multiple orders or paying extra shipping fees to get them.

Overall, our product testers rated the conveniences 4 out of 5 stars. The only reason we docked a point is that we wish the bike came with a wind guard to prevent cold air from blowing in our faces when training in a cold garage. There is one available on the Assault Fitness website, but you have to buy it separately for an additional $39.

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX is a part of the Assault Fitness line of exercise machines that operate using the Assault Fitness app. The app was one of our product testers’ favorite features.

Free to download from the App Store and Google Play, the Assault Fitness App provides you with a multitude of instructor-driven workouts. You can do these workouts on your own or compete against other athletes virtually. Many of the workouts also integrate other types of equipment, such as dumbbells and kettlebells, to help you get more well-rounded programming.

In a recent development, while we enjoyed the app, we only gave it 4 out of 5 stars. As of this writing, it’s not available on the most recent version of Android. Athletes with newer Android phones may not be able to use it.

The Assault Bike ProX is Bluetooth-enabled. We don’t necessarily consider Bluetooth connectivity a standout feature, as dozens of cardio machines we’ve tested now come with it. But we’ve also tried inexpensive cardio equipment that doesn’t have this feature, and even Assault Fitness’s classic AssaultBike lacks Bluetooth capabilities. As such, we rated the ProX 5 out of 5 stars here.

In a recent development, when comparing other fan bikes we tested, the Assault Bike ProX generated less noise due to its belt-driven system. The belt-driven system operates more smoothly than chain-drive systems such as those on the Schwinn Airdyne. A noisier system can make it tough to perform workouts at home, especially if you train early in the morning or late at night when others are sleeping.

That stated, no fan bike will be completely silent, so you should still expect some noise as air travels through the flywheel. Due to this, we give the noise level of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

In a recent development, the Assault Bike ProX offers some portability, thanks to two small transport wheels at the front. To move it, all you need to do is tilt it onto its wheels to help glide it across the floor. However, although it might be easy for some athletes to move this fan bike, others might struggle to relocate it because it weighs 125 pounds. Based on these findings, we give the portability of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

The Assault Bike ProX has a three-year non-wear parts warranty and a seven-year frame warranty. The three-year non-wear parts warranty doesn’t cover normal wear and tear on parts like the seat, pedals, and handle grips. This may seem like a drawback, but in our experience, this is common in warranties on other brands’ fan bikes. But the length of Assault’s warranty is longer compared to Rogue, who only offers a two-year warranty on their Echo Bike, and Titan, who only offers a one-year warranty on their fan bike. We gave the warranty of the Assault Bike ProX 5 out of 5 stars for this reason.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high. Compared to the classic AssaultBike, these dimensions are one to two inches bigger in each category. If you’re between the two, we definitely recommend measuring carefully to ensure you choose the one that will best fit your space.

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX is a fan bike, meaning it builds resistance based on how much air you recruit in the fan wheel as you work. The harder you pedal, the more air resistance is applied, making your workout more challenging.

It has been revealed that in addition to air resistance, the ProX uses a belt-driven system, meaning it only operates when you begin to pedal. If you stop pedaling, the machine stops moving. This makes it harder to operate compared to a chair-driven system, like what you’d see with the AssaultBike Classic.

It has been revealed that the weight capacity of the Assault Bike ProX is 330 pounds. This is more than the Classic bike, which holds 300 pounds, but less than the Elite, which holds up to 350 pounds.

The Assault Bike ProX can accommodate most body sizes with 11 different height settings and six front-to-back settings. These adjustment levels are relatively standard based on what we’ve seen on other fan bikes. However, some competitors like the Rogue Echo Bike only have five front-to-back seat settings.

Recent findings suggest that because the Assault Bike ProX does not require an electrical outlet, you can transport it wherever you want to go —outdoors or indoors. The monitor, however, does require AA batteries to operate.

In a recent development, at first glance, it seems the Assault Bike ProX and Rogue Echo Bike have many similarities. When you analyze them more closely, you’ll find that there are several key differences between the two.

Below are the dimensions of both fan bikes:.

Even though the Rogue Echo Bike is bulkier in material and dimensions, it has the same 330-pound weight capacity as the AssaultBike ProX. Both of these fan bikes are also powered by movement, so no electrical outlet is needed. Further, weighing in at 123 and 125 pounds, respectively, the Rogue Echo Bike and the Assault Bike ProX are equally portable, especially given they both have wheels.

Finally, both products use belt-driven mechanics, providing a smooth and quiet riding experience. But the Assault Bike ProX gives more metrics on the monitor, such as watts and RPM. This feature alone could make or break your decision, depending on how key tracking is to your training.

The Assault Bike ProX comes in with a strong 4.6 out of 5-star rating on the Assault Fitness website. Many consumers claim that it is super easy to set up, requires low maintenance, and is a favorite piece of equipment in their home gyms. Customers also praise its sturdiness and its ability to handle a tough workout.

One user mentioned that the left peg became loose during their workout. Another buyer mentioned that the Assault Bike ProX was very noisy and didn’t think it was as stable as other reviews might suggest — note, however, that complaints like this are in the minority.

In a recent development, after extensive research and testing of the Assault Bike ProX, we can say that this air bike is worth it. Made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat, it can take on the toughest workouts. It’s ideal for anyone looking for a full-body, high-intensity interval training machine for improving both endurance and strength.

It has been revealed that the smoother and quieter experience you get with the Assault Bike ProX is thanks to the belt-driven system integrated into the design. Although this system might require more effort to operate, this bike can still be a great purchase for everyone from CrossFitters to health and fitness enthusiasts.

In a recent development, the Assault Bike provides a great workout, combining air resistance and a belt-driven system for a tough cardio and muscular endurance workout. You can use both the foot pedals and the arm handles to get a full-body workout. Or you can just use the arm handles to work out your upper body exclusively.

The Assault Bike Pro X is a belt-driven system. The fan bike only works when you operate the pedals and/or handlebars. The belt-driven system also offers a smoother and quieter workout.

The AssaultBike alone may not aid fat loss if you’re eating too many calories. However,  it can provide a strong enough stimulus for an intense enough workout to help you burn more calories and hit multiple health and fitness goals.

Because the AssaultBike Pro X requires a full-body effort and utilizes a belt-driven system, you could potentially build a small amount of muscle by using it consistently. However, resistance training with implements like dumbbells or barbells (and following a diet that supports muscle growth) will be your best bet if you want to pack on as much muscle as possible.

Black Friday E-Bike Deals Are Here: Save Big on Editor-Tested Picks From Specialized, Cannondale, Aventon, and Lectric

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that black Friday is here—and so are amazing electric bike deals.
  • There isn’t a single type of electric bike or e-bike rider—and luckily, all sorts of e-bikes are on sale at great prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that black Friday is here—and so are amazing electric bike deals. Several e-bike companies and retailers have rolled out massive discounts and special promotions on some of our favorite and best-tested electric bikes. Whether you’re buying a new e-bike for yourself or a gift for a partner, spouse, or family member, this is your chance to score the best deal of 2026.

There isn’t a single type of electric bike or e-bike rider—and luckily, all sorts of e-bikes are on sale at great prices. These zippy, pedal-assist bikes are perfect for enjoying your local bike paths, riding rail trails with your family, or tackling singletrack adventures. E-bikes are also great for your daily commute, basic transportation, and running errands.

Recent findings suggest that no matter your budget or riding needs—from commuters to mountain bikers, experienced cyclists and brand-newly introduced riders—there is an e-bike for everyone and every age. Our test team rides dozens of electric bikes each year, and these are some of our favorites and the best deals out there right now.

➜ AMAZON ➜ REI ➜ BACKCOUNTRY ➜ COMPETITIVE CYCLIST ➜ SPECIALIZED ➜ TREK ➜ CANNONDALE ➜ AVENTON ➜ LECTRIC ➜ SEGWAY ➜ RIDE1UP ➜ VELOTRIC.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. The Level platform has proven to be reliable, low-maintenance, and fun to ride—and it doesn’t break the bank.

The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. The bike also has regenerative braking, upping the range to 75 miles. For commutes and running errands, the Level comes standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Riders will also find the Level’s connected features very useful. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

In a recent development, compared with earlier Aventure versions, the third-generation model rides smoother and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s new torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found previous models had too much torque, but Aventure fixed that problem. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

In a recent development, the Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-road, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths. However, the bike is burly; its weight and components limit its fun on technical singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price.

Aventon’s Pace 5 REC is a zippy e-bike that’s perfect for weekend cruises around town, the bike path, or even occasional commutes. The brand refined the Pace with a slew of updates, making it one of the best bang-for-your-buck step-throughs on the market. These include connected features (such as GPS tracking and theft deterrence), a powerful 750 Watt motor, regenerative braking, and an impressive 75-mile range. It’s offered in five colors (grey, mint, pink, orange, and teal) and two frame sizes.

According to recent reports, the Pace 5 does not come with a rack, fenders, or a suspension fork. If you commute by bike frequently or use your e-bike for running errands, consider paying $200 more for the Level 4.

Recent findings suggest that A 2024 Bicycling Bike Awards winner, the Cervélo Rouvida is an electric gravel bike that looks and handles like a traditional analog bike—but with a little extra kick. That performance comes from the tiny-but-mighty Fazua motor; the 250-watt/60 N/m Ride 60 system blends smooth feel and good power (especially in Rocket mode). The unit produces a little bit of noise, but it’s less than many other e-bike motors—it’s audible enough that you hear it working, but it’s not annoying or distracting. This is a great bike for getting in gravel or road rides in the winter when you’re pressed for time due to darkness or cold temps.

Industry observers note that electric mountain bikes are a ton of fun and are promptly becoming the go-to choice for performance-minded off-road riders. However, a downside to trail-worthy E-MTBs is often cost: even “budget” models can cost upwards of $5,000, and high-end models often cost more than $10,000.

That’s what makes this deal pretty sweet: The Instinct Powerplay SL C70 features a lightweight carbon frame, 29-inch wheels, Fox Performance Elite suspension, and SRAM GX wireless drivetrain with Code brakes. At the heart of this E-MTB is a lightweight 700-watt/75 Nm motor system, developed in-house by Rocky Mountain in Canada.

It has been revealed that buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have much mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike tech, but it helps you get out and enjoy some rides without busting your budget.

Recent findings suggest that the Cityscape stands out for its combination of low price, practical features (like a rack and fenders), and a UL-certified battery. Unlike some Amazon brands, Heybike offers a U.S. support line for warranty service or product questions.

Includes FREE accessories: Running Boards, Frame Bag, Cushions, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Seat, and Orbitor.

Industry observers note that many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Discounted to $1,699, the dual-battery model has up to 120 miles of range and a 28 mph top speed. A single-battery version is also available for $1,399; it boasts an impressive 60-mile range. Need even more battery power? The $1,999 Long Range model goes up to 170 miles from a single charge.

Recent findings suggest that these prices make the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes on the market. And they’re a solid option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike. “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers and the Essentials package, I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Water-Resistant Panniers, Lock, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Saddle, Phone Mount, and Mirrors.

If you want power and range in a small package, the XP4 750 is right for you. It’s a fast, zippy Class 3 e-bike (pedal assist up to 28 mph) with a 330-pound payload capacity. To increase the XP4’s function and fun, the 750 has a 1310-watt peak motor output (200 watts more than the standard model) and an 85-mile range.

Whether you’re riding city streets on your commute or out for a weekend ride, this bike is fast, easy to ride, and a blast to pedal.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Fenders, Headlight, and Seatpost.

The XP Lite 2.0 scales back the XP4 750’s top speed and power, with pedal assist topping out at 20 mph, a peak motor output of 819 watts, and a reduced payload capacity of 275 pounds. It also drops the suspension fork found on the XP4, but still delivers an impressive range of up to 80 miles.

According to recent reports, however, the XP Lite isn’t simply a stripped-down version of the XP4; it has some major advantages. At 49 pounds (without accessories and options), it’s 26 pounds lighter than the higher-powered model. This makes the Lite much easier to lift and transport. Plus, instead of an 8-speed drivetrain, the XP Lite features a low-maintenance Gates belt drive. That means no greasy chain, no finicky gear adjustments, and a quieter, cleaner ride. Yes, it’s a singlespeed, but the pedal-assist motor easily compensates for all but the steepest hills or heaviest loads.

Includes FREE accessories: Support Seat, Elite Headlight, Suspension Seatpost, and Cargo Package.

Electric trikes are a great choice for many riders, including seniors, people with mobility limitations, and those who need to carry heavy payloads. At $1,699, the Lectric XP Trike2 is an easy-to-ride, stable three-wheeler.

A 750-watt motor with 1,310 peak watts powers the XP Trike up to 17 mph and up to 70 miles of range on a charge. The Trike features a wide, soft seat with back support. Plus, it has a suspension seatpost and suspension fork for added comfort.

According to recent reports, need a lightweight e-bike for city riding, your last-mile commute, or carrying in your car or RV? If so, Brompton’s C-Line Electric 4-speed is your answer. This lightweight (36.5-pound) folding e-bike packs down tiny and can be carried on most trains and buses. Made in England, Brompton bikes have earned a cult following for their quirky-yet-functional design and excellent engineering. And at 20% off, this is a great deal.

With a top speed of 28 mph, 81 miles of range, a 100mm-travel suspension fork, 27.5”x2.6”, a rack, and fenders, the Adventure Neo Allroad Speed’s name fits it to a T. This bike is built for adventures large and small, from commutes to work in the snow or rain, to gravel trails at your local park.

To power the Adventure, Cannondale uses a Bafang 750W rear hub motor and an easy-access 750 Wh removable battery. With its power and wide-range 8-speed drivetrain, you will get up every hill, while Tektro hydraulic disc brakes will control your speed on descents. Plus, it’s available in flashy red or more subdued matte black.

At $1,200, this Cannondale is 45% off its original price and is equipped with better parts than many lesser-known brands’ bikes priced hundreds more.

According to recent reports, many “step-through” e-bikes lack a truly low-step design, making them difficult for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, from REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. This makes the CTY a great choice for older riders, those with mobility limitations, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

According to recent reports, REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor; it provides smooth pedal assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem to custom-tune your riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for improved stopping power. For less than the cost of many unknown e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI’s warranty and service.

Salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs. But don’t let the price fool you; this bike is value-packed. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Newton-meters of torque) and a 430-Watt-hour battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, it has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

The frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system on Pivot bikes), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain, four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the components of this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Sources indicate that electric bikes are great for commuting and city life. However, their added weight (sometimes as much as 90 or 100 pounds) can make e-bikes a pain to carry up flights of stairs, load onto a bus or train, or even move around in your garage.

Weighing only about 40 pounds, the Roadster v3 cuts weight without sacrificing much performance or adding cost. Ride1Up uses a 500 watt/50Nm rear hub motor with an internal battery for a clean, stealthy look. 700x45c gravel tires carry speed on pavement or hardpack dirt roads, and metal fenders keep the road spray off your clothes.

Recent findings suggest that many people know Segway for its original electric stand-up people mover. But did you know the brand also makes e-bikes? Segway offers several electric-assist mini-cargo and commuter bike models, including the sleek Muxi Pro. It also has handy smart features (like traction control, Apple Find My, and hill descent control), plus a 750-watt hub motor with 80 Nm of torque.

This is an absolutely bananas deal for the right rider! If you can ride a size XL frame, you can get a Specialized Turbo Vado SL 4.0—an e-bike that typically sells for $3,500—for less than $1,000. It features Specialized’s excellent Turbo SL 1.1 motor, a 320 Wh internal battery, an 11-speed SRAM drivetrain, and a Lezyne headlight. Run, don’t walk to get this deal!

Industry observers note that over the last 18 months, I’ve probably ridden the Specialized Turbo Vado SL 2 on more days than any other bike. That’s because it’s a super-reliable commuter bike with a great motor, spot-on handling and geometry, and includes extras like a rack, fenders, and lights. At 25 percent off its everyday price, this Turbo Vado doesn’t cost a lot more than some bikes from consumer-direct brands—but you get a higher-performance bike. And it’s often worth paying more on an e-bike to ensure performance and serviceability.

Electric mountain bikes are a ton of fun and help you ride more of your favorite trails. We recommend full-suspension E-MTBs for aggressive and technical trails. But hardtails often work fine on easier trails and mellower terrain, and they cost a lot less than dual-suspension models.

Recent findings suggest that velotric keeps costs low on the Summit 1 by using a rear hub motor instead of a pricier mid-drive unit. The Summit also features an 8-speed Shimano drivetrain rather than more expensive 11- or 12-speed systems. However, Velotric gives the bike a 120mm thru-axle fork to soak up bumps, Shimano hydraulic disc brakes, and a full-color screen with Bluetooth connectivity.

Many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds, so a sub-40-pound e-bike is rather impressive. Unfortunately, e-bikes this light are usually rather expensive. However, Velotric’s Tempo only costs $1,399 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight. Velotric achieves this weight reduction and low cost by ditching the bulky suspension fork and using a smaller battery.

Like most hybrids, and unlike many e-bikes, the Tempo features 700c gravel tires. These tires roll quicker than 26- or 27.5-inch tires on pavement while giving the Tempo improved traction on dirt roads and gravel paths. Velotric offers the Tempo in a traditional double diamond frame and a mid-step design. Both frames are available in two colors and two sizes.

If you’ve been feeling ultra stiff lately, a five-minute yoga-inspired stretching routine break to release physical tension can feel like a full-body reset, helping you feel better in your body—and even more productive—so you can do all of your favorite activities.

It has been revealed that this short practice is ideal when you need a short break during the workday, but it can also serve as a grounding moment before you sit at your desk or when you’re winding down in the evening. You only need a yoga mat and a sturdy surface to practice on. Come exactly as you are.

Industry observers note that lie on your back with your arms and legs straight, as if you were in Savasana. Take some small movements, maybe wiggling your fingers and toes or moving your head side to side. Then let yourself relax for a moment. Inhale as you reach your hands overhead and your feet away from you, stretching your entire body from head to toe. Exhale and release.

Bend your knees, plant your feet on the mat about hip-distance apart, and rest your arms at your sides. Inhale, press your hands and feet into the mat, and lift your hips in Bridge Pose. Exhale and lower your hips to the mat.

Separate your feet slightly wider than your hips. Bend your elbows and draw your arms into a cactus shape. Exhale and allow your knees to lower toward the left. Inhale and return your knees to center. Exhale and lower your knees toward the right. Repeat Windshield Wipers two more times on each side.

Hug both knees toward your chest, grasping your shins or the backs of your thighs with your hands.

Industry observers note that come to a comfortable sitting position. Lift your shoulders toward your ears, then roll them back, down, and forward. Continue drawing circles with your shoulders in one direction for a few rounds, then switch directions.

According to recent reports, interlace your fingers behind your head with your elbows out to the sides. Exhale as you draw your navel toward your spine, round your back, and lower your chin toward your chest in a Cat Pose variation. Inhale as you lift upright and arch your back, drawing your elbows back slightly in a Cow Pose variation. Repeat a few times.

Inhale and reach your arms overhead. Exhale and twist your chest toward the left. Place your right hand on your left knee and your left fingertips on the mat behind you. Take a few breaths here.

Still sitting, come back to center and bring your arms into a cactus shape. Open your hands as wide as you can, spreading your fingers apart. Then shut your hands into tight fists. Repeat opening and closing your hands as many times as feels good.

In a recent development, sit on the mat with your knees bent, your feet flat on the mat, and your hands on the mat behind your hips, fingertips pointing toward you or toward the back of the mat. Press into your hands and feet as you lift your hips off the mat. Draw your chin toward your chest and gaze forward. Take a few breaths here, then lower your hips to the mat.

Draw the soles of your feet together. Inhale and lift your chest. Your feet can come closer to you or stay farther away. Exhale and fold forward, grasping your ankles or feet in Bound Angle Pose. You can stack your fists on top of each other and rest your forehead on them. Breathe here.

Lie on your back with your arms resting at your sides and your palms pressing into the mat. Bend your knees toward your chest and straighten your legs so your feet are reaching toward the ceiling. Keep your legs slightly bent if it’s more comfortable. Take a few breaths here, then shake out your arms and legs and lower your feet to the mat.

Lie on your back, resting your arms, legs, hands, and feet against the mat in Savasana. Or find a comfortable seated position. Take a few deep breaths before returning to the day.

Recent findings suggest that the first snowfall can be magical, but overcast skies and visible breath during a run can dampen the enthusiasm of any runner impatient for spring. To survive the everlasting cold, the trick is to layer properly so you don’t feel miserable during winter training. Stocking up on a winter running jacket, leggings, and pants is a no-brainer, but don’t forget to accessorize. I’m talking gloves here.

In a recent development, as a constantly cold person who has three sweatshirts piled onto the back of her office desk chair, I’ll never forget that one Santa 5-Miler when I left my gloves in my car. As I squeezed my hands into fists trying to retain warmth as I raced, I swore to never again run a winter race without full coverage over my five digits.

Industry observers note that this winter has tested my cold-weather tolerance, dipping below zero degrees Fahrenheit more than once. But it’s a perfect breeding ground for glove—and mitten—testing. Here are my top picks.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve worked at RW for eight years and started running XC in high school. I learned to embrace the cold this year, testing most of the gloves included on this list. I judged them by insulation, dexterity, and fit. I also had a little help from male staffers, who tested the men’s version of gloves—and became aghast learning that the women’s wasn’t similar.

Contributor Nick Hilden also provides tips on what to look for when shopping for gloves and answers your frequently asked questions on when to wear them, and on sizing and fit.

The stitching on the long cuffs ensures a secure, tailored fit around the wrists.

Recent findings suggest that the Active Fleece kept my fingers warm for an hour during 32-degree and slightly below freezing runs. When the temperature dropped to 20, my fingers started to ache after a half hour in the cold.

According to recent reports, my main critique is that they’re unisex sizing only. Even the smallest size, extra small, left some room above my fingertips, which made it difficult to grasp items I pocketed and zippers. The patch on the palm didn’t reach past my thumb and forefinger, which would have provided a soft area for nose wiping.

Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove Review.

According to recent reports, because of their thinness, your fingertips may start to ache once the thermometer hits below freezing. Still, they’re a great pair when you’re transitioning into colder weather or have a higher threshold to the cold.

It has been revealed that when you’re pitting gloves against mittens, it’s dexterity versus warmth. Gloves allow you to use your fingers, but mittens keep them together, thereby minimizing heat loss.

Industry observers note that even though I felt like I was running with oven mitts on my hands (the sizing is small/medium, medium/large), the Convertible Zip Mittens were great for braving workouts that dipped into the teens—and tens. The extra room also allows for doubling up if you really want to head out when it’s minus 1 degree Fahrenheit or less.

The Velcro tabs allow you to tighten the fit around the wrists, and the interior lining feels as plush as the felt on my very authentic Robin Hood hat from Nottingham.

If you’re prone to losing a mate when things come in pairs, TrailHeads sees you: a buckle guarantees your left and right mitt won’t be separated. Afraid of losing both mitts? These gloves aren’t for extreme weather, but they’re great when things start to get nippy or when you’re heading out for a short winter run. However, there’s one thing TrailHeads must rectify: It’s a travesty that only the men’s version has a nose wipe patch. Why did they skimp on this feature with the women’s edition?

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

These aren’t the cotton gloves you wore in grade school. The Smartwool Liner offers so much more in terms of warmth and quality; it all starts with the woven material.

It has been revealed that the fabric is merino wool, which regulates warmth, controls odors, and dries fast. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible, and you’re not limited to a small patch on the thumb when you need to wipe your nose (the glove itself is real estate). The ribbed cuffs fit snug, even on small wrists. They’re great to wear when the temperature is mid-30s; maybe even lower if you don’t have near-Raynaud’s hands like mine.

In a recent development, despite coming in unisex with no extra-small option, I was surprised how well the small Vortex Gloves fit my hands and how easy it was to use my phone and text. That’s not the worst knock, since we’ve had abnormal weather below 10 degrees and most gloves on this list either didn’t make the cut or only lasted for half an hour before I had to ball my hands in the palms.

Prone to losing your gloves? The snap on the lululemon Fast and Free prevents accidental separation and it’s just one standout reason you should buy this pair.
