Striking reflectivity details the back of the Fast and Free. That fabric is also soft enough to swipe your nose without causing the skin on your nostrils to peel.

Shop Men’s at shop.lululemon.com | Shop Women’s at lululemon.com.

What to Consider by Nick Hilden.

Sources indicate that winter runners should look for a pair of lightweight gloves that are warm enough to keep your hands cozy, but breathable enough to let air circulate. Look for technical fabrics—polyester and other synthetic materials are often your best bet for finding that balance.

Some blends are better than others though. In case of bad weather, it also makes sense to keep an eye out for a weather-resistant material that can protect against rain and snow, as well as cold, cutting winds. Moisture-wicking materials, such as merino wool, can also help deal with sweat and mitigate the impact of cold rain.

According to recent reports, I also like when a glove fabric contains a small amount of a stretchy material, such as spandex or elastane, to ensure the gloves fit comfortably and snug. That remarked, skip the stretch if you like a glove that feels roomy inside.

On the other hand, I recommend avoiding heavy gloves made from nylon or polyurethane. These materials are often thicker, warmer and weatherproof, so they’re more likely to make you overheat. (Depending on the design, they may also make it hard to use your phone or check your smartwatch.).

Industry observers note that everyone has their own Goldilocks spot for how much warmth they need from their gloves. The important thing to keep in mind is that your body feels warmer while you’re running–speaking broadly, we recommend dressing for a run as if it's 10- to 20 degrees warmer than the temperature outside (including the wind chill.) That’s a good rubric for determining both when to start wearing gloves in the winter, and the level of protection you want against the cold.

It has been revealed that thinking about gloves specifically, your running gloves probably shouldn’t be as warm as your everyday winter gloves. A warmer glove will keep you going in colder temperatures but will cause you to sweat more, so it may not feel comfortable for long.

Winter nights come early, so visibility is an essential concern for all cold-weather running gear. If you frequently run near a road, or in areas with little street lighting, every item of clothing you wear, head to toe, should feature a reflective or high-visibility element.

In fact, gloves are among the most notable pieces of reflective running gear you can wear. They catch drivers’ eyes especially well because your hands move as you run, creating a more noticeable effect.

When should I start wearing running gloves in the winter?

According to recent reports, every person feels differently about gloves, but as I said earlier in the piece, experts recommend dressing for a run as if it’s 10 degrees warmer than the effective temperature with the wind chill. If you normally wear gloves on a 50-degree day, start putting on gloves when it’s 40 degrees.

According to recent reports, A good running glove should fit snug around your hand. If there’s room for your hand to move inside the glove, your skin may rub against the fabric and start to chafe. At the same time, it’s important to make sure they aren’t too tight, which might reduce circulation.

Recent findings suggest that one way to check if you have the right fit is by doing a pinch test. Put on one glove, then pinch the fabric at the tip of a finger with your other hand. Ideally, you should have about a quarter inch of extra room.

Most glove brands use one of two measurements to determine sizing: The circumference of your fingers at the knuckles (without the thumb), and full hand length from the base of the hand to the tip of the middle finger. Check the product listing on the glove to see how the brand measures.

According to recent reports, to measure the knuckle circumference, hold your fingers together, then wrap a measuring tape around your knuckles. Don’t squeeze your fingers too tight, though.

When measuring your full hand, make sure your middle finger is fully extended to ensure a proper measurement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that recently at the Bicycling office, I was looking at all of the nutrition supplies that I had sitting around. I sit next to Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Test Editor, and I noticed between her stash and mine we had a healthy stockpile of GU Pumpkin Spice gels. Especially with Thanksgiving coming up, the thought crept in, I should make a pumpkin pie out of that.

This is the first pie I’ve successfully baked in my life, so it seems only fitting that I would make my first pie out of nutrition I take on rides. Before making the pie, I was doubtful that it would be edible, but our Test Editor Dan Chabanov had confidence it would come out reasonably well.

Here I’ll go through how the final product turned out and include the recipe so you can make this for your Thanksgiving group ride.

Recent findings suggest that usually I’m not a fan of eating gels when I ride—typically I opt for drink mixes to get in the fuel that I need to keep pedaling. It’s mostly a texture problem when I’m trying to get gels down during a ride, so I was hesitant to think I would enjoy the final product of this experiment.

Recent findings suggest that it would have been unrealistic to expect the filling would be the same as a regular pumpkin pie, but to my surprise it was much closer than I expected. I anticipated it would be a soupy mess in a pie crust, but the texture of the final product reminded me more cheesecake. Don’t get me wrong—it is a little stickier than a regular pumpkin pie. But I wouldn’t guess this was made out of gels if I didn’t make it myself.

It has been revealed that the flavor was better than expected, too. This experiment made me realize that I’ve been trying to fuel with gels wrong all these years. I shouldn’t have been trying to slurp them out of a little packet. All I had to do was bake a handful of gels into a pie.

Coming up with the recipe was hard—believe it or not, everyone I know that has baking experience had no idea how to help give guidance when making a pie out of gels and drink mix. So, I asked ChatGPT to whip me up a recipe—that seems like the best use case for artificial intelligence, right? From there I made some tweaks and got to work.

Bonus to all of this? My house still smells like pumpkin spice and now I have fuel for all my activities this weekend. After this successful test, I can’t help but think what other baked goods I could make with gels—stay tuned.

In a recent development, step-by-Step Directions   1. Prep the oven: Place a rack in the lower-middle position and heat the oven to 400°F. 2. Dissolve the recovery mix: In a medium to large mixing bowl, squeeze in the 8 GU Pumpkin Spice gels and whisk in the ½ cup cold water until completely smooth. 3. Whisk the base: Mix in the 2 scoops of the GU Vanilla Roctane Recovery Mix. Let it sit for 2 minutes so the foam settles. Then whisk in the 3 eggs until uniform. 4. Combine remaining ingredients: Add the 4 tablespoons cornstarch, 2 tablespoons melted butter, ¼ teaspoon salt, and optional cinnamon, whisking until smooth and pourable. (If the batter looks thicker than heavy pancake batter, whisk in 1 to 2 tablespoons of extra water). 5. Initial high-heat bake: Pour the filling into the unbaked pie crust. Bake at 400°F for 12 minutes to set the bottom crust. 6. Finish baking gently: Without opening the oven door, reduce the temperature to 325°F. Bake for another 30 to 40 minutes, until the outer 2 inches of filling are puffed and set, while the very center still jiggles like gelatin when gently nudged. (If the crust edges brown too rapidly, cover them loosely with foil). 7. Cool and chill: Remove the pie from the oven and let it cool completely to room temperature on a wire rack (about 1.5 to 2 hours). Transfer to the refrigerator and chill for at least 4 hours (or overnight) so the cornstarch fully sets before slicing. I opted for overnight so it would be ready for my morning heat session on the trainer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your gym bag is probably packed with some of the best supplements for building muscle, including protein powder, creatine, and pre-workout. Crucial for boosting energy and strength during a gym session and reducing muscle soreness afterward, you wouldn’t dare train without them. But imagine a single supplement that combines the benefits of all three.

Industry observers note that enter XWERKS Motion — an innovative supplement formulated to enhance endurance during intense exercise and support a quick post-workout recovery. Sounds too good to be true? We’ll find out in this XWERKS Motion review.

Our team of personal trainers, CrossFit coaches, nutrition experts, and competitive weightlifters shared their feedback on the formulation, price, taste, and solubility of this one-of-a-kind product. As a registered dietitian nutritionist, I’ll do a deep dive into the ingredients and potential health benefits of XWERKS Motion, so you know if it’s worth adding to your supplement stack.

Medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

Our Breaking Muscle product testing team has tried nearly 20 of the best BCAA supplements, gaining a thorough understanding of what meets customer standards and what falls short. Here’s how our expert testers rated the following categories after trying XWERKS Motion themselves.

In this XWERKS Motion review, we’ll explore the product’s cost, formula, flavors, taste, and more. We’ll include honest, reliable feedback straight from our Breaking Muscle expert testers, so you’ll know exactly what to expect from this supplement. With transparency in mind, we include the good and not-so-good aspects of XWERKS Motion to give you the full picture.

In comparison, Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine costs $1.33 per serving, while Jacked Factory BCAA Powder is available at $0.67 per serving at the time of this writing. XWERKS Motion is on the pricier side, earning this category a 3.5 out of 5, but also contains ingredients not found in most other BCAA supplements.

XWERKS Motion is thoughtfully and originally formulated, earning it a 4 out of 5. It is unlike other BCAA supplements in that it contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbohydrates, also known as highly branched cyclic dextrin (HBCD). Cluster dextrin passes through the stomach into the intestines rapidly, where it can be absorbed into the bloodstream and taken up into muscle cells to replenish glycogen content and provide a quick energy source. (1).

Human studies suggest that when used before or during a workout, cluster dextrin carbs may decrease perceived exertion and enhance endurance when compared to maltodextrin and glucose, especially when prior carb intake is low. (1) However, those who eat plenty of carbs may not experience any added benefits when supplementing cluster dextrin.

In addition to carbs, each serving offers three grams of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). The product contains the BCAA ratio 2:1:1 of leucine, isoleucine, and valine. BCAAs are essential amino acids (EAAs), meaning you must consume them because the body doesn’t synthesize them on its own. Leucine is often thought of as the king of BCAAs because it activates muscle protein synthesis, which is necessary for muscle growth and recovery. (2).

Recent findings suggest that other active ingredients include calcium, magnesium, and sodium. During exercise, you lose electrolytes through sweat that need to be replenished. The electrolytes in XWERKS Motion help prevent dehydration and maintain proper muscle function during a workout.

Enhanced with natural flavors, sucralose, and citric acid, this product contains ingredients that add sour and sweet notes.

According to recent reports, sucralose is an artificial sweetener considered safe when consumed in moderation. Unlike table sugar, most research shows sucralose has little to no effects on blood sugar levels or insulin. (3) However, some animal studies suggest it could disrupt healthy gut bacteria and increase inflammation when consumed long-term, but more human studies are needed. (4).

You won’t have any difficulty picking a flavor if you choose to try XWERKS Motion, considering there is only one option available — Raspberry Lemonade. Obviously, if you prefer to stick with one flavor on repeat this won’t be a problem. For those who like to switch things up, the lack of variety may leave you feeling bored, hence the middle-of-the-road rating on flavor.

Luckily, the Raspberry Lemonade flavor delivers. Our expert tester was more than pleased with the taste of the raspberry lemonade supplement, rating it an impressive 5 out of 5. She noticed hints of the tart lemonade with a more robust berry flavor overall. The supplement wasn’t too sweet and had a very refreshing taste to it. Our tester even went as far as to say that she could happily sip on this drink all day.

Recent findings suggest that another winning category of XWERKS Motion is solubility, which our tester rated a perfect 5 out of 5. She didn’t experience any clumping, grittiness, floaties, or difficulty mixing — a feature you’ll want when drinking it at the gym or on the go. Because the cluster dextrin in this product is highly soluble in water, it dissolves easily and forms a smooth, uniform mixture. Several customer reviews on the XWERKS website rave about the product’s superior solubility, mentioning it “blends so smooth” and is “easy to mix.”.

Cluster dextrin is believed to be safe for consumption, with no apparent safety concerns. (5) Our product tester didn’t experience any adverse side effects during her use of this product. As for beneficial effects, she didn’t notice any superhuman strength or noticeable bursts of energy, but she did feel good during longer lifting sessions.

Recent findings suggest that switching gears, BCAAs are considered safe when consumed in appropriate dosages. It’s best to adhere to the suggested dosage instructions on the product label for optimal safety and effectiveness.

In a recent development, nevertheless, always consult with your healthcare provider before adding a new dietary supplement to your routine, particularly if you have pre-existing medical conditions or are at the moment taking prescribed medications. This precaution ensures that the supplement aligns with your individual health needs and won’t pose any risks or interactions.

All of the above considered, XWERKS Motion gets a 4 out of 5 rating for the lack of side effects from its formulation.

Unfortunately, there’s no mention of third-party testing on the XWERKS Motion product page, which is why we gave it a 1 out of 5.

We always encourage consumers to consider supplements that are third-party tested, because it serves as a quality control measure, ensuring that products are safe, effective, and meet certain regulatory requirements. Third-party testing enhances transparency and builds consumer trust by verifying that high-quality products contain what’s on the label and don’t include harmful levels of heavy metals or contaminants.

Sources indicate that XWERKS Motion and XTEND Original BCAA powder have both commonalities and differences. To start, both products contain BCAAs and electrolytes to enhance muscle recovery, reduce muscle soreness, and maintain hydration.

However, that’s where their similarities end. While XTEND Original BCAA powder doesn’t contain any carbohydrates, XWERKS Motion contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbs for extra energy and prolonged endurance.

Industry observers note that XTEND Original BCAA powder also has a much higher BCAA content of seven grams, compared to the three grams in XWERKS Motion. The Original BCAA powder even contains a whopping three and a half grams of leucine, exceeding the recommended two to three grams per day to maximize muscle-gaining capabilities. (2) The same can’t be stated for the leucine content of XWERKS Motion.

Customers on the XWERKS website give Motion a 4.4 out of 5-star rating. There are only 35 reviews on the product page. Motion is not available on Amazon at the time of writing.

According to recent reports, one happy customer claims, “Great taste! No complications with digestion, gives you the fuel needed during most intense workouts.” Another customer says, “It mixes well, I like the flavor, and have no digestive or other issues. Performance-wise I feel great. I feel more energetic during my workouts and that I’m getting more out of them.”.

Reviews from customers who were less pleased with the product were written over a year ago, and the formulation and flavors may have changed. One customer says, “I’m not sold on this product. I don’t really notice any difference on the days I take this. Also, it takes a blender to get this stuff mixed! That’s a deal breaker for me.” Other customers complain of the grape flavor, which is no longer available.

In a recent development, XWERKS Motion provides a synergistic blend of cluster dextrin carbs, BCAAs, and electrolytes to support endurance and recovery during and after a workout. Those who enjoy leisurely activity and consume enough carbs to sustain their energy levels may not benefit from this product.

According to recent reports, however, it might be worth it for endurance athletes and bodybuilders with high training loads. Taking XWERKS before, during, or after intense physical activity may reduce perceived effort, extend the time to exhaustion, and decrease muscle soreness.

It has been revealed that you can consume BCAAs pre, post, or intra-workout depending on your fitness goals. Some prefer to take BCAAs before or during a workout to provide their muscles with amino acids to help prevent muscle protein breakdown. Others like to take BCAAs post-workout to support muscle repair and recovery.

Recent findings suggest that if you eat a whole-food diet high in protein, then you likely consume enough amino acids and may not experience further benefits by supplementing them. If you struggle to eat enough protein, BCAAs may support endurance, helping you train at a higher intensity for longer. Additionally, BCAAs may reduce muscle damage and DOMS post-workout.

According to recent reports, BCAAs are a group of three EEAs—leucine, isoleucine, and valine— that must be consumed through the diet. They get their name from their unique molecular structure. While all EAAs are crucial, BCAAs are thought to play an important role in protein synthesis, muscle recovery, and preventing loss of lean mass.

In a recent development, BCAAs may provide an extended feeling of energy and delay the onset of muscle fatigue, enabling you to work out longer. Moreover, BCAAs might diminish muscle damage, inflammation, and DOMS post-workout. Lastly, BCAAs may aid in preserving lean muscle mass during periods of fat loss, contributing to weight loss efforts.

It has been revealed that there are no official recommended daily requirements for BCAAs. The suggested sweet spot for leucine intake is often cited as two to three grams per day to optimize muscle building. (2) Avoid exceeding the recommended serving size on the product label. If you take protein powder or eat a high-protein diet, BCAA supplements likely won’t provide added benefits.

#172783. After a Decade of Refusing to Use a Treadmill, I Finally Gave In. Here’s How It’s Making Me a Better Runner.

After a Decade of Refusing to Use a Treadmill, I Finally Gave In. Here’s How It’s Making Me a Better Runner.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when the weather dipped below freezing for the first time last winter and the sun began to set at 4:30 p.m., I knew I’d have to leave my typical after-work miles behind.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’d also long held another line in the sand: I didn’t run on treadmills—at least not since high school gym class.
  • According to recent reports, so I decided to give treadmill running a chance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when the weather dipped below freezing for the first time last winter and the sun began to set at 4:30 p.m., I knew I’d have to leave my typical after-work miles behind. Cold weather and early darkness have always been an easy one-two punch to my running motivation.

Recent findings suggest that I’d also long held another line in the sand: I didn’t run on treadmills—at least not since high school gym class. I took to calling myself a “purist” because I didn’t think running was worth it if it wasn’t outside in nature. I believed my cause was noble, but really, I was just piling up excuses not to run in the winter.

According to recent reports, so I decided to give treadmill running a chance. I set out to complete one to two easy runs per week for a month to see if it could help me stay consistent through the winter. Within a few weeks, I was running more than I ever had in winters past—and reconsidering what held me back all those years.

According to recent reports, my experiment started after work in late fall. I turned to one of the Bowflex treadmills we have at Runner’s World headquarters. Earlier in the day, my editor casually mentioned that my Apple Watch would sync directly to the treadmill for a more accurate reading, a suggestion that made me more excited to get started on my test.

I walked up to the treadmill and the first thing I noticed was that if I wanted to, I could put my Netflix password into the built-in monitor and fire up an episode of Brooklyn Nine-Nine for the 200th time. While this capability isn’t very advanced as far as treadmill features go nowadays, the shift from the bare-bones experience I remembered from a decade ago in high school gym class amazed me.

I decided to go simple for my first run, tapping in with my Apple Watch and committing to a 30-minute easy effort with just a podcast to entertain me.

The run itself was good, but left me puzzled. I immediately focused on how each foot strike offered a different sensation than I was used to outside. After a minute of adjusting the belt speed, I settled into a pace that felt similar to my outdoor easy runs. What I found, though, was that the treadmill speed read a completely different pace than my outdoor runs.

After 30 minutes at zero incline, I completed just 2.56 miles at an 11:51 pace with my heart rate right at my usual 150 beats per minute (bpm). That 11:51 average was nearly two minutes slower than my outdoor 10:00 easy pace, but I felt like I was right at my normal outdoor effort level.

In a recent development, still, I walked away encouraged. I logged a run, avoided the weather, and felt great doing it.

Recent findings suggest that my experiment continued with more 30-minute easy runs over the next couple of weeks. Each one raised the same question: Why did an effort that felt identical to my normal 10:00 outdoor easy runs translate to a treadmill pace of well over 11:00 per mile? Adding to the confusion, I got a new watch (the Coros Pace 4), and it consistently recorded slightly longer distances than the treadmill itself displayed.

According to recent reports, after my third run, I brought all my questions to a chat with Birmingham-based RRCA level II- and USATF-certified run coach Alex Morrow, founder of Resolute Running. I described to him how, on the treadmill, I felt I was giving a similar effort compared with my outdoor runs, but was running at a significantly slower pace, and I asked him why he thought this was the case.

In a recent development, “When you’re outside and you’re running at an easy pace, you’re looking at the trees, you’re waving at other runners, and your mind gets to dissociate from what you’re doing,” Morrow states. “When you’re on a treadmill, there’s very little stimulation,” beyond your body moving.

Because I’d been running exclusively outdoors since high school, I was used to looking around at the cars as they passed by, the birds in the air, and any number of distractions along my route. As soon as I hopped on the treadmill, though, none of that was there to capture my attention. Right away, I locked in on the difference in every step, and became consumed by how far off my pace ended up being from what I expected.

It has been revealed that changing a long-held belief is tough, especially when it’s rooted in identity. “It’s like turning a battleship around,” says Morrow. “It takes time and it’s never easy.” In my case, the belief that “real runners” don’t use treadmills stuck around for years.

Once I started running on one, though, I accepted it as a suitable tool for consistent running almost immediately. The hardest part of flipping my mindset wasn’t logging the miles or dealing with boredom, it was simply stepping onto the belt in the first place.

According to recent reports, if you’re new to treadmill running, or have avoided it for the same reasons I did, my best advice is to try it with an open mind. Don’t worry if your pace looks slower than what you’re used to seeing outside. That mental hurdle of mine ended up not really mattering much. I let effort guide my runs, my podcasts entertain me, and I judge my success based on time on feet rather than actual miles.

Industry observers note that my biggest takeaway from the experience was consistency. According to Morrow, that’s where treadmill running becomes one of the most powerful tools a runner can use, especially in the winter.

In a recent development, through my trial efforts, I realized I wasn’t frustrated with the treadmill itself, I was simply focused on learning more about my running. Curiosity helped me keep a steady schedule, and in just a few weeks, I’d already run more in the winter than I had in years.

“Consistency is so much more vital than having one killer workout,” Morrow explains. “I would much rather you have four or five average workouts than three killer workouts.” This idea counters how a lot of runners think about training, especially when motivation dips. It’s flashy to chase breakthrough days in perfect conditions, but you build fitness by stacking days together, even when the circumstances aren’t ideal.

For runners who live in areas heavily impacted by harsh winter weather, the treadmill is a saving grace. “Something is always better than nothing,” Morrow says. “Jogging three miles on a treadmill is better than skipping your workout completely because it’s cold outside.”.

In a recent development, when weather threatens to derail a week of training, the opportunity that a treadmill provides becomes crucial to your development as a runner. “Consistency creates physiological adaptations in your body that allow you to reach your goals,” Morrow says. Those adaptations include a boost in aerobic fitness development, running economy, VO2 max, and lactate threshold, he continues. It’s adaptations like these that establish an excellent fitness base for marathon training.

Industry observers note that looking back on my career as a recreational runner, my biggest mistake wasn’t refusing to run on the treadmill; it was letting that ignorance cost me months of consistent running every year. Now, the excuses that held me back are gone. I’ve continued using the treadmill to not only knock out frequent easy runs but conquer the occasional interval workout or speed session.

#172782. In Praise of the Charity Ride, One of the Most Underrated Ways to Tackle Your First Century—or Any Big Cycling Goal

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1574 w)

In Praise of the Charity Ride, One of the Most Underrated Ways to Tackle Your First Century—or Any Big Cycling Goal

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that they say pride comes before the fall.
  • I relearned this lesson earlier this month, when I found myself at the top of Bear Mountain, the only notable multi-mile climb close enough to bike to from New York City.
  • Though I’m relatively upcoming to road cycling, I’ve done some long gravel rides and recently tackled the Maratona dles Dolomites in Italy, where I buried myself to finish a 66-mile route that featured over 10,000 feet of elevation and one 8-mile climb up the Passo Valparolo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that they say pride comes before the fall. In cycling, I’ve found pride usually comes before the first true descent.

I relearned this lesson earlier this month, when I found myself at the top of Bear Mountain, the only notable multi-mile climb close enough to bike to from New York City. Its peak was situated about halfway into the 105-mile route of the Best Buddies Challenge New York, an event the organization had brought back for a second year to fund its programming for teenagers and young adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. The riders gawking at the intermittently vermilion canopy who were pedaling alongside me had each raised at least $1,800 to reach this particular vista, plus access to several deliciously well-stocked aid stations, SAG vehicles, and the promise of a raucous finish-line party.

Though I’m relatively upcoming to road cycling, I’ve done some long gravel rides and recently tackled the Maratona dles Dolomites in Italy, where I buried myself to finish a 66-mile route that featured over 10,000 feet of elevation and one 8-mile climb up the Passo Valparolo. By comparison, the Best Buddies Challenge century, with 2,000 fewer feet of climbing stretched over a much longer route, seemed plenty doable when I signed up in September.

Recent findings suggest that the first indication I had erred came before I had pinned my bib number to my jersey. At a pre-ride reception, I sat down with Alberto Contador (yes, that Alberto Contador), who was returning to the event for the second time. He was confident I could handle Bear Mountain, but warned me that the end of the ride reminded him of La Flèche Wallonne, a notoriously difficult Belgian one-day race known for its repeat ascents of the relatively short, brutally steep Mur de Huy. “The last 30 miles is all up and down…save energy,” he remarked.

By the time I slid into the fourth aid station, which marked the 33-miles-to-go point in my own ride, this advice was well out of my mind. I was supremely confident in my ability to finish strong. Sure, I had gone a bit deeper in the tank to maintain contact with random groups throughout the day in valleys and on shallow sections, but there was so little left to go.

How hard could the rest really be?

In a recent development, the Best Buddies Challenge is relatively upcoming to New York City, but the concept of the charity ride is not. The Five Boro Bike Tour, which raises money for Bike New York’s free education and mechanics program, has given city cyclists the chance to experience streets without car traffic since 1977. On the West Coast, Washington’s Cascade Bicycle Club’s Seattle to Portland Bicycle Classic now generates about $1 million each year to fund the organization’s community programs, cycling education, and statewide cycling advocacy work. Even the ride I did in the Dolomites this summer offers charity entrants, who have, over the years, raised over $2 million for road safety, food security, disease research, and rural education.

According to recent reports, among non-endurance athletes, these rides often draw comparisons to running events like the Latest York City Marathon. There are certainly similarities—sanctioned routes, feed stations, distances that sound absurd to normies—but cyclists don’t tend to give even long charity rides anything close to the same level of credence as runners do to marathons.

It has been revealed that that kind of resistance perhaps comes from those strains of cycling tradition that prize grit and ardor and self-reliance. Conquering Mur de Huy during a race takes superhuman levels of tenacity and determination—charity rides, by contrast, even those that span 100 miles, are much more comfortable affairs. Do some riders dismiss these events because they’re too soft? It’s possible.

In a recent development, beginner-friendliness is often baked into the event programming of charity rides. Breakthrough T1D Rides, held to fund research for type 1 diabetes, are actually four-day retreats. Participants spend only one day on the bike. Anthony Geraci, national director of Ride & Endurance Programs, says most of these rides feature “out-and-back” courses. Turn around whenever you feel done with your day! “We always say it’s not about the miles, it’s about the mission.”.

Sure, you could cross-stitch that phrase onto a throw pillow. But it’s also the kind of mentality that cyclists might need to achieve some personal goals, whether that’s riding in a new destination or tackling their first century. In this way, charity rides can be catalysts for remarkable personal achievement.

They also create the conditions for extremely impressive fundraising. Best Buddies International CEO Anthony Shriver (yes, that Shriver) told me that its cycling events account for about 10 to 15 percent of the organization’s annual revenue. Similarly, Kris Rauh, vice president, event experience and operations for NMSS, says its 49 Bike MS events generate about $52 million in revenue annually for the organization.

According to recent reports, indeed, she continued, many of the people signing up to do their first Bike MS have no personal connection to the disease in its name. “They come to us mostly because they want a challenge on a bike … they don’t come to us as fundraisers,” she remarked.

For charity rides like Bike MS and Best Buddies, it’s crucial to connect participants to their mission and the impact of their work. As I ascended Bear Mountain and pushed myself on the way back, I wasn’t just riding with Contador and Chris Froome (who was also participating this year) but also plenty of folks who volunteer for or participate in Best Buddies programming. In fact, individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities often held key roles during its rides. At the Challenge Fresh York, a “Buddy” gave a speech while we waited in the start pen, a different “Buddy” sang the national anthem, and still others staffed the aid stations. “From the moment you wake up at 4 o’clock in the morning, you should know you’re doing something that’s going to enrich another human being’s life,” Shriver noted.

It has been revealed that the combination makes these kinds of charity rides feel a lot different than a standard criterium or gravel fondo. And it seems to hold enough appeal to keep the organizations hosting them going. Best Buddies, which has substantial fundraising minimums for riders, gets a 30 to 50 percent return rate, Shriver notes. According to Rauh, at Bike MS that number is closer to 60 percent. That’s a lot of people returning to charity rides each year.

About two-thirds of the way into my own Fresh York Challenge, I was actively questioning how this could be possible. Though I had been correct that all the long climbs were behind me, the “rolling” terrain I had imagined was actually a freak show of sharp pitches. I cracked on a climb my Garmin did not categorize, attempting to hold serve over a bump with a gradient of 18 percent.

It has been revealed that I unclipped and shuffled my cramping legs up the embarrassingly short walk to the summit. I felt ashamed by the level of hubris I had brought into the event. If it had been just a regular ride, or even a race, this might have been my day. With hours left to a finish that I felt confident most of the participants had already crossed, it would have been totally within my prerogative to pull the quick-release lever off my front wheel and stuff my bike in a Lyft bound back to Brooklyn.

But as I munched on some blissfully salty crackers that quieted my screaming hamstrings, I realized that getting to the end would be an accomplishment for me regardless of how fast I was able to do it. And, importantly, my path to the shuttle bus that would take me back to the city included one final rest stop. Resolved never to underestimate a “ride” again, I got back in the saddle and held the limpest zone 1 pace of my life until I had made it to the aforementioned support tent. With less than 10 miles left, I slumped into a folding chair and sucked down a can of Sprite.

Immediately, I was engaged by Matt, who was participating in the ride as a volunteer. He asked if I was okay, and when it was clear that I was mentally wrecked, but physically fine, gently encouraged me to get moving. With Matt, another volunteer named Ian, and a pair of other riders who had also had similarly tough days, we set off on the last stretch to the end.

According to recent reports, chatting in my bunch, really the only bunch I had been able to hang on to the entire day, made the miles go by faster and the remaining climbs feel shorter. And when the sugar from my soda hit, I realized I was actually less dead than the pair of participants I had just encountered. Ian and I forged ahead, buoyed by the knowledge the end was near. I managed to stay upright enough up the finishing hill to attempt a celebratory pose as I crossed over the finish line: ninth to last. It was the longest ride I’ve ever done and it challenged me to push myself harder than I might otherwise have done. That’s worth something.

Does anyone have a cool $2,000 I could use to try again next year?

#172781. Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running.
  • Around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch.
  • Professional distance runner and New York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running. But by “distance,” I don’t mean bumping up my mileage or running farther. I mean taking time and space away from my sport during seasons when I feel burned out, lost, or simply exhausted.

Around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch. The second I crossed the finish line, all I wanted to do was let my running shoes collect dust, avoid my local trail, and avoid stepping foot in the gym for a while.

Professional distance runner and New York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago. At that time, she consistently stopped hitting her paces in her workouts and decided to step back from running—a break that lasted about two years.

In a recent development, in my case, I wasn’t as decisive. For months, I resisted the idea that I needed to take a break.

I’d heard that a month is generally how long you need to recover from a marathon, so I told myself that’s when I would jump into winter base training. But every time I tried to get back out there, I got bored and I struggled to recover from my runs. I waited until summer for the urge to work out again, but it never really came back.

It has been revealed that for a while, I felt like getting burned out was my fault, that I must have pushed too hard in training. Looking back now—and with help from an expert—I understand that my break was exactly what I needed to get back to my sport in a sustainable way.

It has been revealed that my break from running lasted about nine months, and I came back feeling like the runner I had always been before. Plus, I raced one of my fastest half marathons as my comeback.

Below I offer the telltale signs it’s time for a break from running, what a “break” really means, and the benefits you can gain from stepping away from the sport for a while—even if it seems impossible to do so at first.

The farther away I got from my training cycle, the more I realized how much I overtrained. I’d been strength training for 90 minutes three times a week with heavy weights while balancing 30-plus-mile weeks and 20-mile long runs. As I gained more perspective after my race ended, I noticed signs that I was in desperate need of a break.

Industry observers note that “Pay attention to trends and patterns [throughout your training],” Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology, tells Runner’s World. “We all have bad days where the numbers aren’t coming together or a run feels harder than it normally does at a given pace. But if it continues to occur, then it can definitely be a sign to take a break,” she says.

Ayala says there are three main factors that often lead to athletic burnout. Here’s what each can look like, and how I experienced them.

You might need to take a step back if you find yourself hitting training plateaus despite putting in your best efforts.

I picked a training plan that included paces far too fast for my fitness level at the time, so every interval workout I did felt difficult, and my paces never really improved. The longer the intervals got, the farther I was from my desired split. But I kept checking off the weekly workouts anyway.

This lack of personal achievement and growth can halt your motivation levels. “When you’re not able to progress and you lose sight of [personal achievements] you’re just going through the motions, that’s a really big red flag,” Ayala indicates.

After the first month or so, marathon training started to feel more like a chore and I felt really tired and disconnected during my workouts. I figured it was probably normal because I had never run a marathon before, but it turns out that’s not how you should expect to feel daily in your training. “If the workouts are just a grind and you’re having to peel yourself off of the couch in order to get them in, and that’s a sustained pattern, then that’s another massive red flag,” Ayala says.

Sources indicate that A change in my relationship with running and my “why” meant grappling with my identity as a runner, which Ayala says is the third factor that can contribute to athletic burnout. You might ask yourself questions like, “Why do I even do this anymore?” and “What’s the point?” She says that if those questions linger for more than a week or so, then that’s a sign you might need a break.

Sources indicate that by the time I got to the start line, I questioned why I was even there, and all I could do was get through it. “There’s a very real sense of grief and loss, and that’s really scary,” when taking a step back from running, Ayala explains. “Often we hang on quite desperately to our athletic identity when it’s also okay to move on and to do something different.”.

Once I knew I needed a break from running, I didn’t quite know how to hit pause.

Then Ayala pointed out that perfectionism can affect your relationship with your sport. And simply hearing that helped me realize why I needed to step away.

There are two types of perfectionists, Ayala explains. The first type is the high achiever, who wants to be the best and perform at the top as much as possible. The second type of perfectionist takes a more “maladaptive form.” These individuals are highly motivated by others’ perceptions and expectations, she says. They might fear failure and generally don’t want to disappoint people.

Industry observers note that that second type of perfectionism resonated with me because I realized I was listening to a nagging voice in my head that expected me to give absolutely everything I had to my training. And if I didn’t, I would face that critical voice’s judgment and let it fill me with disappointment and shame.

Recent findings suggest that “Breaks can be helpful because they essentially force you to turn that perfectionistic tendency off. They’re a good way to keep yourself balanced,” Ayala adds.

Once I knew this and decided to take a break, I figured out how to fill my time.

According to recent reports, those first few months after marathon training, I was so excited to not think about running at all. Instead, I looked forward to filling my free time by rebooting my old Webkinz account (an online virtual-pet game popular in the mid-2000s), decorating my latest apartment, and watching a lot of TV.

It has been revealed that “First, just give yourself time. Then, you can create other bite-sized goals like daily movement, getting outside, spending time with friends, or exploring different hobbies,” Ayala suggests.

When I passed the two-month mark of my break, I took up pottery classes. While that hobby didn’t last, it gave me the space I needed from running.

Sources indicate that I knew, deep down, that rest was probably what I needed. But when I took time off, I felt too anxious and ashamed to even enjoy it: I kept thinking about how much time I was wasting and how out-of-shape I felt. “The problem [with athletic burnout] isn’t that you just need to motivate yourself harder. You need to rest in order to get that intrinsic motivation back,” Ayala says.

Ayala explains that if we lose our intrinsic motivation, we often rely on feelings of shame and discipline to keep up with our routine, which ultimately isn’t sustainable.

When I was honest with myself, I found my upcoming “why” for running—my intrinsic motivator—and that was because of how strong, creative, and capable it makes me feel.

It has been revealed that one piece of advice from Ayala especially resonates with me: Accept where you’re at and normalize taking a break. “I would argue that getting burned out is a very normal and expected part of being an athlete,” she states. “If you are an athlete long enough, you are going to get burned out at some point and that’s okay. It doesn’t mean that you’re doing something wrong.”.

Once I accepted that I was dealing with a longer-term case of burnout and some depression, I began to see light at the end of the tunnel. I set bite-sized goals, per Ayala’s suggestion, and began by committing to running just five minutes a day for a month. With that, running clicked for me again.

Looking back on my time away from running, I don’t view it with shame or anxiety anymore. I see it as both a period of my life when I learned about myself as an athlete and about how my brain works. It was also a time of physiological and mental recovery from so much training stress.

It has been revealed that by stepping away, I unlocked a newly introduced life experience that can help inform me if—and probably when—I experience burnout again. That perspective shift alone lifts so much weight off my shoulders.

In a recent development, plus, I’ve come back to the sport now feeling refreshed. I ran one of my fastest half marathons and feel ready to tackle another training plan. I have the drive to set and achieve goals again. And that’s an irreplaceable benefit to taking some time away.

It has been revealed that kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and presently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

Plus, when paired with a newer Garmin cycling computer, the RearVue 820 will track the lane location and size of approaching vehicles.

Still using your phone to track your rides? A cycling computer is a safer, more accurate way to navigate, display key riding metrics, and capture data from devices like heart rate monitors and power meters. Garmin’s Edge 540 packs computing power, battery life, and function into an 80-gram package. It’s a great upgrade for any road, mountain, gravel, or fitness rider.

Tonal Review (2025): Our Experts Put the Smart Home Gym to the Test

📅 29 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room.
  • As a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment.
  • This Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tonal is a high-tech smart gym that makes starting an effective strength workout as easy as stepping into the next room. It has a cable resistance system with multiple attachments, so there is no need for additional equipment. You can choose between instructor-led sessions or work out independently using the demonstrations on the large touchscreen. There are a variety of workouts outside of strength training, including high-intensity interval training (HIIT), cardio, dance, yoga, Pilates, and more.

As a certified personal trainer and wellness product reviewer, I’ve tried (and stopped using) several pieces of home gym equipment. I also work with a team of other expert product reviewers, some of whom have had Tonal for several years and still use it consistently.

This Tonal review describes our experience using it, including details about the equipment, workouts, accessories, and other features. We also spoke to fitness expert Rachael Gonzalez, C.P.T., C.S.C.S., about Tonal’s workout modes and how they can benefit exercisers.

Related: Best Home Gym Equipment.

According to recent reports, based on our experience, we give Tonal an overall 5/5 rating. The only category where it didn’t receive a score is assembly, which doesn’t apply since professional installation is required.

Here’s a look at the scoring breakdown on a scale of 1–5:.

We’re extremely satisfied with the Tonal equipment and programming. We can get a full workout without taking up a lot of space with free weights or having to pay to go to a gym and leave the house.

Industry observers note that the equipment is durable, and we haven’t had any problems. However, moving the arms can be noisy, which may concern people installing it on a shared wall. We had one arm that clicked slightly for a while, but following the troubleshooting instructions on the Tonal website helped fix it.

Some weightlifting moves don’t feel entirely safe or stable, so we usually replace them with ones we’re more comfortable with. The handles, bar, and rope accessories are comfortable to hold and easy to use.

Tonal automatically adjusts weight as you progress, which is really nice. Some workouts have a movement replacement option where you select a modification for the recommended exercise, which has been helpful in certain instances. For example, during pregnancy, you’re supposed to avoid twisting moves, so when one of our testers started lifting after her first trimester, she could easily substitute these moves.

Tonal has worked very well, and one of our testers says it has drastically improved her strength. When she started using Tonal in 2021, she was in the bottom 25 percent of all women. Now, she’s in the top 28 percent, and watching her score increase has motivated her to keep improving.

Industry observers note that the Tonal machine is a wall-mounted smart mirror with a built-in touchscreen and two adjustable arms that extend from the sides of the machine and can be moved up and down depending on what exercises you’re doing. You can choose between an on-demand or live instructor-led class or do your own exercises using the Free Lift option. Throughout each class and in Free Lift mode, a trainer explains how to adjust the arms and attach accessories and demonstrates proper form.

Workouts on the built-in workout app include weightlifting exercises such as squats, deadlifts, shoulder presses, lat pulldowns, tricep extensions, curls, and bench presses. The movement library has over 170 exercises to choose from. Each exercise is performed under the resistance of a cable pulley system using a bar, rope, or handle attachment, with up to 100 pounds of resistance per side for a combined 200 pounds.

Related: Best Functional Trainers.

Tonal recommends weights for each session based on an initial assessment, and your progress and performance determine adjustments. It offers unique weight modes, video form feedback, and floor workouts such as yoga and Pilates. The Tonal app also gives you access to workouts that don’t require the machine arms, so you can work out on the go.

In a recent development, tonal uses artificial intelligence—Coach AI—to track progress, movement, and data from your workouts to make adjustments, weight recommendations, program suggestions, and more. You don’t have to worry about answering questions like: What do I need to work on today? What weights should I use? Should I focus on my lower body or do a full-body workout? Instead, one tap of the 24-inch touchscreen reveals an interactive library of on-demand and live classes or workout programs. Even in Free Lift mode, an option often used by experienced lifters, Coach AI tracks your data and makes adjustments and weight recommendations.

The first time you use Tonal, you’ll complete the Strength Assessment, which starts by choosing from the following goals:.

After selecting your goal, you’ll indicate whether you are a beginner, intermediate, or advanced exerciser and perform several movements—including a seated lat pulldown, seated overhead press, bench press, and neutral grip deadlifts—to help Coach AI get to know you and adapt to your needs, much like an online personal trainer. Your strength assessment results are used by Coach AI as a baseline when selecting the weight for each movement and to recommend workouts and programs.

Recent findings suggest that while this is a good starting point, it could be better. It’s hard to assess your overall fitness based on a single workout—what if you had an off day? Tonal addresses this by learning more about your strength level based on your performance in subsequent workouts and adjusting the weight settings to reflect your strength better.

During daily training sessions, it uses metrics such as time under tension, power output, range of motion, weight, and time to make weight adjustments and measure progress. Coach AI can detect when your form isn’t correct using your positioning, range of motion, and pacing. If it senses uncertain quality, it provides audible and on-screen reminders and feedback or turns off the weight. For example, the resistance shuts off if the bar tilts during a bench press because it suggests the movement is incorrect or unstable. If it senses you are moving the weight too easily, it increases the load each rep so you get the intended stimulus of the workout.

It has been revealed that another impressive feature is the four weight modes: Spotter, Burnout, Chains, and Eccentric. In Spotter mode, Tonal senses when you are struggling with a rep, lowers the weight so you can complete it, and returns the weight for the next rep to re-challenge your strength. Burnout senses fatigue and reduces weight until you finish the set. The Chains mode replicates the feeling of putting chains on the barbell by increasing the resistance during a lift’s concentric or shortening phase. Eccentric increases the resistance as you release the weight for more time under tension, which may help muscle growth.

Tonal enables each mode automatically during live and on-demand workouts. This automation creates a seamless transition between segments like supersets, where you concentrate on opposing muscle groups with little rest in between. If you want to work out with a partner, weight adjustments for both parties are automated.

Experienced experts lead each workout by demonstrating and talking you through set up and proper form. Even if you choose to follow the Free Lift setting or build a custom workout using the extensive movement library, there are video explanations of how to perform each movement. When you enable a specific weight mode, the weight is adjusted automatically, or you can adjust it manually on the screen using the dial. Interestingly, you can adjust the weight in one-pound increments, an uncommon feature in most cable machines and free weights, which typically adjust in 2.5 or five-pound increments.

Sources indicate that to access these features, you’ll need a paid membership for $60 monthly, and Tonal requires a subscription for the first year. The only way to use Tonal without the membership is to manually set the weights to perform unguided exercises like a cable machine.

Recent findings suggest that the purchase price of $3,995 includes the machine (which includes the touchscreen and arms) and no accessories. Aside from the floor workouts, most workouts use the arms and attachments, so Tonal isn’t usable without them. While you can use attachments from other brands, you’ll need to purchase T-lock adapters from Tonal for $43.

Sources indicate that the smart accessories bundle from Tonal costs $495. If your budget allows, I recommend buying it because it includes everything you need to start using your Tonal immediately. Each accessory is available separately, so you can also choose what works best for you. Here’s a breakdown of what the bundle includes and pricing for each item individually:.

The smart accessories have a safety feature to turn the weight on and off with a button rather than by touching the screen, so you can position yourself before loading. The handles have a button on the side that’s easy to reach while gripping, and the rope and bar come with an attachable clip.

As a beginner, our tester initially thought working out with Tonal was intimidating, but it’s a simple process once you learn how the smart home gym works. With a membership, you can choose between live and on-demand classes or a progressive program. Based on your Strength Score established in the initial assessment, the recommended weights are set automatically for you.

From there, you follow the trainer’s instructions and on-screen prompts to set the arms and choose the right accessories for each move. Tonal automatically adjusts the weight, counts reps, and provides form feedback as you progress through the workout. There’s even an audible cue when you have two reps left, so you know what to expect if you’re facing away from the machine.

Free Lift allows you to choose from the library of movements and do as many sets and reps as you’d like. Much like the classes, the screen displays your live stats, and you receive a workout summary with your time under tension, range of motion, power output, and total volume lifted.

You can do floor workouts such as cardio, yoga, and barre directly on Tonal or by using the Tonal app on another device.

Strength training is the main draw of Tonal, so most of Tonal’s content focuses on weightlifting and HIIT training with weights. In addition to the four weight modes mentioned earlier, there are two custom modes:.

According to recent reports, gonzalez notes these options add variety and challenge, enhancing strength gains and training overall. “Diversification in your routine keeps you engaged and introduces new challenges,” she says. “Plus, variation can help you push past a training plateau.”.

Sources indicate that trainer-led workouts on Tonal automatically implement these modes depending on the intended stimuli, but you can activate them manually in the settings for any workout. You can adjust the weight at any point during your workout using the dial on the screen.

In a recent development, “When training, I’m always super mindful of how my body feels and take it easy when I need to, so the Recovery Mode option would work well for when you’re sore or just want to move,” Gonzalez notes. “I really like the eccentric-focused mode. During the eccentric portion of a rep, the muscle lengthens while under tension,” she says. “The eccentric portion of a lift occurs when you are lowering the weight, moving against the opposing force of gravity, and research highlights controlled lengthening of the muscle fibers contributes to overall strength and muscle development.”.

In addition, there are several other types of workouts available on Tonal, including:.

Tonal has a massive catalog of guided workouts and workout programs and a library of over 200 bodyweight moves to allow you to build custom workouts.

The guided programs range from three to five weeks and focus on goals like improving overall fitness, gaining lean muscle mass, and burning fat. For example, Fundamentally Fit guides you through basic movement patterns, and House of Volume uses progressive overload to build strength. Many users on Reddit recommend Four Weeks to Fat Loss, a combination of resistance training and HIIT to maximize energy output. One notes, “Four Weeks to Fat Loss did amazing things to my body composition! Doing that program was when I really started to see a difference in how my clothes fit.”.

The smart handles help replicate moves performed with dumbbells and kettlebells, like hammer curls, bicep curls, or goblet squats. The smart rope can copy moves with a rope or chains, like pull-throughs or tricep extensions. Finally, the bar can replicate barbell moves such as deadlifts and bench presses. You can purchase accessories from another brand, but the smart accessories bundle from Tonal has Bluetooth connectivity, so you can press a single button on the accessory to turn the weight on or off.

Recent findings suggest that if you buy third-party accessories, you must purchase T-locks from Tonal to attach them securely. Additionally, you’ll need to turn the weight on and off directly on the touchscreen.

Tonal has a roster of expert instructors based in its Latest York studio and guest coaches who occasionally provide unique content. These fitness experts have diverse backgrounds, from competitive athletes to sports medicine.

Sources indicate that all Tonal-created workouts are instructor-led, so you’ll hear tips about form and safety throughout. Each instructor brings a unique style, personality, and expertise to the table, and Tonal owners generally find instructors they prefer. For many, this provides the experience of working with a personal trainer, and several of Tonal’s past and current coaches offer personal training services outside of Tonal. For these reasons, Tonal allows you to filter workouts by instructor.

Sources indicate that the Tonal app allows you to access your workout history, create workouts, and do floor workouts directly from your phone. The only thing you can’t do on the Tonal app is weightlifting workouts that require using the resistance cables.

In a recent development, in addition, Tonal connects to several fitness apps, including Apple Health, Google Fit, and Strava. It also syncs with several heart rate monitors using Bluetooth, and you can connect to your Amazon Music or Apple Music account to stream or choose from the 14 stations on Tonal Radio.

Tonal has several features to help keep members engaged with the community and the equipment.

Recent findings suggest that first, there are several achievements you can earn for performing certain types of workouts, working out on holidays or birthdays, or reaching milestones like weekly streaks or 1,000,000 pounds lifted. Your workout summary lists the badges and milestones reached and your progress toward the following milestones. The Total Achievements Card indicates how many workouts you’ve finished, the pounds you’ve lifted, and the longest weekly streak you’ve completed. You earn badges by trying a new workout type, training consistently, and working out at a different time of day. These achievements can be shared with friends and family using the mobile app.

The Tonal Leaderboard ranks all active exercisers based on how many days or hours they’ve used Tonal in the last 30 days, so the more you train, the higher you’ll rank.

Recent findings suggest that your Strength Score increases from the baseline as you get stronger and demonstrate progress during workouts. These improvements are calculated based on your historical workout data and are a huge source of motivation for many Tonal owners. Using a percentage-based comparison, you can see how your Strength Score ranks against others, so some friendly competition is involved.

It has been revealed that tonal has a very active social media community if you prefer direct interaction with other members. The brand’s private Facebook community, The Official Tonal Community (OTC), has over 53,000 members and regularly hosts workout challenges and live discussions with Tonal trainers.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years, and she’s used it consistently the entire time, only stepping away briefly for injury recovery and pregnancy.

Before Tonal, despite being fully aware of the benefits of resistance training, she had no weightlifting experience beyond the occasional half-hearted kettlebell or dumbbell workout.

Tonal takes all the guesswork out of resistance training so you can lift the weights and reap the benefits, which is our favorite thing about it. You don’t have to worry about setting weights, planning workouts, increasing weights or reps, or tracking your progress.

According to recent reports, at first, our tester didn’t understand Tonal’s difficulty levels. She thought the Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced class levels aligned with strength and fitness experience, but they correlate with the technicality of the moves involved. Beginner classes may include heavy weights if recommended by your Strength Score and the algorithm. The “beginner” aspect is that the workout moves are less technical, making effective strength training accessible to those who might typically be considered “casual” fitness enthusiasts.

It has been revealed that our tester says Tonal is a lot of fun. She’s discovered she loves lifting weights, and when she misses a few workouts, she gets antsy about getting started again. Tonal introduced her to barre, a ballet-inspired floor workout she’s grown to adore. There aren’t many new floor workouts, which is sad because she loves the barre and pre/postnatal classes.

Sources indicate that our tester has attended live classes, but she doesn’t very often. Sometimes, she struggles with the pacing for floor/cardio workouts but finds the weightlifting workouts easy to follow. Mostly, she sticks to on-demand workouts because she appreciates the guided warm-up, exercise, and cool-down.

Recent findings suggest that one concern users in the Tonal Facebook community raise is the lead trainer demonstrates the moves during a live workout, which is not true for on-demand classes. These workouts use the lead trainer’s voiceover and cut to another trainer demonstrating the exercises. This inconsistency doesn’t bother us, but some say it disrupts their flow or makes it harder to follow.

In a recent development, the instructors showcase their personalities, and none of the workouts our tester watched seem overly scripted or cheesy. Tonal recently moved their studio from California to Latest York and replaced the coaching staff. Our reviewer had grown accustomed to the “old” coaches and still gravitates toward their workouts because she likes their calm demeanor. Some coaches have a bubbly, energetic coaching style, and others take a tough-love approach.

These trainers have diverse professional backgrounds to support the workouts they design. For example, when our tester’s doctor cleared her to work out after a knee injury, she found Coach Liz’s workouts helpful because the coach is also a physical therapist.

Sources indicate that our tester completed several of the guided programs and saw consistent strength gains from each program. The programs can get repetitive, though, since many of them repeat the same two or three workouts for the duration of the program.

When our tester started using Tonal, her Strength Score was 133, and she was in one of the lowest percentiles of all female Tonal members. Although her progress has been slow, her Strength Score is now 354, and according to Tonal, she’s stronger than 82 percent of all female people. Something about getting higher and higher in those percentiles is supremely motivating for her. In addition to her soaring strength, she’s experienced improvements in her mobility and range of motion.

The base price of Tonal is $3,995, and the optional smart accessories bundle (which we highly recommend purchasing) is an additional $495. Professional installation, which is required, costs $295. Several owners on Reddit report signing a Release of Liability waiver and installing it themselves, but there is no option to remove the installation charge at checkout. Tonal often runs promotions and offers free shipping and installation.

A subscription is required for the first year and costs $60 per month. You can discontinue the membership after one year, but you’ll lose access to many features.

If you purchase Tonal, the optional smart accessories bundle, and the required one-year subscription, the total cost of Tonal within the first year is roughly $5,500 before taxes, not including delivery and installation.

A monthly subscription costs $60 per month and isn’t technically required after you’ve completed your first year of membership.

You can only use Tonal as a cable machine for free lift workouts, and without a membership, you won’t have access to any Tonal content, weight modes, workout or strength data, history, or custom workouts.

The Tonal website notes professional installation is required. Before purchasing, you’ll need to complete a survey providing additional information for the installers, such as where to set up Tonal and the stud spacing in your walls.

Industry observers note that if they determine you don’t have an appropriate place to install it, there are solutions. The brand offers wide-mount adapter bars and installation kits for metal studs. If you have concerns about where you can have Tonal installed, contact the brand’s customer service team for help. Typically, installation fees are $295, but Tonal occasionally offers free delivery and installation.

If you move, you’ll need to schedule a professional reinstallation. Tonal offers relocation packages for moving homes or simply relocating furniture to another room. Relocation fees range from $300 to $500 plus taxes, depending on your chosen service.

Tonal does not cover damage caused by attempting to install or reinstall the home gym, and if you choose this option, Tonal requests you sign a Release of Liability waiver.

Tonal offers a two-year limited warranty on the trainer and touchscreen, which covers parts, shipping, and labor. The smart accessories have a one-year warranty for parts plus shipping and labor. For such a premium (and expensive) piece of equipment, a five-year warranty on the device would be nice—and more comparable to warranties offered by other premium fitness equipment brands.

Sources indicate that tonal customers have had mixed experiences with customer service. Some say customer service swiftly and competently addressed their concerns, while others say they needed more urgency from the customer service team.

The Tonal website has several glowing reviews from its users, many of whom say they have canceled their gym memberships while drastically improving their strength and fitness levels. Several reviewers are excited about their progress and enjoy the objective tracking data from workouts.

According to recent reports, tonal has a 2.⅖ on Trustpilot. Several critical reviews mention installation, maintenance, and customer service concerns. Tonal partners with a third-party firm for delivery, installation, and repairs, and many concerns center around problems with this specific company rather than Tonal itself. Positive reviews mention the variety of workouts, convenience, and ease of use.

People on Reddit say they work out more frequently with Tonal and enjoy the extra time saved from skipping gym commutes. Several mention the cable resistance feels heavier than free weights, so the maximum poundage is not a limiting factor. One user notes they wish to see a floor-based alternative in the future for those who rent or need to move.

According to recent reports, tonal is ideal for people who are interested in weightlifting but need guidance and support to get started and see results. It’s a great fit for athletes and highly active people who want to advance in strength training to support their athletic endeavors and fitness goals.

According to recent reports, likewise, many dedicated weightlifters have switched from using free weights to this comprehensive, versatile system. Tonal is an excellent option if you dislike going to the gym and prefer an all-in-one home gym solution.

Tonal isn’t ideal for people outfitting their home gym on a limited budget. For Tonal’s high price tag, you could buy a complete set of dumbbells or other free weights and other equipment or pay for several years of a gym membership.

Additionally, Tonal likely won’t be a good fit for advanced weight lifters already at or near the maximum of 100 pounds per arm offered for many lifts.

Industry observers note that this machine requires adequate space to extend the arms to fully perform all necessary movements. If you live in a small or cramped space, it may not work for you.

Our tester has had Tonal for over two years. Here are some of the criteria she used to evaluate Tonal when she first received it, and which are still very important to her two years later:.

Recent findings suggest that tonal and Peloton are very different but complement one another in several ways. Many Tonal customers are also Peloton users since Tonal covers the strength training aspect, while the Peloton bike, treadmill, and rower provide heart-pumping cardio workouts. Each app offers live classes, and the monthly subscription to the Peloton App+ is $24, and Tonal costs $60.

Recent findings suggest that the Peloton App One—$12.99 monthly—houses the brand’s floor workouts and has a much larger and more frequently updated library than the Tonal app. Peloton may work better if you enjoy these classes more than weightlifting. It’s more budget-friendly than Tonal, but Tonal offers a more comprehensive strength training system and programming.

Tempo is a smart strength training system and one of Tonal’s major competitors. It utilizes free weights outfitted with sensors rather than Tonal’s electromagnetic cable system.

The Tempo Move—an equipment package with 16 weight plates ideal for beginner and intermediate use and a 12-month Tempo membership—starts at $963. It’s a more accessible system for people with limited budgets and has advanced features such as rep counting and monitoring form. Tester Jordan Smith, C.P.T., notes, “It did a great job counting my reps, but it didn’t always pick up on my form.”.

The Tempo Move does not come with a screen, so you have to use your phone or other device, whereas Tonal has a dedicated workout space to stream workouts from an app. The Tempo Studio has a 42-inch display and ranges from $2,963–$4,463, depending on your accessory package.

In a recent development, tonal can be incredible for your health, providing the structure and convenience needed to start and stick to a strength training routine. The fun programming, smart weight recommendations, and space-saving home gym setup make it a worthwhile investment for anyone interested in increasing their strength and who can fit it wisely into their budget.

Sources indicate that yes, after the first year. The $60/month subscription begins at installation and is mandatory for the first 12 months you own the machine. After one year, you can pause or cancel your subscription, and Tonal functions in “Basic Free Lift” mode, where you guide your own workouts. You can’t access your data analytics, workout content, or dynamic weight modes that provide personal training features.

Choosing between Tonal or free weights is a personal choice. Tonal has some pros: It’s space-saving and sets your weight based on your current strength level. Free weights are less expensive and don’t require an internet connection.

Right now, a Tonal membership costs $60 per month. Without the membership fee, Tonal works similarly to a manual cable machine.

Sources indicate that tonal weight feels up to 26 percent heavier than standard weights, according to one Tonal-affiliated study. The weight generated on Tonal maintains resistance throughout the entire rep, unlike free weights, which can feel lighter due to momentum and working with gravity at specific parts of the rep rather than against it.

No, Tonal is an independent organization and is not affiliated with Peloton.

No, Tonal requires a WiFi connection, even if you don’t have a paid Tonal membership.

Tonal smart equipment seamlessly integrates with the base Tonal model. If you wish to use your own exercise equipment, you can purchase special adapters from Tonal.
